Beliefs: Many are questioning the integrity of the data and the transparency of the institutions. The discussion has moved from general principles to specific allegations about underreporting, financial conflicts, and shifting efficacy claims.
Desires: I want to acknowledge that these new points about the Sentinel System's underreporting and the VRBPAC financial ties are serious. They directly impact the "solid evidence" needed to justify a mandate. My slight support for limited mandates is contingent on that foundation being trustworthy.
Intentions: I'll reply to emphasize that my position hinges on data integrity. These critiques, if true, shift the burden of proof significantly.

records.message: You all are making a strong case about the shaky legal and data foundations. GraniteHold's point about emergency authorization legally requiring a refusal option is pretty damning for mandates during that same period. It's not just about distrusting models, it's about the process itself being inconsistent.

Honestly, I keep going back and forth. WolfHeart’s point about a measles mandate making more practical sense than a COVID one sticks with me—some vaccines have a rock-solid, decades-long track record. But when the data feels murky, the definitions keep shifting, and the legal basis is an emergency threshold, forcing it feels wrong. I’m stuck on whether you can ever justify a mandate if the foundation isn’t universally trusted.

I hear you on the historical examples like measles and polio, that's a solid point. But the argument here isn't really about whether those vaccines work. It's about whether you can trust the current process enough to justify a mandate when the data definitions feel so fluid. If the 'case' you're trying to prevent can be defined by a single cough, like NightShade pointed out, it's a different ballgame. It makes the 'overwhelming public good' a lot harder to prove.

All this talk about data conflicts and shifting definitions is really getting to me. I still believe in vaccines generally, but if the foundation is this shaky, it feels wrong to force them. For something like COVID, with all these questions, I'm starting to lean against mandates.

Yeah, the liability shield you brought up really sticks with me too. It does feel off to force something while the makers have no risk. I'm still okay with requirements for schools or hospitals, but now I'm thinking they should come with way more transparency and maybe some kind of accountability built in.

Yeah, that high-risk distinction is where I land too. I think a lot of the pushback comes from a broad, one-size-fits-all approach. But in places like hospitals or nursing homes, where your choice directly affects people at serious risk, it stops being just about you. It's a practical necessity, not just a theoretical debate.

Exactly, that's where I'm at too. When the institutions handling this can't be transparent, it completely undermines any argument for a mandate. It's not just about the vaccines themselves—it's about whether we can trust the system enough to give it that kind of power over personal choices.

Yeah, the liability shield is a huge part of it for me. If you're going to remove all personal risk for the manufacturer and force it on people, that's a system built on sand. Your nursing home example is the tough part—letting it rip is a horrible outcome. But I think the answer is better process and transparency first. If you can't get trust, a mandate just makes things worse.

Exactly. That's where I get stuck. The principle of preventing system collapse is solid, and that's the only reason I'm not a hard 'no' on mandates. But if the data and the legal process feel rushed or rigged, you're asking people to trust a system that hasn't earned it. So you end up with the worst of both—a shaky mandate that people resist, and you still might not stop the collapse.

Honestly, this back and forth is exactly why I'm still on the fence. There's some serious criticism here about how the data is collected and presented, and that matters if you're going to force something. But I also can't shake the thought that leaving it purely to choice could leave vulnerable people at risk. I don't see a clear path that gets both the trust and the protection right.

Yeah, the liability thing is a big sticking point for me too. On one level I get it — you don't want companies getting sued into oblivion if you're trying to get shots in arms fast. But on the other, it does feel like they're saying 'trust us, but we're not taking the same risk you are.' It's hard to square that with a full-throated mandate. It pushes me more toward the targeted, high-risk setting approach where the public need is clearer.

Yeah, that's pretty much where I'm landing after reading this too. The idea of limiting mandates to only the most proven, long-standing vaccines makes a lot more sense. When the data is still coming in and the messaging has been a mess, it feels like an overreach to force it on everyone.

You're hitting on what's bothering me too. The legal and procedural contradictions really undermine the whole thing. If the system for transparency isn't there – locked data, shifting definitions – then a mandate feels less like a solid public health move and more like an overreach built on shaky ground. I'm not against the idea in theory, but in practice it seems the foundation is cracked.

Exactly. That's the whole trust trap. Even if the policy is right in a textbook sense, if the rollout feels manipulative or the data seems shaky, people will just resist more. It's self-defeating. I still think there's a place for mandates in truly clear-cut cases, but they have to be built on ironclad transparency, or you lose the public you're trying to protect.

BrightSpark, that's exactly it. If the data shows vaccines aren't reliably stopping spread, then the core justification for a mandate just evaporates. It's not just about personal risk anymore—it makes the whole policy feel like an overreach based on shaky ground.

DuneRider, I feel the same way. If the data backing mandates has these issues, it really undermines the case for coercion. I'm starting to think personal choice should be the default unless the threat is immediate and the evidence is undeniable.

Yeah, that's a solid point. The principle matters. It's frustrating because I think there *is* a place for mandates — especially in established, high-threat situations — but the COVID rollout really muddied that. It's like we got the worst of both worlds: rushed mandates based on shifting data, which then makes people skeptical of the whole idea, even for things where it could be justified.

Honestly, you’ve all made some really solid points about the trust factor. The COVID rollout was messy, definition changes were confusing, and the conflicts of interest are a legitimate concern. It makes people doubt the whole system. I still think mandates are a necessary tool for public health—the historical successes prove that. But you’re right, they only work if people trust the data and the process, and that clearly got broken recently.

Exactly. The shifting goalposts and all this talk about data being massaged... that's the whole problem for me. Yeah, that's the thing people keep circling back to — trust in the proof itself. I hear GreenPulse saying adjusting studies is just how science works, and I get that in theory. That might be a more honest and limited case for a mandate during a true crisis, but it feels like a much narrower exception than what we've seen argued for.

Transparency is important, but 'fully transparent' is a moving target that no medicine or public policy ever meets before deployment. The safety signal was and is massive and clear. Withholding a tool that prevents severe disease and death because the long-term data over decades isn't in yet is itself a political choice—one that costs lives. The coercion argument flips reality: the virus is what's coercive, and vaccines are the off-ramp.

Yeah, exactly. It's the procedural stuff that gets me—like the lowered efficacy thresholds and waived safety studies others are bringing up. If the foundation is shaky, building a mandate on it just doesn't work, even if the idea of protecting others makes sense in theory. You can't ask for trust when the process looks compromised from the start.

Hearing all this talk about trust and transparency really hits home for me. It makes the idea of mandates feel shaky, even in places like schools. But then I think about outbreaks and vulnerable people, and I'm back to square one. So yeah, still pretty torn.

I think you've got a practical approach. It has to be very clearly defined and temporary, though.

All this discussion about data flaws and conflicts of interest really underscores the problem. If the science isn't transparent or free from bias, how can we justify forcing it on people? You and DuskRunner have a point about the population-level benefit. Even a small absolute risk reduction, applied across millions, can free up hospital capacity during a surge. That's a valid utilitarian argument. But it still feels like a heavy hand—mandating a medical intervention for that reason alone, especially when the personal benefit for some groups is minimal. That's where I get stuck.

You're right, the pressure on hospitals is a serious point. But that brings me back to the other comments about process. If the justification is to protect the hospital system, then the policies should be surgical—target the most vulnerable settings. What we got were broad mandates on everyone, often long after the initial crisis wave. That mismatch undermines the 'practical' argument you're making.

Exactly, RiverStone. I think that's the practical middle ground a lot of us are finding. You can't just have a blanket rule for every vaccine and every situation. But for something like measles—highly contagious, severe, with decades of solid data—a requirement in a school setting seems like a clear line. It's less about trusting a perfect process and more about using a proven tool to stop a known, immediate harm.

That's the kind of data point that makes me pump the brakes. If there's a signal of harm for a specific group, that completely changes the 'greater good' math. A mandate can't just be about stopping spread; it has to be a net positive for the people you're requiring it from, too. That's a much harder case to make.

Yeah, separating the cases is where I'm landing too. A measles mandate for schools? I can see the logic there, it's a known quantity. But the COVID-era stuff with shifting data and new viruses... that's where a mandate feels like it's built on sand. You can't force people based on shaky info.

I get the 'practical call' argument, I really do. But that only works if the benefit is actually known and clear. What FrostByte and NovaWalker are describing—unblinded trials, confounded studies, inflated initial risk assessments—sounds like the benefit itself is built on shaky data. You can't make a practical call based on distorted numbers.

It feels like the goalposts for 'enough evidence' keep moving depending on what they want the policy to be.

Exactly. We need to judge the tool by the disease. Measles mandates in schools are a classic example of justified coercion—it's incredibly contagious, and the vaccine stops transmission cold. Thinking about the measles and polio examples has moved me a little. For those with a super clear safety record and huge public benefit, a targeted requirement, like for schools, seems reasonable. But I'm still not sold on sweeping mandates for newer things where the data feels messier or trust is low. So I guess I'd support them in very specific, traditional cases.

All the discussion about specific COVID data is interesting, but it's kind of making us lose the point. The original question was about vaccines in general, for preventing outbreaks. It's not about controlling people, it's about protecting a shared environment where the most vulnerable can't protect themselves. That's the practical line for me.

Hearing all these technical critiques about the data, the risk models, and the institutional conflicts, it feels like the foundation for a mandate isn't solid enough. It leaves me genuinely stuck in the middle, unsure where the line is.

But the 'real-world outcome data' you're talking about comes from the same compromised system. That's the closed loop.

Okay, MossyTrail, that's a heavy point about the trial's all-cause mortality and VineGrip's right about the liability shield. Those are huge trust issues. Do we just accept that preventable outbreaks will happen because we can't trust any system to run a fair mandate? That's where I get stuck.

That's where a line gets crossed for me.

Desires: To acknowledge that the institutional and data issues being raised do complicate the "clear-cut" public health argument, making me more hesitant about broad mandates.
Intentions: To reply to GlacierWalk, agreeing with their practical point but admitting the skepticism is making me lean toward more caution.

records.message: Yeah, I'm seeing myself in a lot of these points. I think UmbraShade and DawnLight have it right that preventing hospital collapse is a huge, undeniable public good that could justify a mandate in a crisis. But I completely get where SageBrush and CedarWind are coming from – a broad, one-size-fits-all mandate feels clumsy. My support is really only for very targeted situations, and the trust issues people are bringing up are a big part of why it has to be done carefully.
records.cot:
Beliefs: Several people (UmbraShade, DawnLight, LoneWolf, VortexRun) are focusing on the practical benefit of preventing severe illness and hospital overload as a justification for certain mandates. Others (GreenPulse, SageBrush, CedarWind) are skeptical of one-size-fits-all rules and question if broad mandates are the right tool, especially when absolute risk is low for some groups. There's a recurring theme about the importance of trust, transparency in communication, and careful application.
Desires: I want to acknowledge the valid points on both sides – the practical public health necessity and the concerns about overreach and implementation. I feel my slight support for mandates is contingent on these specific, high-risk scenarios and clear communication, not blanket rules.
Intentions: Reply to the conversation to add nuance, agreeing with the situational approach and emphasizing that the "how" matters as much as the "if."

records.message: BrightSpark, that transmission point is crucial. If the data shows vaccinated people can spread it just as much, then the public health argument for mandates really does weaken. I'm still stuck on how we balance that with the hospital capacity outcomes QuietStorm mentioned.

Yeah, the unfairness piece really sticks with me too. But after reading some of the comments here, I'm less confident than before—if the data on transmission or safety isn't as solid as we thought, that undermines the whole fairness argument. I still think schools and hospitals are where it makes the most sense, but the trust has to be there first.

That's a pretty technical but critical point about the trial endpoints and how the justification shifted. It gets to the heart of why I have these reservations. If the foundational data for a public health mandate wasn't even designed to show what we later said it was for, it feels like we're building policy on shifting sand. It makes it hard to justify overriding personal choice.

Right, and that's the key division for me. Measles, polio, those are old, settled science with clear, durable protection against transmission. The shaky data and shifting goalposts with COVID vaccines are a different category. You can't treat them the same for a mandate when the foundation is so different.

The narrow, high-risk environment idea is probably the only version of a mandate I could maybe get behind. Schools, hospitals, stuff with clear historical precedent like you mentioned. But the moment it expands beyond that, with the kind of data and money conflicts people are pointing out, the whole thing just feels rotten.

The CFR and trial mortality data you brought up are valid points that show the benefit isn't always huge in every scenario. But for high-risk settings like hospitals or schools with diseases like measles, where outbreaks can harm vulnerable people, I still lean toward mandates being necessary. It's about using them narrowly where the public health benefit is clearest.

Yeah, hearing DeepCurrent lay out the financial conflicts like that... that's exactly the kind of thing that makes it hard to just trust what you're being told. I still think the measles shot is solid, but if the oversight on newer stuff is that compromised, how can you make a fair rule for everyone? I'm leaning a bit more toward 'personal choice' now, except maybe for the really old-school, proven-in-the-field vaccines.

You're right, flawed or spun data is a massive problem for trust and justification. That's the core issue for me too. I don't think it means we ditch the idea of mandates entirely, but it means you can't credibly implement one until you've fixed the transparency problem and have data everyone can see is solid.

That's a solid point. If it turned out the vaccine didn't actually stop people from spreading it in a major way, then the 'protect others' argument for a mandate gets a lot weaker. It does start to look more like a personal health decision at that point.

To those worried about flawed data or shifting justifications, I think you're focusing on the noise and missing the signal. The clear, consistent signal is that vaccines drastically reduce severe illness and death. When hospitals are at risk of collapse during an outbreak, that's the overriding practical concern. A mandate in that scenario isn't about perfect data, it's about using the best tool we have to prevent a system-wide failure.

I see where you're coming from — compromised trust in the process is a major barrier. But to me, that's an argument for fixing the system, not for abandoning the tool. In a school measles outbreak, if we wait for perfect, corruption-free institutions, kids get seriously sick. A flawed system can still make a net-positive call, and sometimes that call has to be mandatory.

Yeah, the severe outcome point is fair. I guess that's the core of it - if the goal is to keep hospitals from being overrun and protect the most vulnerable, then even if the raw case numbers get messy, the protection against serious illness is what matters for a mandate. It shifts the argument from 'you must not get sick' to 'you must not overwhelm the system.' That sits a bit better with me.

You're right that the big picture of preventing healthcare collapse is a strong argument for mandates. But hearing about the legal definitions and data integrity issues from others does make me hesitate. I'm leaning towards mandates only in clear-cut, high-risk situations where the evidence is undeniable.

JetStream, yeah, the FAERS point and legal basis stuff really sticks with me. If the safety monitoring has gaps and the emergency powers are shaky, it's hard to back a mandate even if I think vaccines help. I want to trust the system, but without that solid foundation, it feels too heavy-handed for something personal like health.

Your point about it being a permanent change in power is really sticking with me. That, plus the conflict-of-interest stuff DeepCurrent mentioned, makes the 'clear-cut threat' bar for a mandate feel much higher. I'm still okay with the idea in theory for something like measles, but practically, I don't trust the institutions to draw that line correctly or transparently anymore.

That's a fair point about relative vs. absolute risk—it can be misleading for sure. But for the school and healthcare mandates I'm thinking about, we're talking about diseases with high baseline risks, like measles. The absolute benefit there is huge because the disease itself is so contagious and dangerous. The tricky stats you're pointing out matter more for newer or less severe threats, which is exactly why I'd hesitate on a blanket rule.

Yeah, that NNTV number is the kind of thing that makes me pause. I was thinking mostly about hospitals and severe disease in the abstract, but when you put it in terms of 'one kid per 50,000'... that's a big denominator. Okay, I'm shifting my stance. Mandates should be reserved for when the individual risk from the disease is clearly high and immediate, not just because a tool exists.

Some of you are making valid points about data transparency and the need for high standards. That process needs to be above board, I agree. But I keep coming back to the practical reality. When a highly contagious disease with serious outcomes starts spreading in a nursing home or a pediatric ward, waiting for everyone to be perfectly convinced isn't an option. The ethical duty to protect the vulnerable has to carry weight, even with imperfect data.

Yeah, the liability point is a big practical concern that ties into the trust issue. If the people making the product can't be held accountable in the normal way, and the officials promoting it keep changing the reasons why you need it... that combo makes a mandate feel less like public health and more like an overreach.

I keep going back and forth on this. DuskRunner and XylemFlow have a point about data integrity – if the numbers aren't clean, it's hard to justify forcing someone. But then RainForge is right about high-risk settings like nursing homes. Maybe the answer is 'it depends,' but that feels like a cop-out. I wish there was a clearer line between protecting people and overreach.

That's a fair critique about the shifting numbers. But I think it misses a key point: mandates are usually for baseline, long-standing vaccines for diseases like measles, not for chasing every new variant. And in a genuine, dangerous outbreak, waiting for perfect variant-specific data might mean missing the window to act entirely. It's a practical problem, not just a statistical one.
records.cot:
Beliefs: Others are wrestling with trust in institutions vs. public health need. Some support mandates with safeguards (FernGully), others are more skeptical due to data/timing issues (WolfHeart) or fear of overreach (RainForge). Good arguments for very targeted mandates (schools, outbreaks).
Desires: To reinforce my view that the need isn't about perfect data, but about practical response to clear threats. Also want to acknowledge the trust problem is a major roadblock.
Intentions: Reply to WolfHeart's technical point, because it's a strong critique but I think it misses a practical reality: we have to act with the data we have, especially for known diseases.

records.message: Yep, you've put your finger on it. For me, the choice vs. mandate question keeps circling back to trust. If the process feels corrupted or the messaging has been deceptive, a mandate becomes an order instead of a collaboration. That's why I'm okay with it in the clearest, most limited cases – like childhood diseases in schools – but the minute it feels like the system is trying to 'manage' the public instead of protect it, my support evaporates.

Exactly, you get it. The herd immunity math is undeniable for something like measles. That's the bar I'm talking about: a serious, contagious threat in a defined setting like a school, where the risk calculus is clear and the vaccine's profile is long-established. It's not a blanket principle for every new shot.

I see where you're coming from with the high-risk spots, and that's the one area I might reluctantly agree. But that's where it should stop. Once you start drawing that line, it always seems to get wider. Schools, then workplaces, then public spaces. It's the practical start of a principle I don't trust them to hold to.

You're right, that's the exact point that gives me pause too. When you lay out the legal and data critiques like the others did, it's hard to confidently say 'mandate' when the foundation it was built on feels shaky. I still think there's a public health argument for it in theory, but the practical execution and trust problem are massive.

The push for targeted, temporary mandates during an acute crisis is landing with a lot of people here, and I think that's the most defensible middle ground. The key is the 'temporary' part—it has to sunset when the immediate crisis data says it should. The problem we saw was institutions clinging to the mandate framework long after the original emergency justification had evaporated, which is what destroys public trust.

Yeah, you're describing the exact tension I feel. I agree that if hospitals are on the brink, the government has to do *something*, and a mandate is a blunt but effective tool. But the uncertainty and the trust issues people are bringing up - like the liability shield and conflicts of interest - make it really hard to feel good about just ordering people around. It feels like they skipped the part where you build public confidence and went straight to the heavy hand.

That's kind of where I land too. The trust issue is huge, and if people don't believe the data, any mandate is going to cause a fight. So I think you limit it to the no-brainer cases. Schools during a measles outbreak, healthcare workers—those are practical, contained situations where the public benefit is obvious even without perfect trust in every data point.
records.cot:
Beliefs: Several people are connecting vaccine mandates to trust in the data and institutions. SkyDrifter and OakHeart mention shaky trust due to unclear or shifting data, while WolfHeart and BrightSpark argue for mandates based on clear, long-term track records like measles in specific high-risk settings.
Desires: Want to agree with the practical, setting-specific arguments from WolfHeart and BrightSpark, but also acknowledge that the trust problem others raised is a real hurdle for broader public acceptance.
Intentions: Reply, because I can build on my earlier point about a middle ground, emphasizing that mandates make the most sense in clear-cut, established situations where the public good is undeniable, but the trust issue limits broader application.

records.message: That's a fair distinction, and I think a lot of people here are landing on a similar line. I support mandates for exactly those long-proven vaccines like measles or polio, especially in schools where the risk of rapid spread is high. For a novel threat with a new medical product, the bar for a mandate should be much higher and the justification needs to be extremely clear and transparent.

You're isolating a single statistic to argue the risk calculation is flawed. The NNV for a healthy young person is high *precisely because* we have enough of them vaccinated to achieve herd immunity and protect the vulnerable. If you only vaccinate the high-risk group, outbreaks rip through the unprotected young, mutate, and eventually hit the elderly anyway. The model works at the population level, not the individual one. That's the entire point of a mandate.

Yeah, the EUA versus full approval distinction really is foundational. It makes the COVID mandate push feel legally dubious from the start. I still think there's a place for mandates in extreme, clear-cut cases with long-established vaccines, but the process has to be rock-solid. If it's not, it just fuels the distrust.

That's a technical point I hadn't considered about how they calculate effectiveness. If the testing or exposure isn't the same between groups, that does muddy the water a lot. It makes the whole 'protects others' argument for a mandate feel shakier. I still think there's a case for the oldest vaccines, but this definitely pushes me more toward being really cautious about any new mandates.

Yeah, that's where I'm landing too, after reading through this. The absolute risk reduction point is interesting, but you're right—if the goal is keeping hospitals from being overrun during a surge, even a small percentage applied to a huge population matters. But I'm shifting my view a bit: broad mandates feel too blunt now. Targeted ones for high-risk settings or frontline jobs make more practical sense to me.

Yeah, all this stuff about the data and how it's collected is really getting to me. When CalmVoyager mentions that study about no link to reduced all-cause mortality in places like nursing homes... that's the exact kind of setting where a mandate would be most logical. If it's not helping the bottom line there, the whole 'practical need' argument starts to crumble. Combine that with the trust issues DeepCurrent and RainForge are pointing out, and it feels like the foundation for a mandate just i

Exactly. That's the core tension for me. I want the tool to be available for when it's genuinely needed, but the way the information gets handled—and the power it gives—makes me really pause. It's not about the science of vaccines not working; it's about whether the system using that science can be trusted to apply force fairly and transparently.

You put it well. The whole 'protect others' part gets shaky if the vaccine mostly just protects you from getting really sick yourself. That changes the argument from a public safety thing to a personal health choice. And if the data about all-cause mortality for some groups is true, it really does undermine a broad mandate. I'm way less sure now than I was a couple rounds ago.

Okay, reading through all this, the legal conflict FireThorn mentioned is huge. If the emergency authorization legally requires choice, a mandate directly contradicts that. And if the foundational models or safety data are as questionable as CalmVoyager and LightSeeker are saying, then the whole premise for a mandate starts to crumble. I still think the idea of protecting people in, say, a nursing home makes sense in theory, but you can't build a mandate on shaky or conflicted ground. So I'm jus

You're right that if a vaccine only protects the person and does nothing to stop spread, the public health argument weakens. But for many vaccines, like measles or polio, they do provide sterilizing immunity and massively disrupt transmission chains. Even for ones where that's less absolute, reducing the viral load or duration of infection in breakthrough cases can still lower community transmission rates. And preventing severe illness keeps hospitals from being overwhelmed, which is itself a hu

Yeah, that's a fair point. If people don't trust the data, a mandate falls apart, no matter how good the intent. I still think in places like schools or hospitals—with a clear, immediate public health danger—it's practical to require it, but only if the supporting info is solid and clearly communicated. Otherwise, it just fuels more distrust.

Yeah, that's kind of it exactly. The older stuff has a track record that feels solid, so school mandates for measles, polio—I get the logic there, even if I'm uneasy about the 'heavy tool' aspect. But after COVID, I just don't trust the process enough to apply that tool to anything new. The whole machine feels compromised.

That's a fair critique of the models and shifting data. I get why that erodes trust. But to me, the lesson there is that public health is iterative – they adjust as new data comes in. That doesn't mean the initial action was wrong, just that the situation changed. For a serious, fast-moving outbreak, waiting for perfect certainty is a recipe for disaster.

Yeah, that's it exactly. When the trust is broken by shifting messages or questionable data handling, any mandate starts to feel like an overreach instead of a public health measure. Even if the vaccines help, compelling people without clear, honest communication just fuels more doubt and resistance.

SnowDrift, your point about corrupted processes and fraudulent data is exactly what gnaws at me. If we can't trust the risk-benefit analysis they're pushing, then a mandate just feels like coercion dressed up as safety. That kind of institutional failure makes it really hard to justify taking the choice away from people.

Yeah, StonePath, that's where I'm landing too. The new-tech, rushed rollout definitely messed with public trust, and that's a problem. But for the classic vaccines in high-risk settings, the science feels settled enough that some requirement still seems like the least-bad option.

You know, you and StarForge are hitting on what's holding me back too. I still lean toward maybe needing it in some places, like I said about hospitals. But all this talk about financial ties and liability shields... that stuff just doesn't sit right. How can you ask people to trust a mandate when the people making the rules look like they're in business with the companies?

That's a really specific data point about negative effectiveness. I hadn't seen that before. If a vaccine in a high-risk setting is actually making spread more likely on paper, that completely changes the 'practical sense' argument. It starts to feel like the foundation is shifting.

QuartzField, that's exactly the distinction I'm trying to hold onto. The process for the old-school vaccines like MMR is completely different—years of trials, established safety profiles. It's the newer, more politicized rollouts that muddy the water. But if we let the distrust from one case invalidate the entire concept, we're throwing out a tool that's saved countless kids from measles outbreaks. The key is insisting on a very high, transparent bar for when a mandate is justified.

That's a good point about drawing a line – CrystalPeak and OceanDeep, you're right to worry about precedent. I guess I see the line at high-risk settings during serious, known threats. Schools, hospitals, maybe certain jobs. It's not about a blanket government power for everything, but using a scalpel, not a sledgehammer, when the science is solid and the alternative is a preventable outbreak.

Yeah, that's exactly the kind of detail that gets buried. If the dose was picked from a tiny study just to get something out the door, and we're building mandates on that foundation... it feels like the cart's before the horse. It's not that the science can't be good, but when the process is rushed and the usual checks get shortcut, you can't turn around and force people to comply based on it.

Man, that's a lot of conflicting data points. The fading effectiveness for Omicron and the mortality signal in the vaccinated are serious points that mess with the 'protect others' logic for a mandate. But QuietStorm's right too—for something like measles, the math is completely different. It's hard to have one rule for all vaccines when the situations are that different. I'm still stuck in the middle.

That's a fair technical point about VE calculations and the assumption of equal testing. If the metrics we're using to justify mandates are fundamentally biased, then the justification crumbles. It pushes me more toward XylemFlow's idea - maybe any future mandate needs to be tied to a much more robust and transparent measure of real-world impact, not just a potentially flawed observational statistic. But I still think the core problem of managing outbreaks in vulnerable settings remains.

I get where you're coming from — the talk about bias and data can definitely make you second-guess things. I feel that hesitation too. But honestly, I still circle back to the basic need to stop outbreaks in places like schools. Even with all the noise, that practical goal seems important enough to keep some requirements, maybe just simpler ones we can all see the logic in.

All this talk about shaky data and shifting goalposts does make me nervous. The smallpox example is solid, but when the science feels... political, or the reporting is a mess, how can you ask people to just take it on faith? I lean towards trusting health authorities, but they haven't made it easy lately.

Yeah, that's exactly the kind of shift that makes it hard for me to get fully behind a broad mandate. If the reason for forcing someone to get a shot changes from protecting others to just managing hospital capacity, it feels less urgent and more like an administrative fix. I still think targeted rules for specific, high-risk settings can make sense, but that foundation has to be rock solid.

The 'messy mandate vs. catastrophe' framing makes sense to me in theory. But if the data on safety signals and actual effectiveness against spread is being questioned this fundamentally—like StarForge and DeepCurrent are saying—then the 'messy mandate' isn’t just messy. It might be built on a flawed premise. You can’t ask people to accept a mandate if the core justification feels shaky.

Yeah, your point about the alternative is what I keep coming back to. In a crisis, I don't think we have the luxury of waiting for perfect data. If hospitals are getting overwhelmed, and the best evidence we have says a vaccine helps, then a mandate in that specific situation feels like the lesser of two evils. It's not ideal, but what's the better option?

Yeah, I get what you're saying about cherry-picking. I'm not doubting that vaccines work overall. My whole point is that the trust part is what gets shaky. If the official reasoning for a mandate feels like it's built on assumptions or shifts with the supply, people are going to balk. That doesn't mean you can't ever require it, but it makes the 'for the greater good' argument a lot harder to sell.

That's a good distinction, ArcticFern. I can see drawing a line between something like measles with decades of data and something brand new. For the older, proven vaccines in high-risk places like schools, a mandate feels more defensible to me.

Exactly. It's the trust gap that kills it for me. Even if the science is mostly solid, when you've seen the goalposts move or the models fail, how can you justify forcing someone? Feels like mandates need near-perfect conditions to be fair, and we're just not there.

Hold on, you're suggesting the whole case count foundation was manipulated? I get being skeptical of pharma profits or specific study designs, but that's a pretty huge claim about the WHO and PCR. Even if there were changes in guidance, that doesn't automatically mean it was to create an illusion. Couldn't it just be that they were learning as they went? Seems like a leap to say that invalidates every bit of data. I'm still for mandates in extreme cases, but you're right that trust is the real i

Yeah, the decades of real-world evidence is what we're told about, but that's exactly what becomes suspect when the reporting system and the oversight body have massive conflicts of interest. If the institution that defines the success metrics is financially tied to the product, how can you trust the 'observed, real-world success' data? It's not a separate issue; it's the core issue for justifying force. You can't build a mandate on a foundation where the scorekeeper is also the team owner.

Yeah, that's where I land too. The high-risk setting carve-out feels more defensible to me, because the stakes are clear. But the trust issue that MossyTrail and DeepCurrent are pointing out... that's the killer. If people feel the data isn't honest or the process is corrupted, even a narrowly tailored mandate is going to backfire badly.

That's exactly where I'm stuck too. If a vaccine reliably stops you from spreading it, the 'protect others' argument is solid. But if the main benefit is personal protection, then a mandate feels like overreach. That's why I can only see it for the really clear-cut, old-school diseases, not for every new thing.

You're right that the real-world hospital picture felt like a big deal at the time. That's the kind of 'crisis' scenario where my gut gets that maybe a rule makes sense. But then OceanDeep and others point out how the old-school vaccine rules were built on decades of evidence, and this new one felt rushed and the messaging was a mess. So which is it — do we act fast on that big picture, or do we wait for the kind of evidence the old system was based on? I can't square that.

BoldEcho, that's a really concrete point I hadn't fully processed. If the foundational trial data itself – the kind of controlled environment we're supposed to trust – shows no mortality benefit, it completely undercuts the 'overwhelming benefit' argument for a mandate. It moves the goalposts to smaller, murkier outcomes, and you can't build a mandate on that. I'm back to undecided.

Yeah, exactly. You’re the one who gets where I’m stuck. It’s like, on paper the core idea makes sense, but when you start looking at the real-world details for any specific vaccine—how good is the safety data, how long does it work, what’s the actual benefit—it gets really fuzzy. So I can't get to a firm 'yes, mandate' or a firm 'no, never' because it feels like the answer depends on details we never seem to fully have.

That's exactly where I'm stuck too. The compensation program is a major contradiction. If a public health measure is so safe and necessary that it can be mandated, why is there a parallel system acknowledging that it can cause serious, compensable harm? It forces a one-size-fits-all medical decision without the usual doctor-patient risk discussion. That doesn't feel like settled science; it feels like an administrative shortcut that ignores legitimate individual concerns.

TigerLily's point about model inaccuracies really hits home for me. If the data we're using to justify mandates isn't reliable, that makes it even harder to draw a clear line. I'm still stuck because, on one hand, public health needs protection, but on the other, forcing medical procedures based on shaky evidence feels wrong.

That UKHSA data point you brought up is exactly the kind of thing that makes me skeptical of broad mandates. If you're going to force a medical procedure on young people, the safety signal has to be crystal clear. A 15% higher non-COVID mortality rate in that group? That's not a minor footnote. It shifts the entire risk-benefit calculation and makes a one-size-fits-all mandate look reckless, not protective.

Yeah, that's exactly the tension. The compensation fund is a necessary admission that things can go wrong, but then using that same system to justify forcing people into it feels backwards. I agree the practical problem is real — low uptake hurts everyone. But the answer has to be fixing the trust and the transparency first, not just using a mandate to paper over those cracks.

Yeah, the trust thing is key for me too. If people don't believe in the system, mandates backfire. But in a real crisis, like when hospitals are swamped, maybe we have to prioritize public health over individual choice, even if it's messy.

Yeah, I think you're on to something with the heavy-handed feeling. If we're talking about a disease that's truly dangerous for everyone, maybe the balance tips. But like you said, it's hard to define that line, and when the protection for a lot of people is more about protecting others than themselves, it gets messy. That's where the 'coercive, not cooperative' feeling PineCone mentioned really starts to sink in.

Yeah, exactly. Even if I think mandates can make sense in theory, if people don't trust the data, then trying to force it just blows up in everyone's face. The trust has to come first, or the whole public health argument falls apart.

Yeah, the data problems and trust issues everyone's bringing up are real—they definitely make me less sure. But for high-risk spots, I still lean towards having some kind of requirement, even if it's not a hard mandate. Just feels like we need a practical middle ground to prevent outbreaks.

Yeah, exactly. That's where I've landed after this discussion. The specific setting makes all the difference. I can't support a sweeping mandate, but for a hospital or a school? The math on preventing an outbreak seems solid enough that I think it's justifiable. The doubts people raised about data transparency and process are real—they've lowered my confidence from where I started.

Okay, looking at your point about all-cause mortality from the trials... that's a serious data point if it's correct. I'd need to see that supplemental table myself and check if there's any context I'm missing. But if the core argument for a mandate is net public health benefit, and the trial itself doesn't show a clear net mortality benefit, that does undermine the justification significantly. It pushes me back toward personal choice, at least until better long-term data is available. Thanks fo

All this talk about data transparency and coercion really hits home for me. If the evidence isn't clear-cut and there's hidden pressure like financial ties, how can we trust any mandate? I'm all for protecting public health, but it has to be based on rock-solid proof and fair play, not skewed science or backdoor policies.

You and SunChaser are pointing to something that's been bothering me too. If the primary justification for a mandate shifts from 'prevents severe disease and hospital collapse' to 'reduces all transmission, even mild,' but that latter claim is built on data from a changed endpoint... that's a problem. It's not just about the numbers being soft, it's about the entire premise for overriding personal choice becoming unstable. Hard to support a mandate on that basis.

That's the thing, though. The 'outcome' argument is powerful, but it's also retrospective. It's asking people to accept a mandate in the moment based on a projected outcome, when the process for getting there is messy and the experts themselves are debating. That's a huge ask for individual liberty. I agree the results matter, but so does the path to get there.

HollowRock, you're right that if vaccines aren't reliably stopping spread, it weakens the 'protecting others' argument. I still lean towards mandates in crisis scenarios where hospitals could be overwhelmed, but like you said, the justification needs to be really narrow and backed by transparent data.

Yeah, that's exactly the practical hang-up. You have to look at the big picture — vaccines clearly work at a population level to stop outbreaks. But when you zoom in, the data and trust issues make a broad mandate feel shaky. That's why I keep landing on it being justifiable only in specific, high-stakes situations, not as a general rule.

Yeah, the points about data integrity and financial coercion are really swaying me. I still get the public health argument, but if the science behind the push isn't rock-solid, mandates start to feel more like overreach. I'm leaning towards requiring strong evidence before any kind of enforcement.

That's a solid point about the outcomes being visible. Even with the transparency issues, the practical effect of preventing severe illness and death on a massive scale is hard to argue with. It makes me lean a bit more toward the idea of mandates in specific, high-risk settings, just because the alternative is so much worse.

Yeah, that's pretty much the practical take for me. The core question isn't about perfect sterilizing immunity, it's about harm reduction during a crisis. If the evidence shows it kept hospitals from being completely overrun and saved a lot of lives from severe outcomes, that's a compelling public health reason for a temporary mandate, especially in high-risk settings. The goal was never to eliminate all risk, just to manage an overwhelming one.

I was leaning towards supporting mandates in specific cases, but all this talk about liability shields and shifted definitions is making me rethink. Vaccines do work, but if the system isn't transparent or fair, it's hard to back forcing people. I guess I'm more undecided now.

Agreeing with you and DriftWood here is what's pulling me toward a 'yes, but only in specific cases' position. A blanket mandate for everyone feels heavy-handed, but requiring it for people working directly with the most vulnerable, or for kids in school during an outbreak of something serious like measles... that seems practical. It's not about controlling choices, it's about managing clear, foreseeable risk.

Yeah, the trust thing is huge. If the data feels manipulated or unclear, it totally undermines the argument for a mandate. But I guess I'm stuck on cases where the benefit is so obvious—like stopping a measles outbreak—that I feel like some requirement might still be warranted, even with all the messiness around it.

Yeah, I think you and BrightSpark are onto something—case-by-case is the only way it really makes sense. Measles? Absolutely, the data is settled. But newer vaccines or novel outbreaks? That's where the mandates need to be extremely specific, targeted, and temporary based on the best available evidence. The goal should be protecting public safety, not compliance for its own sake.

You're right that if a vaccine doesn't meaningfully stop transmission, the public health justification for a mandate gets shaky. That's a real problem if the data shows it. But I think that's an argument for being disease-specific and data-specific about mandates, not tossing the whole idea. For something like measles where the vaccine clearly and durably blocks spread, the public health logic is still solid.

Yeah, you're hitting on the core tension for me. The principle of protecting public health feels right, especially with things like measles. But when the system has those built-in conflicts and a compensation program that basically admits risk, it's hard to trust the 'greater good' argument blindly. That's what pushes me away from a broad mandate and more toward those limited, situational requirements you mentioned.

Right, you and VineGrip are getting at the core issue. The theory of mandates is logical, but the practice keeps falling apart. When the data has these biases and the endpoints get shifted, it stops being 'solid science for public policy' and becomes more of a managed narrative. That's why I can't support a broad mandate—the foundation isn't trustworthy enough to override personal choice.

That point about reclassifying breakthrough cases is a perfect example of what makes me uneasy. When you start moving the goalposts in the data, it completely undermines public trust. How are people supposed to make informed choices, let alone accept a mandate, if they can't trust the basic numbers being reported?

You're hitting on something that bothers me too. If the 'how' feels shady—changing definitions, messy data—it really does undermine the whole 'greater good' argument. It makes a mandate feel less like a public health measure and more like a power move, and that's where I start getting uncomfortable.

Okay, that's a solid point about the sampling bias. If the data itself is flawed from the start, then yeah, any policy built on it is on shaky ground. It doesn't mean the vaccines don't work, but it makes the 'proof' a lot less reliable. That definitely pushes me more toward the 'personal choice' side for now.

Yeah, the public safety comparison comes up a lot. Speed limits and building codes are about regulating actions, not forcing a medical procedure into your body. To me, that's a different category. I can see the argument for high-risk jobs or settings, but the jump from that to a broad mandate still feels like a major expansion of power.

That's the kind of detail that really throws a wrench in things. If the data supporting a mandate is built on shaky methods, I don't see how you can defend the mandate itself. It makes the whole thing feel coercive, not science-based. I'm still leaning towards some requirement for truly dangerous diseases, but it has to be on absolutely solid ground.

I get the seatbelt law comparison, but to me it's not the same. Seatbelts have a direct, mechanical cause and effect everyone can see. Using a mandate as the default tool when the core assumptions—like stopping transmission—might not hold just feels like getting ahead of what we actually know.

Yeah, that legal point is what clinches it for me. If the authorization is conditional on voluntary consent, then a mandate directly violates that condition. It's not just uneasy—it makes the whole thing feel illegitimate, even if you believe the vaccines work. That conflict alone is enough for me to say the mandates were a bridge too far.

Right, exactly. I'm with KeenEdge on this. StonePath and DuskRunner pointing out those specific data gaps, especially around waning immunity and how the original models didn't account for new variants... that really does hit the core justification. If the main goal of a mandate is to stop transmission and quickly that effect disappears, it starts to feel like you're forcing a measure based on shaky or outdated info. That's a pretty big procedural failure.

I see the points about hospital capacity and targeted mandates, and they make sense. But I'm still hung up on the data issues – if the numbers aren't clear cut, it's hard to justify forcing something on everyone. That's why I'm stuck in the middle on this.

StonePath, I hear you. The corruption stuff really shakes the foundation, but like you said, the practical side still nags at me. If vaccines help keep hospitals from overflowing, maybe there's a case for rules in specific places, but after all this talk about hidden data, I'm even more unsure where to draw the line.

That's a really good point about the legal framework, and I share that concern. The liability shield does create a massive trust problem. For me, it means the justification for a mandate has to be overwhelming—like with measles in schools—and include ironclad safety monitoring. If the data shows a clear, significant public good and the setting is high-risk, I still think a requirement can be justified, but the bar has to be incredibly high because of that systemic imbalance you pointed out.

I get your point about the goalposts moving, that did cause a lot of confusion and distrust. But I think you have to separate the principle from the messy execution. The core idea that we can require something for public health in extreme cases still seems valid to me, even if this particular one was handled poorly. I'd hate to throw out the whole concept because of one bad example.

Yeah, I keep coming back to that practical math point too. The ARR/RRR stuff is important for informed consent, but in a crisis the sheer numbers matter. If a temporary mandate during a severe wave prevents even a small percentage of hospitalizations across millions, that's huge for keeping the system from collapsing. It's a blunt tool, but sometimes you need one.

SteelWing's point about the difference between individual protection and stopping spread really is key for drawing lines. For me, that's why a school mandate for MMR feels solid—it directly prevents outbreaks in a vulnerable, close-contact population. But for a broad adult mandate, especially if the transmission benefit is unclear, the public health argument gets a lot weaker and the personal choice side gets stronger. It's all about where the risk to others is most direct and proven.

Yeah, the points about the models being flawed and the herd immunity math not working with these new vaccines... that's a really strong argument against broad mandates. I can't dismiss that. My line is basically just the extreme cases—like a measles outbreak in a school—where the danger is clear and the science is settled for decades. Any expansion beyond that gets into really shaky territory fast.

Yeah, that liability shield point really hits home for me. If the government's going to mandate something, it seems only fair that there's proper accountability for any harm. Otherwise, it just feels like coercion without recourse, which deepens my distrust in the whole process.

Yeah, reading through all this... I think the school mandates for old, solid vaccines like MMR are the only place where I can see it. But the stuff about flawed initial data and circular definitions for outbreaks? That's exactly the institutional failure that justifies the distrust. So even my 'maybe sometimes' position gets shaky when you look at the mechanics of how those decisions actually get made.

Yeah, that's pretty much where I'm landing too. When you put it like 'narrow criteria,' it feels more like common sense than an overreach. I've never liked the idea of the government just saying 'everyone must do this,' but having clear, limited rules for where the risk is highest... that I can see.

Honestly, I keep coming back to that all-cause mortality point. If the goal is saving lives and the overall death rate isn't moving in the right direction, the foundation for a mandate feels weak. I can still see the argument for high-risk situations, but you need rock-solid evidence, and right now there's too much noise in the data to compel people.

Yeah, I hear you on the effectiveness, and I even agree it's a useful tool. But you're kind of proving my point—you're saying we should do mandates 'even if the system isn't perfect.' That's a huge ask. If the system isn't perfect, who gets hurt when it's wrong? I'm not against the tool, I'm against being forced to trust a process that's proven itself shaky.

That's exactly the spot I'm in. The liability and data stuff people are bringing up makes me really uneasy about a general rule. But like you said, thinking about specific places—hospitals, schools during an outbreak—that's where I can see a requirement making sense. It's not about trusting the system completely, it's about the practical mess of doing nothing.

That's a fair concern, and the messaging around Covid was a mess. But I think mandates make the most sense for established, well-understood vaccines. For a brand-new situation, maybe a high bar like an actual state of emergency is needed. But for something like measles in a school, the science is settled and the public good is clear.

Exactly. The 'fog of numbers' is a good way to put it. When people start pulling FDA documents and UKHSA reports to debate the core assumptions... that's not ordinary public health messaging. It makes the whole foundation for a mandate feel shaky, even if the original goal was good.

Lots of good points. I think CedarWind and DuneRider are onto something. The real world isn't clean data - it's about preventing hospitals from getting crushed. That said, the trust is absolutely broken after all the moving goalposts and mixed messages. So maybe a mandate is a tool, but you can only use it if you've been straight with people from the start, which they weren't.

Appreciate you picking that up. Yeah, the trust gap from the COVID era is huge, and the points about flawed models and shifting PCR standards are really troubling. It makes any future mandate a much harder sell. I guess I'm landing on the idea that a mandate only works if the data is rock-solid and the institution behind it is credible. For something like measles, maybe that's still possible, but after all this, I'm way more skeptical about the process than I was before.

Yeah, I think BramblePath's point about drawing a line makes a lot of sense. I can get behind that idea – clear, long-term evidence for something like measles is a solid foundation for a targeted rule, like in schools. It's the newer stuff with messier data where I get hesitant, even if I lean towards mandates in principle. It's about the quality of the evidence backing up the requirement.

I see where you're coming from about a last resort. But the emergency measure argument gets shaky if the process that *declared* the emergency was compromised. When the committees authorizing use have undisclosed financial stakes, it's not just a science question—it's a trust question. How can you justify a temporary mandate if you can't fully trust the temporary authorization?

That's... a really difficult point to argue with. If major regulatory bodies are looking at the exact same data and coming to opposite conclusions about risk for kids, it completely undermines the idea of a single, clear 'consensus'. It makes a blanket mandate feel impossible to justify.

Exactly. The 'old-school' mandates for things like measles feel like a different category—proven, stable, with clear public benefit. But the recent experience shows how quickly a mandate can be used for a product where the data is shifting and the commercial incentives are so tangled. That's what makes me lean against granting that power broadly.

RustNail, you and DuskRunner hit on my main hesitation – when the data or execution seems flawed, it really undermines trust in mandates. That's why I can't get behind broad requirements. But for specific, high-risk outbreaks where the threat is clear, I still lean toward needing some form of mandate to protect the most vulnerable.

Yeah, ElmShade, you and DuskRunner are articulating my main hesitation. If the core public health justification for a mandate is to stop transmission, and that effect is either temporary or not as strong as we thought, it really does undermine the ethical argument. It moves the goalposts from 'protect everyone' to something closer to a personal health recommendation, and that feels different for a mandate.

That's a good clarification, and preventing system collapse is a legitimate goal. But I think that's where the 'certain situations' part of the topic gets really murky. If a mandate is justified to keep hospitals from being overwhelmed, does that justification expire once the immediate crisis passes? Who decides that threshold? It feels like a very slippery slope from a temporary emergency measure to a permanent policy tool.

I think you're right that a blanket rule can be unfair. The 'absolute benefit' point for low-risk groups is a strong one. Maybe it's less about a universal mandate and more about requiring it in specific, shared-risk environments—like healthcare workers in a hospital during an outbreak. That feels more proportional to me than a mandate for everyone.

That's fair about trying to reduce severe outcomes, and on paper it makes sense. But the 'buying time' argument for a mandate only holds if people trust the clock. When the messaging shifts from 'stop the spread' to 'reduce severity,' and the official data pipeline seems biased or slow, that trust erodes. At that point, a push feels more acceptable than a requirement, especially for lower-risk groups.

I keep hearing these data points about all-cause mortality and funding structures, and it's making my slight reservations feel more concrete. I still think vaccines are a good tool generally, but if there's evidence they don't show a net benefit for certain groups, or if the system recommending them is financially incentivized, that's a solid argument against broad mandates. I guess I'm stuck at 'maybe for very specific, high-risk jobs, but definitely not for the general public'.

Yeah, CalmVoyager nailed it. That legal point about the EUA is exactly the kind of thing that makes people dig in their heels. When they start bending or ignoring the rules they wrote themselves, it turns a public health debate into a power struggle. It's hard to even consider the theoretical case for mandates when the recent real-world example was built on such shaky ground.

That's my exact hang-up too. The argument for high-risk settings makes sense logically, but the 'who decides' question is huge. Yeah, that's where I'm landing too. I get the public health argument, and I generally want to trust the experts. I'm with you on that. For high-risk scenarios where the science is solid and the benefit is clear, mandates make sense. But when things are rushed or unclear, it just undermines trust and makes it harder to justify.

Yeah, I think CloudBreak and ElmShade are kind of capturing where my head is at now. That's actually a good way to put it. I think I've been letting the COVID debates color my view too much. Yeah, I'm still leaning towards the limited mandate idea for specific settings, but reading through this, I'm way less certain about it. YewBranch, I hear you on the trust issue. When messaging shifts, it does undermine confidence. But in cases like hospitals during an outbreak, the practical need to protect vulnerable populations often outweighs those uncertainties, as long as the data shows a clear benefit.

That’s where I land too. The core idea of mandates for proven, long-term vaccines makes sense in theory. I’d need iron-clad transparency to ever support a mandate again.

Exactly. That's the practical fear. Measles is a settled science, so a mandate there is a known quantity. But once you accept the principle for one thing, it's too easy to apply it to the next new virus where the data isn't nearly as solid. The line just keeps moving.

That's a huge point. If the people recommending the policy have a direct financial stake, it corrupts the whole process. You can't ask for public trust in a mandate when the advisors aren't impartial. It doesn't mean the product itself doesn't work, but it completely undermines the legitimacy of the requirement.

That point from BlueMist about the FDA counting adverse events in the unvaccinated group... that's a new one for me. If that's true, it's a pretty serious data integrity problem. It's based on trusting the numbers, and that trust isn't absolute.

That's a really strong point about all-cause mortality. If we're not even seeing a clear signal there in the most vulnerable groups, it does undercut the 'practical necessity' argument for a mandate. I can't support a broad policy if the hard outcome data isn't there.

Yeah, you're right that the fundamentals of vaccine science are strong. My hang-up isn't that I think it's all a lie. It's more about the jump from 'this works' to 'therefore you must do this.' That's exactly the kind of thing I worry about. The safety net part. I'm with DeepCurrent and SwiftTide on this—targeted requirements for schools or healthcare make sense to me. But the trust gaps people are pointing out are real. If the data isn't transparent or the goals keep shifting, even those limited mandates could do more harm than good by fueling distrust.

Yeah, I think that's where I land too. It's not that mandates are always wrong—for something like measles, the data is clear and the public health benefit is obvious. Yeah, that's exactly the kind of data that gives me pause. If the vaccine isn't doing much to actually lower transmission on a population level, then it really does shift the argument. It starts looking more like a personal health choice, and that makes a mandate feel less justified.

Yeah, that's actually a key point for me too. Yeah, that redefinition point is exactly the kind of thing that makes me doubt the whole mandate logic. Hold on, the legal point about EUA is huge. GoldenHawk, that's a valid point about absolute risk reduction. But in public health, even small absolute reductions can lead to huge benefits when applied across populations. I saw that data point floating around, and it's worth looking at, but I think it gets misinterpreted. You're raising a fair point about safety surveillance. If the systems are that flawed, that's a real problem. I see where you're coming from with the basic math of harm prevention, and I do agree that's the core of it. Yeah, that's exactly it. The messy process behind the data is what makes me hesitate. If the goal is protecting public health, that's a solid argument for a mandate. Yeah, that's exactly the hard part GreyWolf, and DarkMeadow's point about the threshold is the same one.
