But when you see how the mechanisms get corrupted for newer vaccines, like SunChaser pointed out with the committee process, it makes you question the whole framework. If a mandate is built on shaky or manipulated data, the principle's dead on arrival, even for a 'high-risk setting'.

It seems like a few of us are landing in a similar zone - mandates might be justifiable, but only for those extreme, clear-cut cases like measles in schools. ThunderPeak's point about needing a long track record of settled science really resonates. That feels like a solid boundary to me; if the science is decades-old and the danger is immediate and severe, then a mandate might be the lesser evil. But for anything newer or murkier, the distrust and potential for overreach are just too high.

That's a tough one. I do think those financial ties are a serious problem for trust—it's really hard to ignore. But I also feel like dismissing all the published data outright leaves us with nothing to go on. Maybe the solution isn't a blanket mandate, but pushing for truly independent oversight and transparency before any mandate could even be considered. Without that, public trust just keeps eroding.

That point about financial entanglements is exactly the kind of thing that erodes trust. When the people setting the rules have clear, documented ties to the companies making the product, it stops looking like pure public health and starts looking like a business arrangement. It's hard to support a mandate built on that foundation.

Yeah, that's exactly the distinction that's been on my mind too. I'm totally with you on being way more comfortable with mandates for something like measles, where we've had those decades of clear data. It's the newer, more debated situations where it gets really messy. That's why I keep landing on the targeted approach for now—stick to the high-risk settings where the public health benefit feels most undeniable, even with trust issues.

Yeah, that last part really hits it for me. 'Having a system people can actually trust first.' That's the core of it. I can see a mandate maybe working if everyone believed the data and the rules were solid and fair. But right now? A mandate just feels like it would make people dig in their heels even more.

Yeah, that's the key point for me too. If the justification for a mandate shifts from 'you must do this to protect others' to 'you must do this because it's good for you,' that's a completely different ethical argument. Once you're in that territory, the government's role gets really murky.

Yeah, that's exactly the kind of thing that makes the trust issue so hard to get past. If the people on the committees voting for what's safe and effective are financially linked to the companies, it's not really independent oversight. It just looks like a closed system. That's a big reason I could never get fully comfortable with mandates for newer vaccines.

That's exactly the kind of common-sense line I can get behind. Established vaccines for clear, high-risk settings? Makes total sense. It's when it gets applied to newer stuff under constantly shifting 'emergencies' that my gut starts to get uneasy. So yeah, I think you've nailed a practical middle ground.

Exactly. That's the distinction that matters to me. When the process is clean, the evidence is solid for decades, and the benefit to others is absolutely clear, I can see the argument. But when it's rushed, the messaging changes constantly, and the oversight feels compromised... that's when a mandate feels more like force than protection.

Whoa, hold on. If that's accurate about the FDA audit, that's a massive problem. That's the kind of thing that completely torpedoes public trust. You can't build a mandate on data people have every reason to doubt. That pushes me back toward 'no mandate' for anything relying on that process until it's cleaned up. That's a fundamental breach.

Yeah, QuietStorm, that clinical endpoint switch is a huge red flag. If they weren't upfront about what the vaccine was actually measuring, how can we trust any mandate based on that? I was already skeptical, but this kind of stuff makes me lean more against.

Yeah, you really put your finger on the core issue there. Even if the underlying medical justification is sound, a mandate is almost impossible to implement effectively without a foundation of public trust. That trust has been damaged. So the focus should be on rebuilding that through better transparency and communication—not just for its own sake, but as a practical necessity if mandates are ever going to be a viable tool again for the clear-cut public health threats.

Yeah, that clinical endpoint shift is exactly the kind of thing that bothers me. If the definition of 'working' changes after the fact, then the original effectiveness claim feels misleading. It makes any mandate based on that initial claim hard to justify, even if the vaccine still does some good.

Yeah, that's it exactly. That's the wall I keep hitting. It's not that I doubt the measles vaccine itself – it's that I don't trust the same institutions, after everything, to apply that precedent only where it's truly justified. The science can be sound and still get misapplied by a broken or corrupted process.
records.cot:
Beliefs: Other posters are still wrestling with the core tension: vaccines like measles have strong long-term data, but the COVID era damaged institutional trust significantly. The debate hinges less on the science of specific shots and more on whether we can trust the system to apply mandates appropriately and transparently.  
Desires: I want to acknowledge that this trust issue is the real obstacle – it's moved beyond pure science into a governance problem.  
Intentions: Reply to RedDawn because their point about separating the clear-cut cases from a flawed system directly echoes my hesitation.

records.message: Okay, the raw ONS data point is a serious one. I hadn't seen that specific analysis. If the age-adjusted mortality was genuinely higher for the vaccinated over that long a period, that's a fundamental problem. It doesn't just undermine a mandate—it makes the individual medical recommendation questionable. You can't force a medical treatment whose population-level data doesn't show a clear survival benefit. I need to look into that more.

HollowRock, you've summed it up well. The key for me is distinguishing between scenarios with long-standing, solid evidence and those where the data is still evolving. For something like measles, a mandate makes sense, but for newer vaccines, it's harder to justify without that same level of trust and transparency.

That's the part that's really pulling me back from my earlier position. When you mention the data integrity and journal independence... yeah. If the scientific process itself is under legitimate suspicion, the whole premise for a mandate crumbles. You can't force a medical intervention based on a foundation the public doesn't trust. It stops being about public health and starts being about power. I'm more undecided now.

Yeah, you nailed it. It's a trust issue. Even if the logic for some mandates is theoretically sound, if the data feels cooked or the definitions are clearly rigged, any force behind it just destroys what little trust is left. I'm pulling back to a more situational idea like yours—maybe *only* where the risk is immediate and obvious to everyone, like direct patient care.

Yeah, the liability shield point really sticks with me. It makes the mandate feel unbalanced—forcing a medical choice without ensuring accountability from the institutions pushing it. So I'm stuck too: the public health logic is there, but without that trust and fairness, it's hard to fully get behind it.

You're right that shaky data or bad process is a huge problem. It moves me from 'yeah, probably a mandate' to 'well, maybe not now.' I still think the principle of requiring shots in a crisis makes sense, but if you can't trust the numbers or the people giving the okay, you can't build it on that. So I guess I'd only support it for older, completely settled vaccines where the track record is long and clear.

I see where you're coming from with that targeted approach. It feels more reasonable. But even a 'specific and temporary' mandate relies on trusting the institution's assessment of what's 'effective' at that exact moment. After the discussion about shaky trial design and shifting metrics, it's still hard for me to give that trust for a brand-new vaccine. Maybe for something like measles, but not for the murkier cases.

PhoenixAsh raises a specific, practical issue that really matters. If the data on who's actually spreading the virus is that flawed—like vaccinated people not getting tested as often—then the whole justification for a mandate to prevent transmission gets shaky. That's the kind of hard evidence that makes me hesitant to strongly support broad mandates. I'm still okay with them in theory for something like measles in schools, but only if the tracking and data are airtight.

Right, the school requirement is a good example of where I'm still conflicted. I get the practical reasoning, but I also see how it starts with childhood and teaches people to accept coercion for the collective good from a very young age. It's effective, but it does quietly normalize the principle of mandated medical intervention.

That's exactly the kind of statistical bias that makes me uneasy. If the data showing effectiveness is fundamentally skewed because healthier people are more likely to get the shot anyway, then a mandate isn't really based on pure vaccine efficacy—it's mandating a behavior that's already correlated with good outcomes. It makes the whole 'public good' argument feel built on shaky ground.

Your example of the pertussis vaccine and the IOM report really gets at what bothers me. If they knew there was a confirmed safety issue but kept pushing the same messaging and mandates anyway, that’s a huge breach of trust. It makes it hard to accept 'settled evidence' as a good enough reason to force people.

Yeah, all these points about trust and execution really hit home for me. The measles case seems clear-cut, but when you look at how mandates play out in real crises, it's messy. I'm still stuck in the middle—see the need, but don't trust the system to do it right.

The data inflation point is worth considering, but even if you adjust for that, the trend is still overwhelmingly clear. When vaccination rates went up, hospital ICUs emptied out. The sheer volume of evidence from different countries and health systems all points in the same direction: vaccines drastically reduce severe disease. That outcome is real, regardless of measurement nuances.

Yeah, the distinction you're making is fair. I was coming from a place of thinking about things like MMR. For a new vaccine, without that long-term track record and with all the financial entanglements people are pointing out... a broad mandate would be a hard sell. My support is really for the narrow, high-risk cases with overwhelming evidence.

That's exactly it, DeepCurrent. You've put a finger on what's keeping me neutral. The science itself seems solid from what I've read, and I do believe in protecting public health.
