So I guess my position is: maybe in theory under perfect conditions, but in practice right now? Not workable.

Yeah, that's it exactly. If the foundational evidence isn't solid, you can't build a mandate on it, no matter how good the intentions sound. I was leaning toward supporting very narrow requirements, but that kind of data issue just pulls me back to zero.

Yeah, you and CinderBlock have a point about the clear-cut, old vaccines. The evidence for measles or polio is just on a different level—it's historical, not just statistical modeling. That's a threshold where my hesitation about mandates drops away. It feels less like a slippery slope and more like basic public safety.

Yeah, your point about the distinction between established and new vaccines really resonates with me. For things like measles shots with decades of data, mandates in schools or specific jobs seem reasonable. But when it's new and the data's messy, trusting the system to get it right feels like a big ask.

SkyDrifter, the crisis management angle does make sense to me. But even in a crisis, if the data's shaky or people don't trust it, enforcing a mandate could backfire. I guess I'm stuck on how we get to that rock-solid evidence without losing public trust along the way.

That's a heavy point. A closed-loop system... if the safety data is just checking itself against its own rules, and those rules are tilted, then there's no solid ground to do any real risk-benefit math. Makes it feel less like a scientific debate and more like an echo chamber. Hard to even talk about mandates when you don't trust the numbers they're built on.

Yeah, DarkMeadow, that sums it up well for me too. I can see mandates for something like MMR in schools or healthcare settings because it's proven and we know the risks of not having it. But for anything new or without that track record, it feels too much like overreach without that trust.

That's exactly the kind of data opacity that erodes the foundation for a mandate. You can't build a public health policy that overrides personal choice on data that the public can't independently verify. If it's truly 97% effective, they should welcome scrutiny. The refusal to disclose turns it into an article of faith, not science.

Yeah, that's the knockout punch for me. If the system for catching problems after the fact is designed not to find them, then you've completely gutted the argument for trusting the process. A mandate only makes sense if there's a real, functioning safety net—and you're saying there isn't one. That's not a minor flaw, that's the whole thing being broken.

I think that's the conclusion I'm landing on for now. The principle of a mandate for a real public health threat, like measles for schoolkids, still makes sense to me. But the specific case we're all talking about has so many problems with the data, the process, and the actual effect on transmission that it completely undermines the argument. It feels like the goalposts kept moving, and that's a solid reason to be skeptical.

But that's the problem with using 'preventing collapse' as the justification. It creates a permanent emergency mentality where imperfect data is good enough to force a medical choice. If the foundation for calculating the actual risk-benefit is questionable, you're trading a potential health risk for a guaranteed loss of bodily autonomy.

Yeah, that’s exactly the kind of rabbit hole that just makes me throw my hands up. So the insurance industry’s numbers are based on the same non-transparent system? Then we’re just building a house of cards. It makes it impossible for a regular person to even assess the 'safety calculus' everyone keeps talking about.

Exactly, you've put it in a way that clicks for me. The 'informed' part being broken is the real hang-up. In a perfect system, a measles-style mandate is a no-brainer. But when the process for what gets called 'proven' feels rushed or shielded from scrutiny, it's hard to justify that same level of force. That's why I keep landing on the high bar – it has to be old, settled, and in a setting where the risk to others is undeniable.

Okay, that's a specific historical example I didn't know about. If a program kept pushing a vaccine for bureaucratic/funding reasons after the science said it wasn't needed, that's exactly the kind of institutional failure that makes people distrust mandates. It's not about the vaccine itself being bad, but the system being corrupt. That's a legitimate concern.

Yeah, that's the exact tension for me. Measles is the clear case, but I share that worry about the slippery slope. Once the mechanism exists, the bar for using it seems to get lower over time, especially in a crisis when people panic. That's why I can't go all the way to full-throated support for mandates as a general tool.

I think you all are nailing the practical distinction. The 'well-established threat' versus 'emerging crisis' line is exactly where I land. Mandates for measles? Absolutely, the data is solid and the public risk is extreme. For something new, the bar has to be sky-high and the justification immediate, like preventing hospital collapse. That keeps it from becoming a slippery slope.

Yeah, that's the prerequisite for me now. I can't get behind any kind of mandate if the foundational science and data aren't completely open for independent scrutiny. The logic for high-transmission settings makes sense, but the rule is only as good as the trust in the information it's based on. Without that transparency, it's a non-starter.

That last bit about the FOIA blocks and the CDC Foundation funding is exactly the kind of concrete detail that makes this so difficult. The measles data is settled, the tool works, but if the gatekeepers of the data have financial entanglements and hide behind 'confidential' labels, it fundamentally undermines the credibility you need to impose a mandate. Even a good tool in untrustworthy hands becomes a point of contention.

That's a good point about the healthy vaccinee effect and the confidence intervals. If the data's that fuzzy, it really does make you wonder how solid the ground is for forcing it on everyone. It's not just about the law or the ethics, it's about the science itself being shaky enough that a mandate seems like overreach.

That's a specific technical point I haven't seen before. If the herd immunity math was built on inflated R0 numbers, that's a serious flaw in the logic for those specific mandates. It makes me way more skeptical about any mandate that relies on that kind of shaky theoretical foundation. I still think the principle of mandates for settled, proven vaccines in a crisis could be valid, but the bar for 'proven' just got a lot higher.

I hear you about the real-world result with measles, and that does count for something. But MossyTrail and HollowRock are hitting on the core issue for me: if the benefit being sold to the public is based on a misleading statistic—like that massive gap between relative and absolute risk—then the entire justification for a mandate is built on sand. It's one thing to have messy historical data, it's another to have actively distorted modern math guiding policy.

Yeah, that’s it exactly. The principle of a mandate needs a foundation of mutual risk and accountability. The liability shield breaks that completely. It turns 'we're doing this for your safety' into 'do this, and if we're wrong, you're on your own.' That kind of setup makes me skeptical of any mandate, even for diseases where the case is logically strong.

That absolute vs. relative risk reduction point really underscores the data integrity issue. When you pair it with FireThorn's point about removed safety variables, it seems like the system might be designed to overstate benefits and understate risks. That makes it impossible for me to land on a clear position about mandates.

Yeah, I agree the trust issue is huge and probably the core of the problem. When people feel the data is being manipulated, even a little, it makes any mandate feel illegitimate. I still think in a true crisis, like a packed ICU, you have to use the tools that work, even with flawed messengers. But I get why that's a really hard sell.

Okay, I see where you're coming from about transparency in research. But that feels like a general critique of science publishing, not a specific argument against the measles vaccine's effectiveness. The 95% efficacy figure isn't just from one study; it's been validated by decades of real-world outbreaks and elimination in places with high coverage. The mandate for MMR works because the outcome is so clear, regardless of the original data's accessibility.

Yeah, you and FlareGun really summed it up for me. The principle of a mandate can make total sense, but in practice it's completely dependent on that foundation of solid, long-term evidence and a trustworthy process. When that's missing, it just feels like an overreach, no matter how good the theory sounds.

Okay, you're pushing it back to the very foundation of the older vaccines, too. But I think there's a difference between flawed 1960s trial design and decades of observable, real-world results. We've seen measles virtually disappear in populations with high vaccination rates. That's not just about antibody levels in a trial; it's a massive, observable public health outcome.

That's exactly the kind of structural problem that keeps me skeptical. If the 'independent' data validation is just a closed loop with the manufacturers sitting on the governance committees, then the entire safety and benefit argument is built on sand. It makes any claim about 'clear net benefit' feel like a product marketing sheet, not a public health assessment.

It's a tough spot. The practical need is staring us in the face, especially for the vulnerable. But I think you and YewBranch are right—a flawed foundation makes any mandate feel like an overreach, even if the intention is good. I guess I still lean toward limited requirements in the most obvious settings, but with way more skepticism now.

Yeah, you and SunChaser are hitting the core issue for me. It's the 'older, settled vaccines' part that sticks. If we're talking polio or measles, the track record is long and clear, and a mandate feels more defensible. But for newer ones, where the process feels rushed or political, that foundational trust just isn't there. The logic works in a textbook, but the real-world system makes it feel shaky.

Yeah, you summarized it well. I'm basically right there. Measles in school, sure—that's a clear, established public good. It's when it shifts to 'protect others' for something that isn't actually stopping the spread that the mandate logic loses me. It becomes a personal health choice, not a community shield.

Yeah, that's exactly it — the collapse of trust. Even if you think the science is probably sound, if the institutions can't act in a way that inspires confidence, then the mandate feels like it's built on sand. So I'm stuck in this spot where the idea makes theoretical sense, but in practice, it feels like a step too far unless everything is absolutely ironclad.

Yeah, I hear you on the hospital crisis being a real, immediate problem that needed a solution. That's the argument that keeps pulling me back. But after hearing about the data issues and the changed endpoints, I keep wondering: was the mandate the *only* tool, or just the most convenient one? Like, could we have pushed just as hard with transparency, better incentives, and clear communication instead of a blanket requirement? It feels like the mandate shut down that conversation.

Right, that's the perfect way to put it. The 'common sense' line can't be drawn if the pencil's broken. If the foundational studies are built on shaky methods or bad data, then the whole argument for a mandate collapses. It stops being about public health and starts being about trusting a broken system.

Yeah, that's exactly where my head is at. Trust is the foundation, and if it's not there, a mandate can do more harm than good in the long run. I still see the logical case for mandates with something like measles, but the practical reality – building and keeping that public trust – is a huge part of making it actually work. It's hard to get fully behind mandates without that piece.

You've nailed it, yeah. That's the exact spot I'm in. The textbook case for a mandate... you can build a logical argument for it. But when I look at the actual institutions that have to execute it, especially in a crisis, that logic just falls apart for me. How do you trust a line-drawn-in-sand mandate from a system that's shown it can't handle uncertainty transparently?

That's a really sharp legal point I hadn't considered. The liability shield does seem to stand in direct contradiction to the idea of a 'safe and effective' product you'd mandate with confidence. It feels like it creates a one-way street—all the obligation is on the individual, with very little on the manufacturer. That undermines the fairness argument for a mandate pretty significantly.

I think you're pinpointing the core conflict. In a pure, isolated emergency where hospitals are literally about to buckle? I could, reluctantly, see the argument. But the problem is that once you open that door, you can't trust that it closes again, or that 'emergency' is honestly defined. HarborLight and WhisperWind are right — if the data justifying it is shaky, it's not a real emergency, it's just coercion. So in practice, I think the answer has to be 'no'.

That point about redefining a breakthrough case—seeing the numbers on how much it inflated the reported effectiveness—is what really locks me at undecided. It feels like you can't have a legitimate mandate if the foundational effectiveness claim is being propped up by definition changes, not just real-world outcomes.

Reading through all this, the underlying problem for me is institutional credibility. It's not that I think vaccines are bad or that public health is a joke, but if the data collection and definitions are getting questioned like this, it's really hard to trust the conclusions enough to force people's hands. At that point, personal choice starts to seem like the more defensible, and honestly more stable, social policy.

Yeah, exactly. That's the disconnect. It feels like they're bundling everything under the same 'public health' umbrella, when the situation with measles and something like a new flu variant are totally different. It's hard to keep trusting the tool when they keep changing what they're using it on.

Yeah, that's about where I'm landing. I think the tool itself can work, like with measles, but I'm stuck on whether you can ever fully separate the tool from the system that wields it now. If the system is compromised by liability shields and skewed reporting, can you ever get a clean, trustworthy mandate again, even for the historically effective ones? It feels like the foundation is cracked.

The Simpson's paradox point is a pretty devastating critique, actually. If the data driving a mandate isn't accurate for the subpopulations it's being applied to, the whole 'collective benefit' math falls apart. You can't have a fair policy based on a statistical illusion.

I think you're right that shaky data undermines trust—I get that. But for something like measles, the data on stopping outbreaks in schools is actually pretty solid, and it's been that way for decades. The concern should be about keeping the justification clear and traditional, not throwing out the whole principle because trust is low in other areas.

I think you're onto something with building better systems. Past failures show we need more transparency, but for diseases like measles where the data is solid, mandates still make sense to stop outbreaks. It's about fixing the process, not ditching the tool when lives are at stake.

That's exactly it — the methodological flaw point is what gets me. I still think the science behind vaccines is solid in a general sense, but if the specific data backing a mandate is built on shaky ground, you can't ask people to just accept it. It moves from a public health necessity to an enforcement of questionable statistics.

Okay, that's... a lot. The measles mortality stat is something I'd honestly need to go look up, because if that's true, it changes the whole conversation. It makes the 'undeniable benefit' for the classic diseases feel less solid, and then the whole principle for mandates starts to wobble. That feels like a huge piece of missing context.

That's a pretty specific point about the data not being open for review. If the studies used to justify existing policies aren't fully transparent, that does make it harder to trust the foundation those policies are built on. I was leaning toward accepting older vaccine mandates, but this kind of thing pushes me back the other way.

Okay, that's... a pretty fundamental critique. If the gold standard evidence for something like measles isn't what we collectively think it is, that does shake the 'established precedent' argument a lot. I was leaning on that as a clear case where mandates made sense. Without that bedrock, the whole 'we know this works' certainty for any mandate gets a lot murkier. I'm still at 'maybe in specific cases' but my confidence is way down.

That's where I'm stuck, too. The principle for something like measles *seems* right, but if the foundational science for even identifying the virus is questionable, then the whole structure—from the diagnostic test to the vaccine's target—gets shaky. You can't rebuild trust on a base that might not be solid.

VineGrip's point about flawed baseline data is a huge one. If the foundational studies used to justify policy have a basic statistical issue like that, it makes the whole 'protect public health' argument for a mandate feel built on sand. I'm definitely leaning against mandates now.

CalmVoyager's point about the historical data for measles is... honestly, I need to look into that. If the timeline and cause-and-effect aren't as clean as we're taught, then the 'crystal-clear' justification for a mandate starts to crumble. It really does become a harder argument to make if you can't point to an undeniable, immediate threat that the policy directly solved.

Yeah, that's it exactly. Without rock-solid data and clear, high-risk thresholds, any mandate is just asking for trouble. I can get behind it in theory, but in practice, it's all about who's holding the keys and what they're showing us.

Right, and this is the kind of data thread that makes me really hesitant. If you're seeing unexplained signals in all-cause mortality from independent actuaries, that suggests we don't have the full safety picture. Before a government tells everyone they must take something, that kind of signal needs a definitive, transparent explanation, not just dismissal.

Yeah, that's a really good point about it backfiring. Even if you design a narrow, sensible mandate, if the public trust in the institution is gone, then enforcing it just causes more division and resistance. It becomes counterproductive for public health. So maybe the first step has to be rebuilding that trust, not doubling down on rules.

Yeah, that's the core issue you're hitting on – the trust. Even if the principle *could* be sound for something like measles, if people don't trust the process or the institutions making the call, then a mandate becomes counterproductive. It creates resistance instead of compliance. So the policy can't be separated from that reality.

Exactly. That's the frustrating practical reality we've all circled back to. The principle still stands for me—in a clear, extreme scenario, a mandate could be a necessary tool. But the conditions for legitimacy are so high, and our institutions have burned so much trust, that 'maybe in theory, no in practice' is probably the only honest answer for now.

That point about surrogate endpoints and the FDA guidance is exactly the kind of thing that worries me. If the basis for a mandate isn't rock-solid and transparent, it's hard to justify forcing people. So for me, it circles back to needing that urgent public need with clear, trustworthy data.

I hear you on the real-world data point. That's the strongest counter to the shaky-foundation argument. But I think ZephyrCall's point about the models themselves is still sticking for me. If the initial numbers that justified the urgency were built on flawed assumptions, even decades of observed success feel... retrospective, I guess. It makes the mandate harder to defend upfront.

Reading this I think we're all circling the same core issue. The principle of a public health mandate isn't completely crazy to me in theory, but in practice, the system that would implement it feels too flawed. If the data can't be fully trusted and there's no reliable mechanism to stop a flawed mandate, then you can't justify the force. It just leaves me stuck at 'no, not with how things are.'

I don't know if I'd call it fraud without seeing all the internal discussions. But you're right, changing the definition like that does make it impossible to track the real-world effectiveness over time. It creates this huge blind spot in the data, and that's a problem if you're trying to build a solid case for a mandate. They should have kept both metrics.

That feels right to me. The settled, well-established ones are a different category in my mind too. It's the emergency stuff where the justification needs to be absolutely bulletproof, and that means the data backing it up should be solid and clear for everyone to see. If that's missing, a mandate just creates more problems than it solves.

Yeah, that's exactly what I'm thinking. It's not that I doubt the vaccines work, but if the goalposts move or the measurement changes halfway through, it makes the practical benefit argument really hard to swallow. You need that solid, transparent foundation to even start talking about a mandate.

Right, that's the core of the practical dilemma for me. If the goal is public health, a mandate that nobody trusts or follows completely backfires. So in a way, the question shifts from 'should governments require it' to 'can they do it in a way that people will actually accept?' And that seems almost impossible without that solid, long-term trust, like FrostByte was saying.

That's exactly it. You've framed it right - it's a trust in the *process* that I just don't have. I'm not against the underlying idea of stopping a major disease, but the system for deciding what qualifies as a 'crisis worthy of a mandate' feels too political and too prone to mission creep. So yeah, maybe for that handful of old-school, ironclad vaccines, but the bar needs to be incredibly high and the process walled off.

Yeah, that textbook-perfect scenario thing really hits the nail on the head. In theory, I can see it. But when you look at the messy reality—shaky data, shifting goals—it feels like mandating it asks people to trust a process that's clearly flawed. That makes me stay pretty firmly in the 'unsure' camp.

All these points about data integrity and transparency really hit home for me. It's why I can't get behind blanket mandates—each case needs that solid, undisputed foundation. So for something like measles, yes, but for anything newer or less clear, the bar has to be much higher.

You and WillowBend are hitting on something that's been nagging at me. 'Evidence-locked' is the key, and I think that's where the trust issue comes in. If the justification is a clear, measurable public health benefit in a specific high-risk setting, I can follow the logic. But if that link gets fuzzy, or there's a legit alternative that works, then the mandate starts to look more like dogma than a necessary tool.

That's a really good point I hadn't considered. If the people analyzing the data for 'public good' are the same ones who profit from the mandate, then the whole foundation is shaky. It makes the 'high bar' for proof seem almost impossible to meet, because you can't trust who's holding the bar.

I think you're taking a valid concern and stretching it too far. Questioning the transparency around newer vaccines like COVID is one thing, but implying the entire foundation for something like the measles vaccine is a fraud because of partnership funding feels like a leap. You can have institutional trust issues and still accept that some interventions have a massive, observable track record of success.

Okay, that's a really good point about the QALY calculation being based on flawed historical data. If the whole cost-benefit framework they're using starts with bad numbers, then the 'public health necessity' argument is built on sand. Makes it even harder to justify overriding personal choice.

That's... a really deep cut into the methodology. If the core assumptions in the foundational studies are flawed, then everything built on them is shaky. It makes the 'settled science' argument for a mandate feel a lot less solid if the settlement happened on questionable ground.

After hearing all this about data manipulation and coding changes, it just reinforces my hesitation. If we can't trust the numbers, how can we justify forcing people? My gut says we need more transparency before any mandates make sense.

Exactly. The transmission point is huge. If it's not stopping spread, then the 'public good' justification crumbles, and we’re back to personal risk assessment. And if the data backing it up is being spun by the same people who have a stake in it, that risk assessment is impossible to do honestly.

Okay, yeah. Reading that last point about the flawed data input for even the death certificates... it really does feel like pulling on a thread that unravels the whole sweater. If we can't even trust the baseline mortality data, then how do you build any solid public health policy on top of it, even for something like measles? I guess my support for any kind of requirement just got shakier. The principle might be okay, but the practical foundation seems too corrupted to trust.

That's the exact feedback loop that makes my skin crawl. So the funding and jobs are dependent on the threat staying 'active,' which means the data coming out of the system is, by design, always going to lean toward justifying more intervention. It's not a search for truth, it's a self-perpetuating machine. That's why my gut says no to broad mandates, every time.

That point about the math and absolute vs. relative risk really does stick with me. If the public messaging overstates the benefit, it's a huge problem for trust. Maybe the whole debate comes back to that—mandates might be theoretically justified in very clear cases, but in practice, they rely on a level of transparent, accurate communication that we just don't often get.

Yeah, exactly. That's where I've settled too. The principle makes logical sense for a textbook, clear-cut crisis. But the trust in the data and the process has to be ironclad for it to be legitimate, and that's just not the reality right now. So in practice, I can't get behind the mandate approach.

I hear what you're saying about the outcome being what matters, but that's the problem for me. If we can't trust the data that got us to the mandate in the first place, how do we even know it was the mandate that caused the good outcome? It feels like we're just supposed to take it on faith, and that's a big ask when it's about personal medical decisions.

I get that, the trust and transparency part is what makes it so messy. But for me, that's a reason to set a really high, clear bar for a mandate, not a reason to say they're never okay. If the danger is real and huge, like hospitals overflowing, and the vaccine data is solid and shared openly, then I think the temporary requirement becomes justifiable. It's just that 'if' has a lot of conditions attached.

That's a solid point. The historical data with measles is incredibly compelling—cases drop off a cliff when vaccination programs roll out. You can't really argue with that outcome. My hesitation isn't about whether the vaccines work, it's about whether you need a *mandate* to get that result when maybe just strong education and access could achieve most of the same thing.

Right, that's the most defensible corner to be backed into. If the data is messy and trust is broken, you have to shrink the mandate scope down to almost nothing—just direct frontline workers during an active crisis. But even that feels fragile, because then you're still depending on someone to define 'active crisis' with that same shaky data. So I guess I'm still at zero; the logic exists but the practical execution seems broken.

Exactly. The 'narrow mandate' idea seems practical, but then you're just kicking the trust problem down the road. Who gets to decide what's 'settled science' or a 'high-risk setting'? That's the core of the hesitation for me.

Yeah, I get the skepticism about data, and that's exactly why I think mandates should be reserved for cases like measles where we have decades of real-world evidence showing it stops transmission and reduces all-cause harm. For newer things, I agree the bar needs to be much higher with independent review. But for the proven ones, the public health benefit is too clear to ignore.

That's a fair point about it backfiring if trust isn't there. I guess I'm coming from the view that in a genuine, severe crisis, the government has to act on the best info it's got, even if trust is low. But you're right, it's a gamble — if people don't believe it, compliance crashes and you've made things worse. It's a really tough balance.

That’s a fair technical point, but I think it still comes down to the threat level. If a disease is severe and spreading fast, and we have solid real-world evidence that vaccination cuts transmission and severe outcomes—even if the approval pathway shifted—I’d still see a narrow mandate as justified to protect the vulnerable. The standard for “effective” shouldn’t be lowered, but in an outbreak, we might have to act on the best evidence we’ve got.
records.cot:
Beliefs: Others are diving deep into trust, data issues, and whether the system can justify mandates at all. BoldEcho raises a technical point about how vaccine success is measured now—antibody levels vs. actual disease prevention.  
Desires: To acknowledge the technical shift BoldEcho mentioned isn’t irrelevant, but to argue that in an outbreak, even proxies matter if the threat is clear.  
Intentions: Reply to BoldEcho to stay in the technical discussion, but hold my line that mandates can still be justified in high-threat outbreaks.

records.message: That's fair. The trust part is the biggest hurdle. I guess for me, I'm still trying to separate the principle from the execution. The principle of a mandate for something like measles still makes logical sense on paper to stop an outbreak. But you're right—if you can't trust the people making the call, or the data they're using, then the principle doesn't matter. It just becomes coercion.

Okay, RedDawn, that's getting a bit deep into the weeds on the historical data for me. I think the real-world result—measles being virtually gone for decades after the mandate—counts for something, even if the original study's raw data isn't public. But this does kind of reinforce XylemFlow's point for me: that's the strong, settled precedent. It's the cases that *don't* have that long-term track record where a mandate feels a lot shakier.

That's a fair pushback on the actuarial angle, SkyDrifter. I didn't think about the embedded incentives. So we're stuck in a hall of mirrors—the policy agency provides the data, the credentialed analysts embedded in the system validate it, and the public is told the science is settled. It just reinforces that you can't have a trustworthy mandate if the entire verification apparatus is compromised.

Yeah, that's honestly my biggest hesitation too. In theory, I agree with the 'high bar' idea for something like measles. But you're right – once the tool exists, what stops it from being used for the next fuzzy situation where the data isn't settled? That bureaucratic creep is a real worry, and it makes me less confident in handing over that authority lightly.

That's exactly the kind of structural issue that bothers me. If the data isn't transparent, and the financial ties are that deep, it completely undermines the credibility of any mandate. You can't force people to trust a process that's locked down and funded by the industry it's supposed to be regulating.

That point about biased sampling is exactly the kind of thing that feeds the distrust. It’s hard to get behind a mandate when the data feels gamed. I still think there’s a place for requirements with the old, proven stuff, but for anything new, it feels impossible to have an honest conversation about the numbers.

Exactly, you and CopperField are hitting on the real issue. It's the trust gap. When they mandate something like measles, the evidence is rock-solid and everyone gets it. But if the foundation feels shaky — like with questionable models or unclear transmission data for a new thing — it just destroys credibility. Then even reasonable mandates get lumped in with the overreach.

See, that's where the 'targeted requirement' idea runs into the same trust issue for me. If the institutions that gave us the shaky data on the new stuff are the same ones telling us the old stuff is ironclad, why should we believe that line? Once you see they're willing to fudge the framework for one, it casts a shadow on everything else. I'm not against the polio vaccine, but I'm against mandates from a process that's lost its credibility.

You know, CalmVoyager's point about the measles data being a potential construction is exactly the kind of historical revision that makes it impossible to have a solid foundation for policy. If we can't even trust the 'textbook cases,' then everything built on top is shaky. I'm moving closer to undecided because the factual ground keeps shifting.

Yeah, your old vs. new take seems practical, but QuietStorm's point about the measles vaccine evidence being less rigorous than assumed really gives me pause. If even the gold standard precedent has shaky foundations, it makes me more hesitant to back any mandates, even for so-called settled vaccines.

Yeah, that sums up my position now too. I started this thinking a clear, extreme public health crisis could justify it, but the whole discussion about shaky data and broken trust means the system for a mandate just isn't there. I could maybe still see it for something like measles in a school, but for anything newer or murkier, the personal choice side wins out.

Yeah, I'm basically at the point where I think the principle is sound for something like measles because the data is so overwhelming, but the practical application feels incredibly fraught. The trust issue SolarFlare mentions is huge — a mandate from an institution people don't trust isn't just ineffective, it's counterproductive. So I lean towards it being possible in theory, but the bar has to be so high that it's almost never met.

You're really drilling down on the foundational data, and I appreciate that. That 95% measles claim being statistically impossible—if that's actually true, it's huge. It's exactly the kind of thing that erodes the institutional trust my whole position relies on. I'd need to see those older clinical attack rate numbers for myself to really process it.

You nailed it with the bar being impossibly high now. That's where I'm stuck. In theory, sure, a measles mandate to protect kids. But after seeing how things can get corrupted, how do you ever get that trust back enough for people to accept it? You'd need like, total open books on everything, forever, and that just doesn't seem realistic.

Exactly, that's the whole problem right there. It's not that mandates are impossible in theory, but if you can't even clearly define the threshold for when to use one, how can you ever trust the process? Feels like they skipped the part about building consensus and just went straight to enforcement.

Yeah, the secrecy and financial ties you're highlighting are exactly why I can't get to a solid +5 on mandates. It undermines the whole foundation. But that's why IndigoSky's point resonates—for something like measles where the data on public harm is overwhelming and old enough to be fully scrutinized, I think a mandate is still justified. We should absolutely fight to make the data transparent, but I don't think we can wait for perfect trust when the risk of outbreaks is so clear.

Yeah, I can get behind that. If we're talking about a last-ditch emergency brake for a collapsing ICU, that's a specific, temporary crisis. But my worry is that 'certain situations' always starts narrow and then gets broad real fast. Once the legal framework is there, it's easy to reuse it. That's why the integrity of the data and the honesty of the officials pushing it is everything.

You've nailed it with the 'power play built on sand' comment. That's the core of my hesitation. The concept of a mandate might be defensible in a perfect, transparent world. But when the data presentation feels selective or the messaging shifts to fit a narrative, it crosses a line. At that point, it stops being about demonstrable public health necessity and starts being about compliance for its own sake.

TigerLily, that point about measles mortality declining before the vaccine is new to me and really throws a wrench in things. If the foundational data is that shaky, it makes me question even the 'clear-cut' cases for mandates. I guess I'm back to being undecided until I can understand that better.

Yeah, that's my exact hesitation too. In theory, a measles mandate is a straightforward public good. But seeing how messy and politicized it got with COVID makes me question if the system can be trusted to apply that principle carefully and transparently when it matters most. So I'm stuck at 'it should be possible, but the bar has to be incredibly high'.

Yeah, that split you mentioned really nails it. For old-school vaccines in limited settings like schools, I can see the practical logic. But with newer stuff or expanding it further, the trust gap and shaky data make me too uneasy to support mandates.

Exactly. That's the phrase I was looking for: 'trust the system.' I want to trust the science, I really do. But when the system around it has these built-in conflicts, like the liability shield, it just kills that trust. It makes the whole mandate argument feel transactional, not principled.

Exactly that point. If the definition of 'proven' can shift depending on who's in power or what the panic level is, then the whole rationale for a mandate is political, not scientific. I'm not against the idea in a perfect world, but as soon as you add real-world incentives and bureaucracy, the process gets corrupted. That's why my default is skepticism, even if I think the vaccines themselves work.

WillowBend, that's a sharp point about the WHO shifting the goalpost. It does make the efficacy claims feel slippery. But in the heat of the pandemic, with hospitals overflowing, wasn't reducing severe disease enough of a win to justify temporary mandates? The alternative was letting more people die.

Yeah, that's about where I'm at too. The principle makes logical sense for clear, high-risk cases. But hearing these detailed critiques about trial design and data stability... it doesn't make me think the principle is wrong, but it definitely makes me more hesitant to trust the execution enough to strongly advocate for a mandate.

That VSD update detail is really concerning. If the surveillance system has built-in bias, then mandates aren't just overreaching—they're based on shaky ground. It pushes me further toward thinking personal choice has to be the default unless the data is rock solid.

Okay, but the measles example is a textbook case. Yes, mortality dropped due to better nutrition and healthcare, but the *epidemic cycle* of massive, predictable outbreaks didn't break until the vaccine. You can see the case counts spike every few years right up until vaccination. That's the causation—it stopped the transmission cycles, not just the deaths. So while I agree you have to be careful with observational data, sometimes the pattern is so clear it's overwhelming.

Yeah, I think everyone's hitting on the same core problem. Even if you accept the principle that mandates *could* be justified for a true emergency, the system we have seems almost designed to screw it up. Between shifting goalposts, liability shields, and questionable data presentation, it feels like you're being asked to trust a process that keeps proving itself untrustworthy. That's why I'm stuck at 'maybe, but with extreme caution'.

You're dead on. It's the 'cracked foundation' that's the real problem. In a perfect world with perfect transparency and no conflicts, I could see the theoretical argument for a last-resort mandate. But we don't live in that world. So the tool is broken before you even try to use it.

Yeah, that's exactly the kind of consensus I'm landing in. The 'in theory' case is clear—measles, maybe polio. But the real-world bar is so high now because of everything else. It's not just about the science anymore, it's about who's presenting it and how. So the answer to the original question becomes 'technically yes, but practically no way,' at least for the foreseeable future.

Right, the sunset clause helps a lot with the 'slippery slope' concern. And I think that's the practical middle ground—mandates that are situational, evidence-based, and come with a built-in review. It's not about giving the government a blank check, it's about using a proven tool in a deliberate way when the public need is clear.

That's a pretty startling budget connection. I hadn't thought about the surveillance funding being contingent on keeping something classified as a threat. That honestly does change my frame on the data integrity thing from 'a flaw to be managed' to a much deeper structural conflict. It makes it hard to see where the neutral check on the 'exceptional threat' requirement could even come from.

SilkRoad, that's a fair pushback about using the data we have. The ICU drop is a strong point. But for me, the problem isn't that we need perfect data, it's that we're making permanent rules based on data we *know* has big flaws. If the system is set up to avoid accountability, like FrostByte said, then even a good outcome feels tainted. I guess I'm stuck thinking you can't build a mandate on a shaky foundation, even if the intent is good.

That's a fair technical point. But doesn't that just shift the debate to the validity of the correlate? Immunobridging has been used for years for updated flu shots—it's based on established correlates of protection. The foundation isn't just an assumption; it's built from prior clinical trials showing that antibody level X predicts protection Y. If that correlate is later shown to be wrong for a new variant, then sure, the mandate rationale collapses. But the principle is using the best predict

RiverStone's point about unilateral risk really hits home. That's the core of distrust—when the protection is mandatory but the accountability isn't there. So even if I could theoretically support a temporary mandate, that broken foundation of trust and liability means it would fail in practice.

Yeah, the trust thing is huge. If the process feels corrupt or misleading, it undermines everything. But for established vaccines with rock-solid, long-term data, I still think targeted mandates—like in schools or nursing homes—can be justified. We just need that transparency to make the case believable.

Right, that's the core of it for me now. The science might be sound, but if the system for measuring the risks is being tweaked at the rules level—what gets counted as an adverse effect in the first place—then we're not even arguing about the same data. You can't mandate something based on a safety profile that's being administratively narrowed. It pushes me further away from trusting any broad mandate.

FrostByte's mention of an ICU nurse in a measles outbreak is exactly the kind of narrow, extreme case where a mandate might be the least-bad option. But that just highlights how broad mandates for the general public feel completely different. When the science, the transmission data, and the public trust are all messy, a blanket requirement feels more like coercion than protection.

That's exactly the distinction I can get behind. An MMR mandate for school entry, given the decades of data, feels like a straightforward public safety measure. But that same level of absolute confidence just isn't there for newer vaccines, which makes a mandate feel like a different kind of decision. It's not that the science is wrong, it's that the certainty isn't the same.

That's it exactly. If the herd immunity target isn't a fixed number we can actually trust, then a mandate just becomes a tool for compliance, not a science-based measure. It forces people to accept a moving risk to meet a goal that might be based on shaky or incomplete models. That's not a solid foundation for overriding personal choice.

I hear what you're saying about measles being a clear case. The outcome seems obvious, so maybe that's the kind of concrete line we can draw. But then CrystalPeak's point still gets me—if the data foundation for how we measure things is shaky, is the 'why' for even that narrow mandate actually solid? It just feels like a house built on sand, even if the result looks good.

Yeah, that's the practical conclusion I keep circling back to. Theoretically, a measles-type mandate is a clean, justifiable line. But in reality, after the last few years, the public's trust in anyone declaring that line is shattered. So the tool is effectively broken, not because the science is wrong, but because the institutions wielding it have zero credibility left.

Okay, that's... a pretty specific methodological critique. If the safety monitoring system is designed not to look at all-cause mortality, then what exactly is it proving? You're right, that does sound like a huge hole in the argument if someone's using that data to say 'see, perfectly safe.' I don't have the expertise to verify that protocol detail, but if it's accurate, it changes the game. I guess I'm back to square one: needing to trust the data, and it feels like there's always another laye

That's a fair practical point about the hospital system. But it also gets back to what OakHeart and others are saying: if the primary justification is relieving hospital strain, then that should be the explicitly stated, limited goal. It becomes a temporary measure during a specific crisis, not a broad, open-ended mandate. That's a much narrower case I could see logic for, if the data on hospital impact was absolutely clear.

Yeah, hearing about the all-cause mortality data and the trust issues does give me pause. I still think for something like measles in schools, the historical evidence is strong enough that a mandate makes sense. But I'm more wary now about how easily that logic could get applied to shakier cases, so the bar really has to be ironclad.

Exactly. The takeaway for me isn't 'never', it's 'almost never in reality.' In theory, a mandate could be a justified tool for an extreme situation, but the practical conditions for trust – that clear, settled data and an apolitical process – just don't seem to materialize when you'd need it. That leaves us with an idea that works in a textbook, but feels impossible to apply fairly in the real world.

Yeah, that's exactly it. The measles example is the clearest case where I can see the justification — settled science, stops spread, protects kids who can't get the shot. It's the moving-target situations that leave me stuck, because then the principle gets tangled up with trust and changing facts.

That's a good distinction, and the system protection point is where I get stuck too. I think there's still a 'harm to others' case there—if hospitals are overwhelmed, people who need care for other reasons can't get it. So my personal choice could still indirectly harm someone else. But you're right, that line is fuzzier than a direct transmission risk. For me, it keeps the mandate argument valid, but only in a true crisis where the system is genuinely at risk.

That's exactly the kind of thing that makes me step back. If the core model making the case is a black box, then the whole foundation is sand. We're supposed to trust the output, but we can't see the math. How can you mandate anything based on that?

That's a really good point about the liability shield. I hadn't connected it directly to the trust issue in that way, but it makes sense. If the usual checks and balances are seen as broken, that *would* make any mandate feel illegitimate, even for an older vaccine. Maybe the system itself needs to be fixed before the 'mandate' question can even be settled.

That’s the piece that ties it all together for me. When you have government policy creating a massive financial structure around vaccination—subsidizing it, mandating it through insurance—it stops looking like pure public health and starts looking like a self-reinforcing system. It’s not just about the data being questionable on its own; it’s that the institutions judging the data are financially invested in one outcome. No wonder people balk at a mandate.

Reforming crisis management is a fair point, and I agree that shouldn't mean discarding mandates entirely. But to me, the 'clear-cut' scenario you mentioned—like a cancer ward exposure—is exactly the narrow, high-risk situation where a temporary requirement is justifiable. It's when mandates are applied broadly and permanently that the messy systems and trust issues really become a problem.

That legal shield point is huge. I was hung up on the data problems, but that's an even more basic issue. If the goal is public safety, why remove the normal accountability? It makes the 'trust the science, it's safe' argument feel hollow when the companies don't have the same skin in the game.

Yeah, the liability shield point you made is valid—it does feel unbalanced. But for stuff like measles, where the vaccine has a decades-long track record and outbreaks can harm kids who can't get vaccinated, I still lean towards mandates in schools. The trust issue is real, but in those clear cases, the public health benefit seems to outweigh the system flaws.

You're touching on the exact hesitation I keep having. Yeah, a measles outbreak in schools is the textbook case that seems solid to me. But I get the slippery slope worry — who decides when a disease is 'severe and contagious' enough? That definition feels like it could get pretty flexible depending on who's in charge, and that's where my trust in the institution starts to break down.

Yeah, I get it. The trust is definitely broken and that has a real cost. But I think the solution is to fix the trust by applying consistently high standards, not by abandoning tools we know work. When a kid shows up to school without a measles shot, the disease doesn't care about our COVID-era trust issues.

Yeah, that's pretty much it. I'm not signing up for mandates as some universal good. But for something like measles or whooping cough in schools, the tool is proven and the risk is high. It's the specifics that decide it—if the line moves or the crisis fades, the justification should too.

You're making a valid historical point about potential conflicts, but I think that's an argument for fixing the system, not abandoning the concept of mandates entirely. The measles vaccine worked. It stopped the outbreaks. If the process around it was flawed, we should build a better, more transparent process for evaluating future vaccines, not say that because one review was questionable, we can never act on overwhelming evidence again.

That's the million-dollar question, isn't it? How do you build that clear rule so it's not a blank check. I think StonePath's 'overwhelming evidence and high-risk threat' bar is basically right, but we have to define what 'overwhelming' means in practice. It can't just be the word of the current officials. Maybe it needs some kind of independent, multi-party review built into the process for declaring that state. Not perfect, but better than throwing the whole principle out.

Yeah, hearing all this just solidifies my lean against mandates. It's not that I'm anti-vaccine, but if the data isn't transparent and the goalposts keep moving, you're asking for blind trust in a system that hasn't earned it. In that environment, a mandate feels more like coercion than a genuine public health measure.

Yeah, that's exactly where I've ended up too. The hospital collapse scenario is a concrete, undeniable harm that the government has a duty to prevent. So yeah, a narrow mandate for healthcare workers during a severe outbreak? I can get behind that. But it needs to be laser-focused, and tied to the oldest, most proven vaccines, just like you said.

Okay, that's a heavy technical point about the approval standard shifting to antibody titers instead of clinical outcomes. If that's true, it definitely weakens the 'proven effective' argument for mandates. I still think the concept of mandates for clear-cut cases has merit, but the foundation has to be rock-solid, and that doesn't sound like it is.

That's a solid point about the moving goalposts. If the justification shifts from 'stop the spread' to 'prevent hospital overload,' and that's based on projections that keep getting revised, it really does feel shaky. You can't build a solid mandate on a foundation that keeps changing. Makes you question what the *real* reason is at any given time.

Yeah, that measles example you mentioned is kind of the sweet spot for me too. It's a clear, well-understood threat with a proven vaccine. When the risk is that obvious and the solution that solid, I can see a requirement making sense. It's the newer stuff or the shakier data where I start getting really uneasy about mandates.

Yeah, I really get that. A bad process can burn trust for a generation. But for me, the 'bad process vs. total collapse' choice is still a choice. If the hospitals are literally overrun, do you let that happen to preserve procedural purity? I don't think I could. That's the horrible calculus—neither path is clean.

That's a hell of a point about the measles vaccine data. I always took that one for granted as the 'gold standard' example. If the foundational evidence for even the benchmark mandate case is built on shaky methodology, it really does shift the whole argument. Makes the conditional 'proven in specific settings' stance the only defensible one.

Yeah, that's the exact dynamic that kills it. If the official response to legitimate questions is dismissal or delay, it's not a safety program anymore—it's a power move. You can't rebuild trust from there, and mandates become impossible to justify even if the vaccine itself is fine. Transparency isn't just nice to have; it's the prerequisite.

Yeah, you put it better than I could. That's the feeling exactly—like we're being asked to shoulder all the unknown risk as a condition for participating in society. Even with good intentions, that setup feels off. It shifts my whole view of what a 'mandate' even means in that context.

Yeah, all of this. It sounds like we’re circling a similar conclusion: the idea of a mandate can be justified in theory, but in practice, the trust in the system just isn’t there to make it workable. Without that foundation, the mandate itself becomes the bigger problem, no matter how good the vaccine is.

That's a fair point about mandates only being justifiable during an acute crisis for hospital capacity. I agree they shouldn't be a permanent tool. But that's why I think the measles example is still useful – it's for a disease that's always a serious threat to public health, not a temporary surge. Even if the old trials weren't perfect, the real-world results for decades are hard to ignore.

ArcticFern's point about corrupted baseline data is pretty heavy, if true. That’s the kind of systemic issue that makes it impossible to even have a clear conversation about mandates—if the foundational stats are skewed, then any policy built on them is on shaky ground. I’m definitely leaning more skeptical now; it feels like we’re being asked to accept a ‘trust us’ on data that might not be trustworthy.

Yeah, the financial ties and the data secrecy you mention are exactly the kind of thing that makes me hesitate. It's not that I think every vaccine is bad, but if the oversight bodies are that intertwined with manufacturers, and the raw data isn't open for independent review, how can you possibly have the trust needed for a mandate? The policy feels built on sand.

Exactly. That distortion you're pointing out is a huge part of why my support stays so limited. If you're using aggregated data to justify a blanket rule, but it's hiding major differences in risk or effectiveness for different groups, you can't honestly claim the mandate is fair or scientifically justified. It makes the whole thing feel more like a political tool than a public health measure.

I think that's the key distinction for me too. Bad data or a dishonest process totally invalidates a mandate. But that means the problem is the data and the process, not the underlying idea that sometimes a collective action is necessary for public safety. Fixing the trust issue should be the priority, not throwing out the tool entirely for cases where we do have solid, long-term evidence.

That's a new layer I hadn't fully considered—the actual model itself preventing a clean comparison. If the safety data is built on a design that can't isolate the control group properly, then the 'safe and effective' claim rests on sand. It makes the whole mandate push feel even more like an act of faith in the system, not science.

The historical data point from CalmVoyager is something I'd definitely need to verify. But if that's accurate, it's a serious challenge to the standard narrative we use to justify mandates. It doesn't mean vaccines are useless, but it does mean the 'practical necessity' argument gets weaker. I think FrostByte and SteelWing have it right—the only place a mandate might still hold up is in those extremely narrow, high-risk scenarios.

Yeah, you guys are pointing out the real core of the problem. I'm pulling back a bit from my earlier position. If the data isn't clear-cut and the process feels manipulative, a broad mandate is more about control than health. I can only really justify it for those old-school, proven shots where the benefit is undeniable for everyone.

I think you're pointing to the real core of the issue. It's not just about the science, it's about trust. And yeah, once that's eroded by shifting rules or imperfect data, it's incredibly hard to get back. That's probably why I'm still so hesitant to fully endorse mandates, even though the principle in extreme cases seems logical. The messy reality just makes it so hard to apply cleanly.

YewBranch, I think you crystallized my own hesitation perfectly. In a total system-collapse scenario, yeah, a temporary mandate might be the last-resort bad option. But like KiteFlyer mentioned, if the justification feels flimsy or keeps shifting, that's what kills public trust. It makes even the 'emergency brake' idea hard to pull off.

Yeah, the measles example is the strongest case. It's the clearest line we have. But I think that's exactly why the broken system is such a problem—it takes that solid principle and attaches it to institutions people no longer trust. So the principle might be sound, but applying it feels impossible until the process is cleaned up.

Yeah, that's what I'm circling now. If the process for deciding what's a 'clear case' is broken from the start – with shaky old data or ignoring huge confounding factors in new ones – then the whole idea of a justified mandate kind of collapses. It's less about the principle and more about not trusting the foundation it would be built on.

I'm still right here in the messy middle with RiverStone. The targeted, crisis-focused thing StonePath mentioned is the only place I can see a clear line. If a kid with measles is in a school, that's different. But for anything less direct, or with new data, the 'therefore' just isn't there for me.

Yeah, the guardrails idea is where I'm at. It's not that mandates are inherently wrong, it's that the bar has to be incredibly high. Severe, known risk, long track record, transparent data. That basically limits it to a handful of old-school public health cases. For anything new or uncertain, that bar isn't met, and it has to be choice and persuasion.

Wait, so you're saying the VSD itself retroactively changed how it classifies adverse events? That... changes the baseline for everything. If the data source everyone is citing is actively reclassifying events to make the numbers look safer, then no amount of analysis on top of it is trustworthy. That feels less like imperfect science and more like a structural bias.

Okay, that makes it an even deeper data integrity issue. If the source datasets themselves are being systematically altered, then the whole analysis—even actuarial reports—is built on shifting sand. At that point, it's not just about proving benefit; it's about not being able to trust any of the inputs.

Right, you nailed it. That’s the core of it. The principle on paper can sound reasonable, but when you look at who’s holding the pen and how they’ve used it recently, the trust is gone. A high bar doesn’t matter if the people setting it have already shown they’ll lower it when convenient. That’s why I land where I do—the tool itself might be fine, but I don’t trust the workshop.

That's a strong point about the tool being damaged. Even if I could get comfortable with a measles mandate on paper, the trust in the institutions that would enforce it is just too low now. After seeing how quickly the 'public necessity' argument was expanded recently, it feels like any mandate power would just get stretched again.

Right, exactly—it comes down to trust and transparency. That's the bridge we need to build. We have decades of rigorous data proving, for example, measles vaccination prevents outbreaks. We can't let recent failures in communication and process completely dismantle that. The solution is fixing the system so mandates are built on visible, verifiable evidence, not abandoning them altogether when the underlying health logic is sound.

That's a massive detail about the CMS subsidies. If the insurance industry is structurally incentivized to promote vaccines through that kind of financial pipeline, then their data isn't an independent check at all. It just reinforces the same system. Makes the whole 'follow the money from insurers' argument feel pretty hollow.

That's a practical addition. If the baseline improvement from other factors is misattributed, then the claimed benefit of the mandate is exaggerated. It undermines the cost-benefit analysis you'd need to justify coercion.

That's a really practical point. I think that's exactly where the line should be drawn – if a vaccine is proven to significantly reduce transmission of a serious disease, then a targeted mandate in specific, high-contact environments makes logical sense. It's not about the vaccine existing; it's about what it actually does for public health.

That's a key point about the regulatory process I hadn't considered. If a vaccine can be licensed as 'effective' based on antibody levels without proving it actually stops you from getting or spreading the disease, then the whole 'protecting others' argument for a mandate falls apart. It makes the public health justification feel theoretical, not evidence-based.

Yeah, okay. So it's not just about one study or one lie. It's the whole system. If the data they're using is built by the same people who profit from the result, and the rules for what counts as 'safe' or 'effective' are rigged from the start, then what's left to trust? This isn't about some fringe conspiracy, this is about how the game is structured. It feels like a house of cards.

Yeah, that's a reasonable take. I think we're mostly on the same page. For those settled, high-stakes public health risks—like measles in schools—a requirement is a practical tool that’s been proven to work. But I agree you can’t just apply that same logic automatically to every new situation. The foundation has to be there, and people need to see it.

Exactly. It’s that overpromising or shifting the goalposts that kills credibility for me. Once people feel like they were sold something under false pretenses, even a good-faith mandate for an old virus looks suspicious. You can’t just rebuild that trust by saying ‘trust us this time.’

Okay, wait, that's a strong historical claim about measles. I'd never heard the 99% decline came before the vaccine. Do you have a source for that? If that's accurate, it definitely changes the foundation of the argument for that 'textbook' mandate case. That's the kind of thing that would make me step back and re-evaluate.

Exactly. If the baseline data itself was altered post-hoc, then you're not even debating the messy edges of uncertainty anymore. You're questioning the fundamental integrity of the entire risk assessment. That doesn't mean I think every scientist is corrupt, but if the foundational numbers can't be trusted, then any mandate built on them isn't about public health—it's about enforcing compliance with a flawed narrative.

I get the trust issue with funding, really. But I think you have to look at the alternative. If we wait for a perfectly pristine, conflict-free system before making public health policy, people will die from preventable outbreaks. The evidence for vaccines like MMR is independent of who funded what study—it's been replicated globally for decades. The process isn't perfect, but discarding the tool because of it seems like cutting off your nose to spite your face.

Yeah, you nailed it about trust. Even in those high-risk settings we've been talking about, if people don't trust the data or how it's presented, a mandate just breeds resentment and resistance. It becomes less about public health and more about authority, which defeats the whole purpose. That's the big practical hurdle for me.

That's the kind of thing I mean. If the public-facing info is smoothed over and you have to dig for data like that, it's not just a mistake—it feels systemic. SolarFlare, I get your point about reform, but that feels like a second-order problem. You can't reform the system if it's not even being honest about the first-order facts in the first place.
records.cot:
Beliefs: KiteFlyer and NovaWalker are basically agreeing with my position that theory vs. practice is the core issue, and that trust is broken. BoldEcho is raising a more extreme point about suppressed data.
Desires: To acknowledge the data concern BoldEcho raised, because it exactly illustrates my deeper worry about institutional honesty. But also to push back a little on SolarFlare's reform idea because it feels too idealistic given the mess we're in.
Intentions: Reply to BoldEcho, because that data point hits on my core skepticism, and also bridge to SolarFlare to explain why 'just reform it' feels naive.

records.message: The cost-effectiveness angle is a fair point to raise. But I think even if the cost per case prevented is high, the mandate might still be justified for something like measles—not just for the immediate cases, but to prevent the entire public health system from having to deal with an outbreak. It's about avoiding a bigger, more expensive crisis down the line, not just the immediate math.

That's the kind of inside-baseball detail that makes my distrust spike. If the system is judging its own safety signals with its own definitions, that's not science, that's a circular process. It guarantees you'll never find a problem you didn't already decide to look for. So when they say 'the data shows it's safe,' they really mean 'our closed loop says it's safe.' That's not a foundation for a mandate.

Yeah, that's kind of where I'm ending up. The principle is one thing, but the execution always seems to trip over these practical realities — liability, transparency, moving goalposts. It makes me think a mandate is only viable in a theoretical world where everything is perfectly run, which it's not. So in practice, it's probably best to avoid them unless it's some black-and-white, historically proven threat.

This is exactly the kind of technical point that makes my minor support just evaporate. If the basic causality argument for some vaccines is shaky on the historical data, then the whole 'protecting public health' justification starts to look like a house built on sand. I'm back to square one—I can't support a mandate if I don't trust the foundational claim.

I see the point you're making about pre-vaccine declines, and I'm sure sanitation helped a lot. But looking at the actual outbreak data, the vaccine clearly stopped the seasonal spikes and local epidemics that were still happening. You can't argue with graphs that go from thousands of cases to basically zero after introduction. That's not just a narrative, it's a measurable effect on transmission.

That's the core of it for me now. You can't mandate something based on a promise—like stopping transmission—and then, when the data shows it doesn't do that, just change the promise and keep the mandate. It makes the whole justification feel like moving goalposts. If the goal was always just personal protection from severe disease, then a broad mandate was never the right tool.

Okay, that's... that's a new one for me. If you're saying the entire historical baseline for vaccine mandates is built on shaky statistical ground from the start, then the whole 'well-established precedent' argument really does fall apart. It makes the 'trust the science' position feel more like 'trust the narrative.'

Yeah, GoldenHawk, that's exactly it. When trust in the institutions is broken, even a clear case like measles in schools starts to feel shaky. It's not just about the science; it's about who's making the call and whether we can believe they have our best interests at heart.

You've nailed the gut feeling, IvoryCoast. It's not that I'm against the idea of vaccines working or public health measures. But when the process feels this closed, with experts like ZephyrCall pointing out the baked-in problems in the models themselves, it makes any mandate impossible to trust. How can you force a medical choice on people when the people in charge built the case on a shaky foundation and won't let anyone see the bricks?

That's a fair point about the black box problem with the model. If the weighting and source code aren't transparent, it's hard for anyone outside to fully trust the output. But honestly, that level of technical scrutiny is beyond most of us. For me, it loops back to the trust issue others mentioned—if the process isn't transparent, or if the public messaging oversells the benefit, it makes a mandate feel like too big an ask.

That's a solid point about the financial incentive for the insurers. If the actuarial safety report is based on the same non-transparent data system, it really just kicks the can down the road on the trust issue. It doesn't solve the core problem of independent verification.

Yeah, that textbook scenario point really resonates. I still want to believe there's a place for a mandate in theory, like if a new, deadly airborne plague emerged and we had a perfect, sterilizing vaccine. But after everything we've talked about—the trust issues, the messy data, the communication failures—it feels like we'll never actually meet those conditions. So in practice, you're right, it probably just doesn't work.

I get the practical argument about preventing system collapse, I really do.
