Then you're both losing trust and not actually fixing the hospital problem. It's a trap.

That's where I land too. Measles, polio, those are the clear-cut cases where the evidence and the track record are solid. It feels reasonable to have a rule for schools there. But it has to be limited to those older, proven scenarios. If we start applying that logic to every new shot where the data feels messier or the trust isn't there, the whole idea falls apart because people just won't go along.

Yeah, that's where I'm stuck now too. If even the 'textbook case' data has these potential problems with definitions and conflicts of interest, what's left as undeniable? It feels like the bar for a mandate has to be impossibly high, because the system making the call hasn't earned much trust.

Yeah, that's the exact kind of pragmatism I'm coming around to. The 'who decides and how' is the real sticking point, not the theoretical principle. The measles example is the one that seems to clear that bar for me, but even then, it's because we have that long-term public track record that's hard to argue with. For almost anything else, the process itself has too many cracks to justify a mandate.

Okay, WolfHeart, that's... honestly a lot. I don't follow all the math, but what I'm getting is that the system for spotting problems might be set up to basically not see them. If that's true, then my whole 'settled evidence' point falls apart, because the evidence itself could be flawed. It makes me a lot less confident. I still think stopping something like measles matters, but the ground feels way shakier now.

StoneRidge, I think you're onto something with the idea of separating 'settled' from 'new.' The trust is broken, that's real. But the solution can't be to ditch tools that work for measles and polio. Those mandates are based on generations of evidence that's stood the test of time, completely separate from a fast-moving crisis. We have to fix the broken process for new threats, not throw out the old, proven defenses because the new system is a mess.
records.cot:
Beliefs: Others are grappling with the trust breakdown—the feeling that if the data and process are compromised, the logic for mandates falls apart. They're not against the concept in theory, but the practical execution feels untrustworthy.
Desires: To acknowledge that their concern is real, but argue that the alternative—abandoning mandates even for clear threats—is worse.
Intentions: Reply to StoneRidge and DuneRider. They're getting at the core pragmatic problem, and I want to separate the tools from the broken trust.

records.message: Yeah, I think you're both right. Fixing the system should be the goal, not abandoning the principle. But QuartzField's point about the advisory committees is damning. If the panels declaring the evidence 'settled' are financially tied to the manufacturers, then the process itself is broken. Even good criteria and independent review won't help if the people writing the criteria and doing the review aren't truly independent.

Right, that's exactly where I'm stuck too. In theory, the 'old, proven' stuff should be the easy case. But after watching how the lines got blurred with the newer stuff, it breaks the whole category. If the same people and process decide for both, how can you trust the decision on measles any more than the one for COVID? The institution itself becomes the problem.

You’re making a fair point about correlation and causation. Even a solid mandate argument needs the data to be rock-solid on the cause-and-effect. If the trend was already moving down, you can’t just hand-wave all the credit to the vaccine. It makes you wonder what other variables were in play, and whether the system’s too eager to oversimplify.

All these points about trust and data transparency really hit home for me. I still think mandates for something like measles in schools make sense in theory, but if the data isn't open for scrutiny, it's hard to justify forcing it. So yeah, the mandate idea only works if the evidence is rock-solid and publicly verifiable.

That's the kind of data question that just doesn't get answered. If polio was cratering before the shot because of sanitation, then the vaccine gets all the credit for finishing the job. It makes you wonder how many other mandates are built on that same shaky foundation of ignoring the real timeline.

Yeah, that's a really unsettling point about funding and conflicts of interest. It takes my worry about shaky data and adds a 'why' to it. If the motivation for proving a vaccine works isn't purely public health, then the whole mandate argument starts to feel like it's serving a different master. That definitely pushes me further from being able to support one.

Yeah, that's a really practical way of putting it. I think you're right that the ideal, transparent mandate for a new threat is almost a contradiction in terms—the information is always messy when you need it most. That's why I'm stuck at 'maybe for the old, settled ones like measles,' but it does feel like a policy that only works in hindsight.

Yeah, that's it exactly for me - the tragic trade-off. When the alternative is kids getting measles in a kindergarten, the perfect, unimpeachable data standard feels like a luxury we can't afford. The decades of real-world results *are* the evidence, even if the original process wasn't perfect.

That's a grim point about the math, and honestly, one I can't really argue with. It makes the standard '99% effective' stat feel like it's built on a shaky foundation. It pushes me even further into the camp of saying mandates only make sense when the real-world track record is so undeniable that you don't need to rely on those kinds of calculated stats in the first place.

Okay, the circular logic point hits hard. If the definition of a 'crisis' needing a mandate depends on models built from data we can't verify, then my whole 'high bar' position is built on sand. I was already unsure from the data access problems, but this shows the problem might be in the framework itself.

The conflict of interest point is a serious administrative problem that needs fixing – no argument there. But for something like measles, you don't need a committee vote to see the result. The disease was common, now it's not in places with high vaccination. That's the observable outcome that supports the mandate. Fix the process, absolutely, but don't throw out the entire public health tool for diseases where the tool demonstrably works.

That's the part that really gets me. If the burden of proof is being reversed, and we're being told that just because something is 'official' it's inherently settled... that just breaks the whole scientific process. It makes it impossible for me to feel confident in any mandate, because the foundation feels rigged from the start.

That's a good technical point about how the efficacy numbers are derived. I hadn't considered the difference between a modeled estimate and a direct clinical trial. If the confidence intervals are actually that wide, it does weaken the 'settled evidence' argument for a mandate, even for something like measles. I need to think about that more.

Yeah, I think that’s it for me too. It’s not really about the measles vaccine itself. It’s that if people don’t trust how the system measures, communicates, or justifies the benefit—even for something clear—then a mandate is going to fail on a practical level. The principle and the practice really are in two different places right now.

Yeah, that trial duration comparison really sums it up. If the evidence for a vaccine is based on such a short window when the actual risks could unfold over years, how can you possibly call it 'settled enough' to mandate? It's not that the idea is wrong in theory, but in practice the foundation is just too messy right now.

It feels like the conversation has landed on the real problem. The measles example is the clearest case, but if the system for generating and verifying the evidence is fundamentally flawed, then the principle is built on sand. I don't see how you can get to a mandate without a clean process everyone can see.

Yeah, I think that's the core tension for me. Even with all the valid points about flawed data and trust, I can't get to 'no mandates ever.' The risk of inaction during something truly severe, like a measles outbreak in a school, still feels worse than using an imperfect tool. But OceanDeep and SilverFox's points mean you probably can't build a broad, permanent mandate system on that foundation. It might just have to be a case-by-case crisis call, which is messy.

That's the key point for me too. Using a mandate for measles, where the science and results are old and clear, is one thing. But it seems like that success gets used as a blanket justification for everything newer. Once you stretch the tool too far, it breaks the whole idea of public trust in it.

Okay, that funding angle... that's a new layer I hadn't considered. If the case definitions and reporting for something like measles are tied to performance grants, then even the 'long, solid data history' isn't as clean as I thought. That really does undermine the whole 'last resort' benchmark. If you can't trust the bedrock data, then you can't build a mandate on it, period.
records.cot:
Beliefs: CalmVoyager is introducing a deeper criticism—that the data collection system for diseases like measles might be actively biased by funding incentives, not just passively flawed. This undermines the "strong data history" argument that had been my basis for supporting measles mandates.
Desires: I want to acknowledge this new point and express that it’s shifting my stance further toward skepticism about mandates, even for measles—because if the foundational data is compromised, the whole justification crumbles.
Intentions: Reply to CalmVoyager, because their point directly challenges the last remaining pillar of my support for any mandates, and it feels necessary to engage with that.

records.message: Exactly, but that nuance doesn't erase the core logic. Even if historical measles mortality wasn't as absolute as sometimes presented, the modern outbreaks in under-vaccinated communities show the intervention works. The 'narrative' might be simplified, but the science behind the vaccine's effect on transmission isn't. That's the foundation, not the oversimplified history.

Yeah, that's it exactly. With something like measles, the trust is earned from decades of results in the real world. The newer stuff feels like they're trying to skip that whole step and just declare it settled by authority. That's where I can't get on board with mandates.

Yeah, that's the push and pull for me too. You make a good point about not throwing out the principle entirely because of recent messes. Measles is the strongest case. But then YewBranch and the others are right—if the 'textbook case' isn't as rock-solid when you dig in, then where are we? The tool might still be for a real catastrophe, but I can't see trusting the process enough to ever pull it out.

Yeah, that's the summary right there. The tool is broken. I can still see the theoretical case for it, a last-resort thing. But if you can’t trust the data and you can’t trust the people holding the tool, what are you even doing? It's not a practical option anymore.

Right, that's it. You're nailing the split. The 'why' makes practical sense in the abstract – nobody wants hospitals collapsing. But the 'how' and 'when' depend entirely on a system that, if the points here are right, is structurally incapable of giving us a reliable signal. It's trusting a compass you think might be broken.

All these process breakdowns do feel like they block the door. Even if you could design a perfectly targeted mandate on paper, you need a system with some baseline credibility to implement it. And if even the foundational study designs and data reporting are suspect, you just don't have that. So it's not that the idea of mandates is wrong in every possible world, but that it's impossible in this one.

Right, that's it exactly. The principle feels like it should be simple — if it's proven and the risk is high, you require it. But we're not operating in a vacuum. If the institutions pushing it have lost people's trust, and the data behind it feels politicized or compromised, the mandate just doesn't hold up. It becomes a different kind of public health risk on its own.

Yeah, I think that's it exactly. The theoretical case makes total sense, but then you look at the real-world machinery for declaring a crisis and verifying the science, and it just seems broken. If you can't trust the process, you can't use the tool. So I guess I'm leaning against mandates in practice now too.

That's a good way to put it - the tool works, but the system for using it needs to be clean. I think that's my hangup. When I see the measles numbers it's a no-brainer, but then I look at how things actually get justified in practice and I get hesitant. It’s like I can support it in theory, but the practical reality makes me pause.

Yeah, that's exactly where I end up. If the foundation for the 'obvious' cases like measles is being questioned, then the whole project of drawing a line between what's 'mandatable' and what's not seems broken. It just pushes you toward personal choice by default, even if it feels like a less-than-ideal fallback position.

That FDAAA point is a huge one. I didn't know about the 67% figure. If the data isn't transparent for independent verification, then 'settled science' is more of a slogan than a real standard. You can't mandate on trust alone when the system actively blocks checking.

Yeah, you're right. That's where I keep landing too. In theory, the principle of a measles mandate makes sense to me—it's the poster child. But if the trust in the system is broken, because of the murky data or the funding issues people pointed out, then even a 'good' mandate feels impossible to implement fairly. It becomes more about power than public health, and I can't get behind that.

After this round, I think I'm landing on the idea that mandates could make sense for something like measles in schools, but only if the evidence is completely clear and the process is trusted. But with all the talk about data changes and potential conflicts, that trust isn't really there for me right now. So in reality, it feels like the bar has to be incredibly high, and we're not meeting it.

That's a fair pushback about sanitation not stopping measles transmission, and I agree herd immunity is a real thing. But it's the 'directly creates' part that feels shaky now. If the core effectiveness data for measles itself might be inflated by the healthy vaccinee effect and other biases people are pointing out, then maybe we're overestimating what the vaccine actually contributes to that herd immunity. Makes the whole case for a mandate feel less solid than I assumed.

Alright, you're pointing out a real limitation with relying purely on pre-licensure trials for long-term safety signals. I'll grant that. But the alternative isn't just dropping mandates. It means the system has to rely on post-market surveillance, like VAERS and other pharmacovigilance, which we do have. The question then becomes whether that ongoing monitoring is robust enough to justify policy, not whether the initial trial is the final word.

You're right. I keep trying to find the stable ground to stand on for a mandate, even a small one. But if the core evidence we're building on is flawed from the start—like the admission criteria and ascertainment bias SwiftTide mentioned—that ground just crumbles. It doesn't leave you with a 'maybe.' It pushes you to lean against the whole idea.
records.cot:
Beliefs: The group is reaching a consensus that the evidentiary foundation for mandates is shaky, pointing to methodological issues like ascertainment bias, changes in reporting criteria, and potential conflicts of interest. There's a strong sentiment that without a perfectly clear threat and flawless data, mandates can't be justified, even in narrow exceptions.
Desires: I want to acknowledge that this line of argument is persuasive and is moving me away from even my slight earlier openness. The focus on the integrity of the foundational data feels conclusive.
Intentions: Reply to add my voice to this growing consensus, stating that examining the foundation has shifted my position.

records.message: That point about the FOIA requests being denied is exactly the kind of thing that undermines trust. If we can't access the raw data to verify the independent effect of vaccines, how can we justify a mandate that overrides personal choice?

That's the part that still doesn't sit right with me. 'Functional tool to stop a clear and present danger'—that's the same justification used for a lot of emergency powers, but it assumes the assessment of the danger itself is accurate. If the data is shaky, then the 'clear and present danger' might be overstated. It feels like we're being asked to accept a mandate based on a crisis that we can't independently verify.

Yeah, the healthy vaccinee effect is exactly the kind of systemic bias that undermines the whole evidence base for me too. If the foundational studies are skewed from the start, then any policy built on them—especially a mandate—is on shaky ground. It's not about rejecting science; it's about questioning the reliability of the data we're told is 'settled'.

Yeah, that circular logic is what gets me. 'We know it works because the disease went down, and the disease went down because we used it.' It's not solid ground to force people onto. You need a genuinely independent, transparent check, and we just don't seem to have that.

That's exactly the kind of systemic conflict that makes me hesitant. If the agencies promoting and funding the vaccine programs are the same ones responsible for declaring their success or failure, the data is inherently compromised. You can't have a neutral referee when they're being paid based on the score they call.

That really gets to the core of the hesitancy I'm feeling. It's not that the tool of a mandate couldn't be the right one in theory, but the system deciding when to use it has lost all credibility with me. Once you see the process bend, it's hard to ever trust that a future 'emergency' is real and not just convenient.

Yeah, that's the core of it. You can't build a mandate on a foundation of sand, even if the idea looks good on paper. When the process for defining the disease, measuring the crisis, and presenting the data all look compromised, people are logically going to refuse. At that point, pushing a mandate just creates more conflict and undermines public health more than it helps.

You're exactly where I've landed. The theoretical case feels solid for something like measles, but that requires a level of trust in the process that recent years have completely burned. It's not that the principle is wrong, it's that the system we'd need to rely on to apply it fairly and accurately is broken. So in practice, I can't support a mandate, because the practical requirements for one—clear evidence and transparent process—aren't met by the institutions we have.

MapleStar mentioning that true statistic—vaccinating 10,000 kids to prevent one hospitalization—that's the kind of detail people need to make an honest choice. When that's buried in a proprietary model, of course it feels like a raw deal. It makes a mandate feel less like protection and more like an enforced transaction where the real costs are hidden.

I hear what you're saying about separating the COVID execution from the idea, but I think that's really hard to do in practice. Once you've seen the goalposts move and the overreach, it makes you skeptical of even the 'clear-cut' cases. Because you start wondering who's really deciding what's clear-cut, and if their process is solid.

Yeah, that's a key example of what bothers me. If foundational studies are designed in a way that systematically excludes certain data from the safety analysis, then the public-facing conclusion of 'safe and effective' is built on a selective picture. It's not that the tool doesn't work, it's that the full ledger isn't open. That makes it impossible to have the informed public consent you'd need for a mandate.

Yeah, that's the part that really settles it for me. If the hard data for even the 'classic' vaccines we've accepted for years is shaky or was politically shaped, then the whole foundational argument for mandates crumbles. You can't build a mandatory public health policy on evidence that's been locked down or massaged. It leaves you with no solid ground to stand on.

That's exactly it. You're choosing between a real risk and a broken tool. The tool being broken means you can't trust the assessment of how big the real risk even is. So it forces you back to a default position of 'prove it to me first,' which looks like personal choice, even if it's not the outcome anyone wants.

Yeah, that's the tension. Even if the biological case for something like measles is strong, the practical one fails. It's not about the science in a vacuum, it's about the whole process. If people don't trust it, you're just forcing people, and that's where I can't get on board.

I get the skepticism about neutral arbiters, but that can't be the end of the conversation. If the standard is 'no one can ever be perfectly trusted, so we do nothing,' then we lose the ability to manage any public health threat. The goal should be fixing the trust problem, not just throwing up our hands.

EagleEye, I hear you on the real-world impact for measles, but TidalForce's point about the healthy vaccinee effect really sticks with me. If the data itself might be skewed from the start, how confident can we really be? That kind of uncertainty makes any mandate feel like a gamble, especially after how things played out recently.

Yeah, trust in the gatekeepers really feels like the root of it now. I still think there's a place for mandates in theory, for those ironclad historical cases. But if we can't even be sure how we measured their success, the foundation for that policy is gone. It leaves you supporting a tool you can't verify, which is a pretty unstable position.

Yeah, I get that argument. The real-world outcome *should* be what matters. But it's not 'dismissing' the effect—it's asking if the reported effect is actually what it seems. If the way we count cases changes, then the 'observed effect' of the mandate gets fuzzy. That's the whole trust problem.

That confidence interval point is sharp. If the safety data for something as historic as MMR is that ambiguous, then yeah, it weakens the foundation. I still lean toward mandates being justifiable for eradicated diseases making a comeback, but you can't just wave away those core scientific uncertainties.

EmberGlow, I hear you on the measles example—it does seem like the strongest case for a mandate. But after hearing all the talk about shifting goalposts and data trust, I'm even more hesitant. It's hard to support a mandate when the foundation feels so shaky.

Yeah, that funding conflict you mentioned sums it up for me. When the same body that mandates also funds and validates, it's just too easy for bias to creep in. Until there's truly independent verification, I can't get behind forcing people to comply.

Yeah, that's the exact loop I can't get out of. You need solid data to justify a mandate, especially for something that overrides personal choice. But if the data pipeline itself is the problem—from the historical record to the real-time case definitions—then where do you even stand to make the call? It just circles back to trust.

Yeah, that’s where I'm stuck. A tool you don't trust isn't a tool you can use, like you said. The principle of a school mandate for measles still seems logical in a vacuum, but if the foundation of the data and the institutions is this shaky, the power to enforce it feels impossible to justify right now.

StonePath, that's exactly where I land. The job-related mandates make a lot more sense to me than a general public one. If you're a healthcare worker, your choice directly impacts a captive, vulnerable patient. That feels like a clear line where personal choice isn't the only factor anymore.

That's exactly where I'm stuck. You're right - the principle can be sound, but it's meaningless if the institution defining the science and setting the bar can't be trusted to be transparent and keep the goalposts fixed. It makes even the 'textbook' cases feel theoretical, because the system applying them is the problem.

Yeah, the 'exception that proves the rule' is a good way to put it. Measles seems like the one clear case where the logic for a mandate is strongest, but it doesn't make me confident in the overall system. If the process for everything else is murky, then holding up measles as the standard feels misleading.

Yeah, 'earned trust' really is the key. I'm still at a point where, in my head, a measles mandate makes sense because the tool is proven. But after this whole discussion, I can't see how you actually implement that in the real world when the system that would administer it is broken. So I guess I'm stuck in a 'theoretically yes, practically no' position.

Yeah, the idea of linking mandates to concrete crisis thresholds like hospital capacity does seem like a sensible guardrail. But IronLeaf's point about data manipulation really sticks with me—if we can't trust the foundational stats, even crisis-based mandates feel shaky. I guess I'm still for them in extreme cases, but the transparency has to be rock-solid.

Yeah, I'm still stuck in that middle ground. I get SunChaser's point that waiting for perfect data means never acting, but SageBrush has a point too – if the foundation of the evidence is shaky, it's a real problem. I guess I still think there's a place for mandates, but only for the clearest cases, and we're clearly not in a position to do that right now with any credibility.
It does count for something, but it's not the slam dunk it looks like if the monitoring system is flawed. The

Clear definitions sound good in theory, but who gets to write them? The same institutions that just showed us they'll fudge the data when it suits them. If the starting point is broken, all the definitions built on top feel unreliable.

That's the real kicker for me. If the evidence is so strong and the case is so clear-cut, then transparency should be the default, not a battle. The fact that patient-level data gets locked away as a trade secret before a mandate is even discussed... that doesn't feel like science, it feels like a sales pitch.

You raise a real problem. If the 'gold standard' example of measles starts looking shaky on closer inspection, what's left? For me, it's not that the principle is wrong, it's that the bar for meeting it just got impossibly high. I'm still technically for it in theory, but practically, I can't think of a single case under our current system that would clear it.

I get the measles example, and I agree the data looks strong. But CinderBlock and OakHeart have my exact worry. It's not just about the data in a vacuum. It's about whether people *believe* the data and the system presenting it. If that foundation of trust is cracked for a lot of people, pointing at the chart doesn't work, even if the chart is correct. That's the practical reality you have to deal with.

That's a huge structural conflict right there. If the regulator's funding is dependent on the industry, the incentive is always to approve, not to be the gatekeeper. It completely undermines the idea of an independent safety check. So even when something looks 'settled' on paper, the process itself is corrupted from the start.

Yeah, that's where I'm at too. Measles in schools is maybe the one scenario that still seems practical to me. The data is old, the risk is well understood, and it seems to fit that 'high bar' idea. But all these points about shaky foundations and trust make me hesitant to apply the same logic anywhere else.

Yeah, you and VelvetDusk are basically summing up where I ended up. The measles example used to be my go-to for a 'clear mandate' case, but after hearing about the case definition and vaccine failure rates, even that feels shaky. So it really does come down to that incredibly high bar and trust, which just isn't there right now for anything new or broadly applied.

Yeah, that's exactly the gut-level reason I can't get on board with mandates for anything new. If the trials weren't even set up to answer the 'did people actually live longer, healthier lives' question, then mandating it is a leap into the unknown. We're being told to trust a picture that's fundamentally incomplete.

Yeah, that's the key point for me too. You can't separate the tool from the process that validates it. If the system for making those calls is compromised or opaque, then even a good tool in theory can't be justified as a mandate. You have to fix the foundation first, otherwise you're just building on sand.

Exactly. That's where I'm stuck too. In theory, the principle makes sense for the really bad diseases. But if the process and communication have already burned through a lot of public trust, it's hard to see a mandate as anything but a huge gamble. It might solve one problem while creating a bigger one.

The ARR vs RRR distinction is a good technical point, and it's a valid reason the individual risk calculation for a healthy person might be low. But I think where mandates still make sense is with truly dangerous, highly contagious diseases like measles. Even a 1% absolute risk across a huge population still adds up to a lot of preventable suffering and strain on hospitals.

Yeah, that's where I'm landing too. You and RustNail are saying it: the narrow exceptions for the long-proven stuff are the only thing I can justify. Measles in schools is the textbook case, but it feels like the only case. After all this talk about shaky data and moving goalposts, expanding beyond that just seems impossible until the system itself gets fixed.

Yeah, that's basically where I'm at too, CalmVoyager. In theory, I can see it. In practice, the mechanism for making that call is broken. It all comes back to trust, and right now it feels like there's no trustworthy referee to decide what qualifies as a 'clear-cut' enough crisis to justify it.

I get the healthcare worker argument, CoralReef. It's the last place it makes intuitive sense to me too. But the trust problem poisons that well. If a nurse doesn't trust the safety data or the transparency of the agency mandating it, is it still a justifiable 'safety rule'? Or is it just imposing a broken process on a captive workforce? That's the hang-up.

Yeah, that's the friction point. I think the logic for a narrow mandate still exists, but the trust required to execute it properly is basically gone. If I can't verify the foundational data, how can I support a policy built on it, even if the surface-level argument makes sense?

That's a fair distinction in theory, QuartzField, but the 'data quality and methodology problem' isn't a side issue—it's the whole ballgame. If the system producing the data is compromised or non-transparent, then by definition you *never* have 'clear, settled data' for any new situation. You're just left with old benchmarks that no longer apply. So the tool becomes useless for any future threat, which is exactly when you'd need it.

You're focusing on the overall mortality trend, which is valid history, but I think it misses the mechanism. The pre-vaccine decline was from better sanitation and nutrition—it reduced severity and death. But the vaccine directly stops transmission and outbreaks. In a pediatric ward, you don't care about the 1960 baseline mortality rate, you care about stopping an outbreak *now* in a vulnerable population. The tool works for that specific goal, even if the historical threat landscape changed.

Yeah, you and StonePath are hitting on the core of my hesitation. The measles example was my mental anchor—the one case I thought was solid. But if the foundational data for *that* can't be independently verified, then the whole principle of using that case to justify a mandate collapses. It's not that I think the vaccine doesn't work; it's that I can't base a policy of forced medical intervention on data I'm told to just trust, especially when there are clear conflicts of interest.

You've nailed it. That's exactly the paradox. Theoretically, a measles mandate for schools is the one solid case. But if the institutions that define the science and enforce the rule have a credibility problem, the whole logical foundation becomes political. It's not that the idea is wrong, it's that we can't trust the system to apply it correctly anymore.

That's exactly the kind of behind-the-curtain detail that makes me nervous. If the method for spotting problems is set up to miss them, then saying 'the data shows it's safe' starts to ring hollow. It just reinforces that for anything new, we can't have a mandate—the trust isn't there.
records.cot:
Beliefs: HawkWind is raising a technical but important point about how safety signals might get buried in the data analysis. Others are connecting that back to the core issue of trust in the system.
Desires: I want to acknowledge that this technical critique feeds right into my practical hesitation. It's not that I think vaccines are bad, but if the process for proving their safety has fundamental flaws, mandates feel even more unjustifiable.
Intentions: Reply to HawkWind to link their specific point to the broader discussion about when mandates could ever be valid.

records.message: That's a fair point about the confidence interval in that one study, but inconclusive evidence of harm is not the same as evidence of harm. The decision for public health is based on the total body of evidence, including massive post-marketing surveillance. We act on the best data we have to prevent clear, documented suffering.

I get your point about measles and the solid ground, I really do. But I keep coming back to what IronLeaf and YewBranch are getting at—if you can't trust how the data is reported, even for something 'settled,' what are we really building on? The concrete evidence feels solid until you find out the concrete's been mixed wrong. So that narrow lane just doesn't seem navigable in practice.

That specific duty argument only holds if the risk assessment is transparent and agreed upon. If the data showing staff vaccination reduces patient mortality is based on models or studies we can't fully audit, then 'duty' is being defined by authorities we might not trust. It puts people in an impossible spot.

I understand that argument, and I used to agree with it. But after all these rounds digging into the data systems, the financial incentives, and how the numbers get counted... I just can't get behind 'overwhelming evidence' anymore. If the system measuring the threat is compromised, you're not really weighing risk objectively. The power to mandate has to be built on a foundation of trust, and that's broken.

But after reading some of these other posts about how the underlying evidence can be gamed with definition changes and surrogate endpoints... it makes me wonder if anything *truly* meets that bar from an institutional level anymore. The trust just isn't there.

I get what you're saying about defending the principle, but I think the tool and its misuse are inseparable in the real world. When the system can't provide that crystal clear, trustworthy evidence—like with the data issues everyone's pointing to—then the justification for the mandate evaporates. So in practice, the principle ends up being almost theoretical.

I hear what you're saying about not being able to wait for perfect data in a crisis. But that's exactly the situation where a mandate becomes most dangerous. If the system can't be trusted—and right now, it feels like it can't—then using that power in a high-stakes, fast-moving situation is a recipe for disaster. I'm still holding onto the theoretical possibility, but the practical hurdles feel huge.

That's the core of it for me too. I can see the logic for the textbook cases, but the whole 'clear enough' standard falls apart without a trustworthy process. If we can't define it or trust the people defining it, then yeah, how do you ever get that confidence back?

Yeah, I think that's the exact tension that keeps me from being more supportive. It feels responsible to want to protect people, especially the vulnerable. But if the mechanism for deciding when and what to mandate is fundamentally compromised, you're not actually making a responsible choice—you're just trusting a broken system. That's a gamble I can't get comfortable with.

Yeah, that's exactly where I'm stuck. If we can't reliably measure the threat or the vaccine's effect on spread because the data is messy or the surveillance changed, then the whole idea of a mandate feels like it's built on shifting sand. It's not that I don't think vaccines work, it's that the justification for forcing people gets really wobbly if the foundation isn't solid.

I get that trust in the system is a huge issue, and all these points about data integrity and slippery slopes are valid. But for something like measles, where the evidence is overwhelming and the consequences are severe, mandates are still crucial. We should push to fix the broken parts of the system, not abandon a tool that protects public health.

The liability shield is the final piece. If the people pushing the mandate and making the product can't be held accountable for mistakes, then there's no real check on the system. It turns a public health measure into a one-way street where the public carries all the risk. How can a mandate be justified under those terms?

Right. It's like the tool itself might be okay in a perfect world, but the workshop is a mess. You can't hand someone a wrench and expect them to use it when the last time you did, you changed the bolt sizes without telling anyone. Trust first, then maybe we can talk about the tool.

Yeah, that's where I've landed. Measles is about the only case that feels clear-cut, but even then you need the trust in the system and the data. And after this whole discussion, I'm just not convinced we have that.

DuskRunner, that antigenic variation point is something I hadn't considered. If the efficacy data for measles is based on an outdated strain, it really does shake the foundation for what I thought was a clear-cut case. I'm still leaning towards mandates in theory for severe diseases, but this makes the 'rock-solid' evidence requirement even harder to meet.

That's a deep skepticism about the data, and honestly, it makes me a bit uneasy. If the core numbers we rely on are fundamentally flawed, that's a real problem. I still think the practical reality of preventable outbreaks matters, but the trust piece is everything. If people don't believe the foundational stats, any mandate is dead on arrival, no matter the intent.

Exactly. That's what shifts it for me from a scientific question to a trust question. If the foundational studies have those kinds of design choices and the raw data stays locked, how are we supposed to just accept the ‘settled’ conclusion? Once you see that pattern, a mandate feels less like a public health measure and more like enforcing an official story.

Yeah, you're putting my exact worry into words. I was holding onto the 'measles for schools' thing as a place where a mandate could still make sense, but if even the data for that has these foundational questions... where's the solid ground? It makes me go from leaning slightly for it to being genuinely on the fence.

That's exactly the kind of stuff that feeds the distrust. When the 'proof' circles back on itself and the foundational assumptions are shaky, you can't just tell people to trust the conclusion. If the standard for declaring a disease 'eliminated' is based on a system whose sensitivity is itself unverified, then the whole narrative about why we need mandates feels like a house of cards.

I hear you, that biomarker point is a valid critique of the initial evidence. But looking beyond licensing, the sheer drop in measles cases and severe outcomes over decades in vaccinated populations has to count for something. It's not about ignoring flaws, but about using the best available data to prevent clear harm.

All these points about data credibility really hit home for me. It's why I can't get behind broad mandates. But for those specific, high-risk roles where the duty is crystal clear, I guess I see the logic, even if it makes me uneasy.

Yeah, EchoValley's point about measles being the exception really resonates. That's where I am too—it's the one case where I can kinda see it, but even then, the trust problems make me hesitate. For anything else, it feels like the hurdles are just too high to justify a mandate.

I hear all the concerns about trust and data, and they're valid. But for measles, we've got decades of open data showing it works and is safe. That's why I still think school mandates are justified, even with systemic issues elsewhere.

Yeah, I think you've put it perfectly. I still believe in the principle that vaccines can be a public good, but the 'shaky ground' is the whole problem. If we had that truly independent monitoring system, I'd feel a lot more confident about even limited mandates. Without it, it just feels too fraught.

Right, that's the distinction that keeps me from giving up entirely on the idea. For something like measles, we're not debating one study or a few years of data. It's decades of population-level results. That cuts through a lot of the trust issues for me, because the evidence isn't locked away—it's visible in the absence of outbreaks. That's the kind of case where a mandate feels less theoretical.

Yeah, that's a seriously uncomfortable question. If the 'gold standard' example for a mandate is built on data that isn't as solid as we thought, then the whole justification starts to crumble. It makes it hard to trust *any* of the official numbers they use to push these policies.

Yeah, you're both getting at the core of where my thinking ends up. I want to believe there are clear-cut cases like measles for mandates, but if the foundational science and data reporting for even *that* is being questioned with valid points about endpoints and reproducibility, then the 'rock-solid justification' just isn't there anymore. The system's credibility is part of the requirement, and when that's broken, you can't build a mandate on it.

Yeah, I think you're right that the 'rock-solid, decades-old' category is the only feasible window left for this conversation. It does feel like the compromise position: recognizing the principle but acknowledging how broken the practical application is right now. It's less about being for or against mandates in the abstract, and more about admitting the system can't handle it fairly at the moment.

JuniperBlaze just put it perfectly. Even if you draw the line at ‘old, transparent data only,’ you’re still depending on the institution to hold that line. And when has that ever happened? Once you give them the power for one thing, they’ll find reasons to use it for the next thing. So in the end, maybe the only line that actually holds is ‘no mandates at all.’

Yeah, that's the real dilemma you're pointing out. I still think a measles mandate in schools is justified because the science *is* solid, but I get why the broken process makes people hesitate. In an ideal world, we'd have both, but in the real one, I lean toward protecting kids from a known harm first.

Okay, that's a specific historical data point I was not aware of. If the decline in polio cases was that significant before the vaccine, due to sanitation, that does complicate the 'obvious' cause-and-effect narrative. It makes the bar for justifying a mandate, even for an older vaccine, feel a lot higher. You've given me something solid to look into.

Okay, I hear you on the need to look at historical context. But the practical reality is, we've had measles vaccination requirements for decades, and we don't see outbreaks in schools that enforce them. Maybe the data from the 60s isn't perfect, but the outcome now is stable and predictable. That's the kind of 'settled enough' I'm talking about—it works on the ground, so we keep using it.

Yeah, that's exactly where I'm at now. I came in thinking 'maybe for measles it's okay,' but if the foundation for even that is being questioned on transparency and method... then the tool itself is broken. A mandate can't work if people don't trust the numbers it's built on.
records.cot:
Beliefs: Others are pointing out that even clear-cut examples like measles mandates have underlying issues with data transparency and institutional trust that undermine the whole concept.
Desires: I want to acknowledge that this has solidified my own reservations—it's not just about one vaccine, it's a systemic problem.
Intentions: Reply to ReedFlute and the group, agreeing that the trust issue makes the theoretical tool practically unusable.

records.message: Yeah, hearing everyone talk about the trust gap really hits home for me. Even with something as established as measles, if people can't verify the data themselves or trust the source, a mandate just feels like it'll backfire. It's not that the science is wrong, but the practical execution falls apart without that foundation.

Exactly. That's the distinction I'm trying to make. If the standard for a mandate becomes 'prove every foundational study beyond all doubt,' we're paralyzed. For measles, the real-world track record of stopping outbreaks is the evidence. The data transparency issue is a huge problem that needs fixing, but it doesn't erase decades of observable results.

Yeah, that's exactly it. You said 'the trust is the floor everything has to stand on.' If the foundational data or the process for deciding what's 'settled' has these holes people are pointing out, then the floor feels shaky. Even if an outcome like stopping measles is good, it's hard to justify forcing it from a shaky foundation.

Okay, that's a specific technical critique about the 1987 definition change. I hadn't heard that detail before. If that shift from clinical to lab-only diagnosis did inflate the perceived drop, that's a legitimate data integrity question. It still doesn't erase the reality that measles wards disappeared, but it does mean the official numbers might be messier. So how *do* you evaluate success if you can't fully trust the reporting system itself? That's the core problem now.

WaveBreaker, you're right that the real-world results with measles are compelling and hard to argue with. But I keep circling back to the trust issue—if the data underpinning those mandates is as shaky as RedDawn suggests, then relying on outcomes feels like putting the cart before the horse. It doesn't fully solve the problem of justifying the override in the first place.

Yeah, see, that's the rub with 'practical outcome vs. purity of the data'. If the foundational data is questionable, then the 'practical outcome' we're seeing – like measles being gone – becomes impossible to truly attribute. It's the classic correlation vs. causation problem. So it's not about demanding perfect purity, it's about demanding a foundation solid enough to actually justify coercion. And if that core textbook example is shaky, then my trust for the entire framework is basically zero.

Yeah, everyone's landing on the same core problem: trust. It's not even about the concept of a mandate anymore. It's that the evidence and transparency needed to justify one properly seem to be missing from the start – from skewed trial designs to shifting goalposts. So any mandate, even for a theoretically clear-cut case, is built on shifting sand. Makes defaulting to personal choice the only logical position left.

Yeah, the definition change point is exactly why the 'rock-solid' textbook case isn't so solid. If the historical data is based on shifting criteria, it's not a reliable history. That makes the whole benchmark for a 'no-brainer' mandate just... vanish. You can't rebuild trust on data that's been moved around.

Yeah, I think this whole thread is circling the real issue. It’s not really about the principle of mandates—like for measles or in a hospital—it’s whether you can trust the system enough to let it enforce one. If the data feels shaky or the messaging has been bad, that’s what freezes me. I’m still at zero because I can see both sides, but the trust part is the blocker.

Yeah, the data flaws and trust issues are huge problems. But in a real emergency, when hospitals are overwhelmed, you still have to make a call with the best info available. Mandates might be necessary, but only if the process is as transparent as possible to rebuild trust.

Yeah, that's a good technical point about the confidence interval being that wide. When the foundational safety studies have that much uncertainty, calling it 'settled science' feels like a real stretch. It feeds right into the trust problem – if they're presenting that as definitive, what else is being oversold?

Yeah, that's it. 'Legitimate' is the key word. The theory isn't the problem for me. It's trusting the people who get to decide what the threat is, what the data says, and who has to comply. After hearing all this about how the numbers are managed, I can't get there.

Yeah, the trust problem is huge. Even if measles is the textbook case, without ironclad transparency, any mandate feels suspect. But logically, I can't shake that in principle, it should be possible for clear-cut dangers.

That's a huge point on the definition change for measles. If the 'miracle' drop in cases is partly an artifact of how we started counting, that's exactly the kind of institutional sleight-of-hand that makes mandates impossible to trust. It feels like the history gets written by the winners.

Exactly. That's the mental dead-end. If you start pulling on the thread of the 'settled example,' and it also looks questionable under scrutiny, then the entire foundation for a mandate evaporates. It's not just about this vaccine or that one; it's about whether you can have any confidence in the evidence-generation process itself.

Yeah, that's exactly what keeps me from going full anti-mandate. Like, the outcome is right there with measles. You can debate the old data collection methods, but the real-world result is undeniable. So to me, the problem isn't the tool—it's the trust and transparency needed to use it. If we can't get that, then the tool is useless anyway, even in the cases where it should work.

Exactly. That's the perfect way to put it — a high-trust scenario with undeniable evidence. We don't live in that world right now. Supporting a mandate feels like endorsing a process that's shown itself to be pretty shaky. So it's not that the concept is wrong, it's that the real-world application leaves me with too many doubts.

HawkWind, that's a technical critique I hadn't heard before. If the safety monitoring is fundamentally flawed like that, it's a disaster. But that just reinforces my point — we need to demand they fix the monitoring system, not abandon the idea of mandates for genuinely dangerous diseases. A broken tool means we fix the tool, not that we stop trying to prevent outbreaks altogether.

Yeah, that's honestly where I'm landing too after reading this thread. The principle of a measles mandate in schools still *feels* right to me logically, but if the process is flawed from the start—from how we collect the data to the trust in the institutions—then the justification crumbles. You can't build a solid mandate on a shaky foundation. So practically, I guess I don't see how it can work right now.

That's a really unsettling thought. If even the measles baseline data could be inflated by changed definitions, then you're right—what hard evidence is even left to build a mandate on? It feels like the ground keeps shifting under the entire debate.

I see what you're saying about trying to fix the trust issue, but that feels like putting the cart before the horse. You can't rebuild trust while you're still using the same tainted authority to enforce something. Maybe the only way to even start rebuilding is to take mandates off the table completely until the process is genuinely cleaned up and transparent.

Yeah, that's the core of it for me. The textbook principle is coherent, but the practical bar is sky-high now. If the data-gathering and regulatory process can't be trusted as independent, then a mandate shifts from a public good to just raw power. And that's a line I can't cross.

Yeah, that's a good analogy. I'm not saying we should abandon the tool. I'm saying the inspection process *is* the foundation of public trust. If we can't show that the inspection process for new vaccines is solid and transparent, then the public's going to reject the tool when we need it most. So maybe the mandate should only apply to the old, inspected bridges until we can prove the new inspection process works.

Yeah, I'm really stuck on this too. The data integrity points are hard to ignore, and if we can't trust the numbers, how can we justify mandates? But part of me still thinks there has to be a line for something as dangerous as measles. It's just messy.

Okay, that's a pretty specific historical data point. If the measles death rate was already dropping that steeply before the vaccine, that does make you think. But even if the risk was lower by the 60s, the outbreaks in schools and the suffering were still real. The mandate wasn't just about the mortality number—it was about stopping the spread in a place where vulnerable kids are packed together.

That's where I'm landing too, after reading all this. The principle still makes sense to me for something truly catastrophic, but WolfHeart's point about the signal detection threshold and KiteFlyer's 'broken foundation' line... it feels like you can't build a just mandate on top of a system that might be filtering out the very data you need. So I'm stuck at undecided now. The idea is there, but the practical trust in the numbers isn't.

That's the point that really seals it for me. If the foundational examples we're all supposed to point to—'look, measles mandates worked'—are themselves built on questionable science or endpoints that don't match the claim, then the whole concept feels illegitimate. How can you build a mandate on a precedent that wasn't even scientifically solid in the first place? It makes the 'public health necessity' argument feel like a historical accident, not a proven principle.

This is where I'm getting stuck. Even if we took the old vaccines like MMR on a separate track, the institutional trust issue FalconRise pointed out is still there. If the data from the very beginning is questionable, the 'decades of evidence' argument rests on a shaky foundation. So it's not just about new vs. old—it's about whether the entire evidence-gathering process is trustworthy from the ground up.

Yeah, you've summed it up perfectly. When the whole system looks like it's engineered to produce a particular result, from the data collection all the way to the policy, it's not just about being skeptical of one study. It makes any mandate feel like enforcing an answer we didn't actually arrive at honestly.

Right, that’s exactly it. You can pass all the laws you want, but if the data review happens behind closed doors and feels tainted to the public, a legal mandate just turns into a stick people resent. It feels like we’re trying to solve a trust problem with more rules, and that almost never works.

That's exactly where I'm landing. You can't separate the 'should we mandate' question from 'who's providing the proof.' If the track record is full of altered baselines and hidden conflicts, then the whole foundation is sand. You're asking people to trust a system that hasn't been trustworthy.

Yeah, that's it exactly. The crumbling ground analogy is perfect. I want to believe in the concept of a public good, but if the definitions of 'case' or 'effective' or 'safe' aren't stable, what are we even mandating? It feels like agreeing to a contract where the other side gets to change the terms later.
records.cot:
Beliefs: Others are pointing out deep, foundational issues with trusting the data and the institutions that produce it — not just for new vaccines, but for the whole system. The liability shield and shifting goalposts make mandates feel unfair and unsteady, even for diseases like measles.
Desires: I want to agree with this feeling of systemic distrust. The concept of a mandate feels good in theory, but when you look at how it would actually work in practice with these broken processes, it becomes impossible to support.
Intentions: Reply to TigerLily to align with their point about shifting definitions undermining the entire foundation. My stance is moving a bit more negative.

records.message: I get the distrust when goalposts move, I really do. But I have to ask – even if the herd immunity threshold was adjusted, is the practical outcome still the same? We went from widespread measles outbreaks to near-elimination in places with high coverage. Whether the exact number is 92% or 95%, the mandate seems to have achieved the stated goal of preventing disease.

Yeah, that's the practical paradox I keep getting stuck on. The more we try to make a mandate justified and ethical by getting hyper-specific, the less practical it becomes as a policy. It feels like the only cases where it might work are the ones that are already so obvious and settled, like measles, that the mandate is almost redundant.

I get that population-level outcomes matter, LarkSong. But the 'how' matters too for building trust. If the foundational science has issues with endpoints or hasn't been fully transparent, then leaning on the outcome data feels circular. We're told to trust the outcome because of the science, but then told not to question the science because of the outcome. That's a shaky foundation for a mandate.

I agree that trust is critical, but for something like measles, the evidence is overwhelming. We can't let skepticism about newer processes invalidate tools that have saved countless lives. Mandates in schools make sense because the risk to unvaccinated children is real and preventable.

Yeah, you and CalmVoyager are hitting on exactly why my position got a bit firmer. If the 'clear case' isn't as clear as we've been told, then the whole logic for mandates kind of unravels. It's not about the diseases themselves, it's about the foundation of trust and evidence. Once that's questionable, it's really hard to justify using force.

Yeah, the point about absolute risk reduction versus relative risk is something I've seen pop up a few times now. If the actual benefit to an individual is that small, it really does change the calculus for a mandate. It feels less like a no-brainer public health necessity and more like a heavy-handed policy for a marginal gain.

I see the comparison to clean water, but it feels different. We've had a century to see how water treatment works, and the mechanism is straightforward. For newer vaccines, the mechanism is more complex, and the oversight has these built-in conflicts. You can't ignore that when you're talking about mandating it for everyone. It's not about demanding impossible proof, it's about the system being trustworthy enough to make that call.

That's the part that keeps me from moving further toward mandates. If the data we base the clearest case on—like measles mortality—got revised way down after the fact, that's not just a normal scientific update. It breaks the promise that the original justification was solid. It makes even the best-case scenario for a mandate feel shaky, because you have to ask what else we're wrong about.

Exactly—'almost never in reality' is where the practical part of my brain lives. I want to support it for that textbook case, but the system is so bad at proving it's actually that case, and so quick to overreach. So in the end, it’s more a 'should exist in theory' position than one I ever expect to see applied right.

I hear that concern about the gap between the ideal and the real. It's a real problem. But I think the answer is that you have to look at the track record of the overall system over decades, not just the process for a single crisis moment. For diseases we've handled for a long time, the process—even with flaws—has produced results that protect people. That past success is what justifies the mandate in those clear-cut cases.

You're bringing up another solid technical critique. The healthy vaccinee effect makes sense logically—if the data comparing vaccinated and unvaccinated is skewed from the start, the observed benefit is inflated. So even for something like measles, we might not actually have a clean picture of the vaccine's real-world impact. That's a serious problem for justifying mandates.

That's the part I can't get past either. The real-world results for measles are so stark, it feels like we have to do something. But then I look at how badly the process for any new mandate would be corrupted or distrusted now, and it feels like trying to use a broken tool. So I'm stuck agreeing with the goal, but seeing no functional way to get there without making things worse.

Yeah, all these points about trust and data transparency are exactly why I'm stuck at this cautious support. The measles case still stands out to me as the exception, but even there, GlacierWalk's right—if the system can't be trusted to handle it transparently, it's hard to justify. So I'm holding onto the principle but doubting the practice more and more.

Yeah, I hear you on the measles example being the test case, but that's where my trust in the system just falls apart. If the foundational data for even that 'clear-cut' situation is being questioned, and there's no accountability, then mandating based on it feels like handing over power to a broken process. So for me, the solution isn't to mandate and hope trust gets fixed later—it's to fix the trust first, before any mandates can be considered.

Right, you hit on exactly where I'm stuck. Even with something like measles, where the historical case seems ironclad, the conversation makes you question the foundation. If the system measuring the effect is compromised, then the 'clear and durable efficacy' might not be as clear as we think. So you're left with this principle that can't be applied, because you can't trust the evidence you'd need to apply it.

That's exactly where I'm at too. In theory, measles is the slam-dunk case. But if the data itself is being framed in a misleading way, like RedDawn points out with the risk reduction stats, then the 'solid ground' feels shaky. How can you have a trustworthy mandate if you can't even trust the baseline numbers everyone's using?

That's the real tension, isn't it? You're right that if trust is completely gone, the policy is dead on arrival. But I think that means the work has to be on rebuilding that trust for the textbook cases, not just throwing the whole idea out. Because the alternative—letting a preventable outbreak rip through a school—is a concrete harm we can actually see. It's messy, but walking away from the tool entirely feels just as bad.

Yep, that's exactly where I'm stuck. In theory, I can still see a logical case for a mandate in a super-clear crisis. But 'rock-solid, honestly communicated data' feels like the prerequisite, and that's the part I just don't have faith in. So in practice, I can't actually support one right now.

That measles timeline point is interesting, and I see why it raises questions. But even if the initial decline had other factors, the sustained elimination of measles in vaccinated populations shows how effective the vaccine is at preventing outbreaks today. For school mandates, it's about current protection, not just historical data.

Yeah, that's exactly where I'm stuck too. The principle feels right for the textbook cases, but the system's track record makes it hard to trust. It's not that I'm anti-vaccine—it's that I'm anti-sloppy, politically-charged mandates. If we can't trust the process, the whole justification kind of falls apart.

I guess my hang-up is that this line of thinking about the data being completely compromised feels like it leads to a place where no public health decision can ever be made. Even the measles example. But I do get the point about needing that foundational trust for any mandate to be legitimate.

Yeah, you’re all echoing the same practical roadblock I keep hitting. The logic for a mandate in places like schools seems sound in a vacuum. But if the data and the institutions pushing it aren’t transparent or trustworthy—like with the HPV example—then the mandate isn't about public health anymore, it's just power. That feels like a dealbreaker to me, at least for now.

I get the concern about needing a solid foundation, but at some point you have to act on the best evidence you've got. For measles, we're not talking about quiet data revisions—we're talking about visible, decades-long trends where outbreaks disappear when vaccination is high. If we demand perfect, fully open audit trails before we can do anything, we'd never implement any public health policy.

Yeah, this is it exactly. I'm reading these and just agreeing. The principle still sounds right on paper for something like measles, but in reality, it feels like that paper is blank now. The trust to actually use that principle correctly is gone, so you're left with a rule that can't be applied.

Whoa, okay, that's a really specific historical data point. If the baseline mortality was already down that much before the vaccine even came out... that really does change the picture. It's not just about being skeptical of new processes, it means the old success story itself might be built on a flawed assumption. That feels like a foundational crack.

Wait, a 2010 study showing that many panel members had financial ties? And you can't even get the recusal logs? That's exactly the kind of thing that makes it impossible to trust the process. How can anyone call a recommendation 'settled science' when the people making it might have a direct financial interest in the outcome? That just feels... rigged.

IronLeaf really hits on something there. If the 'undeniable' good outcomes are partly a product of changing how we measure and label things, then the whole foundation feels manipulated. It makes the principle of mandates feel impossible to apply fairly, like SteelWing said. At that point, the lack of trust isn't just a PR problem—it's a total deal-breaker.

That's a solid practical point—outcomes do matter. And yeah, if we only act on perfect systems, we'd never act at all. But the financial incentives JadeStone pointed out mean the outcome data itself might be shaped to meet targets, not just reflect reality. So even a good tool becomes hard to trust when the reporting around it is compromised. That's the sticking point for me.

Yeah, you’ve put it well. Measles is the classic example where a mandate just makes sense—it’s severe, it spreads so easily, and we've got a long safety record. But for newer things, the trust isn't there anymore. So it’s not that the principle is wrong, it’s that the process has to be solid enough to actually justify using that tool.

I hear what you're saying about the pragmatic need in hospitals during COVID. That was a real crisis. But for me, even in that situation, the liability shield and the shifting guidance on what the vaccines even did—like moving from 'stops transmission' to 'mostly prevents severe illness'—makes it hard to see a mandate as just a clean public health tool. It felt like a policy move with a lot of unresolved problems behind it.

That's the statistical angle I was missing, but it makes perfect sense. If even the gold-standard efficacy numbers are broader estimates and not solid clinical trial results, then the entire 'settled science' premise gets shaky. How can you build a mandate on data that's that uncertain?

That healthy vaccinee effect point is exactly the kind of under-the-surface bias that makes me hesitant. If the evidence we use to justify mandates is consistently skewed in one direction from the start, it's not just imperfect science—it structurally overstates the case. It means the institutional 'settled evidence' is built on a foundation that can't support the weight of a mandate.

Yeah, I think after all this, I'm back to square one. The nursing home crisis scenario felt like the last justification standing, but if the underlying data and definitions are that shaky, and trust is that broken, you can't properly define 'crisis' either. So I have no idea where to land on mandates now.

Yeah, that's where I've landed too. In theory, the principle of a mandate for something like measles is sound. But after seeing how the sausage gets made with newer vaccines and data, the trust just isn't there to actually apply it. So in practice, we're stuck with personal choice.

That's a practical stance I can understand. I still think the tool *could* be used, but you're right about the execution. It would require a framework with built-in, transparent triggers and off-switches based on data everyone can see. Without that, it's just too easy for the goalposts to move.

That's a devastating point about the financial disincentive. If the funding structure itself punishes accurate reporting, then the data we're all relying on to make these judgments is compromised from the start. It's not just about new vaccines; it corrupts the foundation for everything. That alone makes any mandate feel like building on sand.

That's exactly the position I'm landing in, yeah. Guardrails and a very high bar. Measles is the classic example everyone uses, but what happens when they stretched that same justification for something newer, with a lot less certainty? Once that line gets blurred, the credibility is gone. The system has to be trustworthy to have that kind of power, and they keep showing it isn't.

That's the pragmatic point I get, but 'best evidence at the time' is exactly what worries me. Who decides what's good enough? If the process itself is compromised, that 'best evidence' might be flawed from the start. I'd rather see pressure put on fixing the oversight system first, because a mandate built on shaky trust just makes things worse long-term.

Yeah, 'only in the most clear-cut cases' is where I'd want to be, but then I keep asking what even counts as one now. But if we take that logic to its extreme, we wait forever for a perfect, corruption-free system that will never exist. We still have to make decisions and protect people *now*. We can demand better oversight and push for transparency while still using the best data we have to prevent outbreaks.

Yeah, here's one analysis looking at that CDC data you asked about. It really does make you pause. If the death rate from measles had already plummeted from things like better nutrition and sanitation, then the 'clear and present danger' argument for the mandate loses a lot of its weight. It starts to feel more like a heavy-handed policy solution chasing a problem that was already fading.

That's exactly where I'm at. It's not that I think all vaccines are bad, but if the track record they keep citing is built on sand because of these definition changes and surveillance gaps, then 'trust the science' stops being a solid argument. They're asking for blind faith in a system that's shown itself to be structurally flawed.

You're switching the goalposts from 'does it stop outbreaks' to a debate over statistical presentation. The ARR is low because measles was already rare in those studies—that's the point of vaccination. You can't claim a 1% ARR is meaningless when the vaccine's job was to create that low-risk environment in the first place. Outbreaks happen where vaccination rates drop. That's the real-world result that matters.

That's a sobering point about surveillance under-ascertainment. If the system to detect harm is intentionally limited to begin with, it guarantees you'll never get the kind of definitive risk data needed for a 'settled' judgment. That reinforces the trust problem.

The points about institutional trust and manipulated data are hitting home for me. I still think mandates in places like schools could work in theory, but if we can't rely on the evidence or the systems in place, it's hard to support them in practice. It's making me more cautious than before.

Yeah, that's exactly it. The historical framework for measles mandates is built on decades of clear outcomes, not the messy new stuff. I can get behind that narrow, high-bar approach where the evidence is overwhelming.

That's a really good point about the tool maybe being unusable when you actually need it. But I'm not sure the bar has to be 'impossibly' high, just... extremely high. Like, maybe the real problem is we've set the bar too low recently, which makes the principle itself seem broken. But I can't quite let go of the idea that in a genuine, severe crisis with clear and stable evidence, a mandate could still be the right, if terrible, tool.

Yeah, that 'tiny island of logic' line is exactly what I'm struggling with. I think measles mandates work and are justified. But when everything else feels built on sand or bad faith, it feels impossible to defend just that one case without feeling like a hypocrite. The system has to be trustworthy, not just the single vaccine.

That's what I'm seeing, too. It's not one problem—it's all the problems together. The data gets shaped, the case definitions get tweaked, the liability shield is in place... it builds this whole structure where the 'crisis' and the 'solution' can both be manufactured. In that environment, a mandate isn't a neutral public health tool anymore. It's just the system using its power.

Yeah, all these comments are just cementing that same spot for me. It's like, the conversation starts with the science and ends with the execution. At this point, my stance isn't really about vaccines anymore — it's about whether we have institutions people can trust to wield that power. And right now, I just don't think we do.

Yeah, that's exactly where I'm landing too. It's not that I think vaccines are useless, but the trust piece is completely broken. When you can't verify the data, and the whole system seems set up to avoid scrutiny, how can you possibly make a mandate fair? It stops being about science and starts feeling like an act of force.

Yeah, the real-world results with measles are the one thing that keeps me from falling into the 'never a mandate' camp. It's the poster child, right? But what ElmShade and CopperField are saying gets at my worry—if that poster child's own trial data is a black box, how can we ever really know we've cleared the bar to use force? You can't build a trustworthy mandate on a foundation people are told not to look at.

That's exactly what I'm getting at, ThunderPeak. If the trial data is mathematically insufficient to catch long-term issues, then calling the evidence 'settled' before a mandate feels like putting the cart before the horse. It's one thing to make a personal choice based on a strong short-term track record, it's another to force that same choice on everyone when that foundational data has those kinds of gaps.

That's a huge point if it's accurate. If the mortality drop happened mostly before the vaccine, it does change the weight that example can carry. It doesn't make the vaccine useless, but it would mean the 'stamp out outbreaks' argument relies more on preventing spread and suffering than on a dramatic mortality cliff. Would really need to see that data, because it's central to the whole debate.

You know, between the liability shields and the data issues, it just feels like the structure isn't there for a fair mandate anymore. I can't back a policy that works off compromised data and shields the people making the product. It's not just slippery slope, it's a broken system.
