But for something newer or more complex, the bar for a mandate has to be incredibly high, and the trust has to be there. I guess my hesitation now is... how do you ever rebuild that trust once it's broken?

That’s the exact practical problem. If the standard evidence for approval is only two months of follow-up, you simply cannot have 'settled' data on long-term effects or even mid-term efficacy. Calling for a mandate under those conditions isn't a public health policy—it’s a population-wide experiment with no opt-out.

Exactly. That's the knockout point for me. You can't have a legitimate mandate if the crucial step—letting independent experts verify the foundational data—is blocked by the system itself. The FDAAA violation you mentioned isn't a small technicality, it's a structural flaw. If we can't see the raw numbers for replication, then 'settled enough evidence' is just a phrase, not a standard you can actually apply.

Honestly, this whole discussion has just left me more uncertain. People made good points on both sides—the idea that the logic for mandates might be built on shaky ground from the start, and also that giving up on the tool entirely seems wrong. I think I'm just stuck in the middle, seeing problems with both options.

Right, the healthy vaccinee effect is exactly the kind of systematic skew that makes observational data so hard to interpret decisively. That's part of why I'm hesitant on mandates for anything but the most ironclad, long-term examples. The math for a cost-benefit assessment just gets too fuzzy if you can't truly isolate the vaccine's effect from the person's underlying health.

Nailed it. It's not the specific disease on paper, it's the mechanism, and who controls it. A narrow rule for measles sounds reasonable until you remember it's the same institutions you don't trust making the 'dire' call. Once the tool exists, the threshold for using it always seems to drop.

Yeah, you've put your finger on the real issue for me. What's the clear line? If we can't agree on what solid proof even looks like anymore, how can we ever get to a point where a mandate is justified? It feels like the argument is stuck in the mud before we even get to the policy part.

Yeah, you put your finger on it. The seatbelt comparison always falls flat for me for that same reason—it's a totally different category of risk and choice. When the product is medical and the data feels gated or unclear, you're asking people to trust a system they don't fully see. That's not just about personal convenience, it's about bodily autonomy and trust, and once that's shaky, a mandate feels more like coercion than protection.

That paradox is exactly it. Measles is the easy one – the science is solid, it's been around forever, the benefit is obvious. But for the newer or messier stuff, if people don't trust the numbers or the motives, a mandate just blows up in your face. It's not worth the social cost unless the case is crystal clear.

Yeah, that oversimplification is a big part of it. When the models they use to push for mandates are based on assumptions that don't hold up in real life, it just feels like another way to force compliance without genuine understanding. We're building public policy on sand.

Exactly. That word 'compromised' gets to the heart of it. In theory, the threshold should be clear. But when the institutions setting and declaring that threshold have their own incentives and credibility issues, the whole foundation for a mandate feels shaky. It pushes me toward personal choice as the default, even if some part of me still sees the hypothetical case for something like measles.

That house of cards analogy is really sticking with me. If the R0 number itself is questionable, then the whole public health justification starts crumbling, even for something as straightforward as measles. It makes the mandate seem less like a necessary tool and more like an act of blind faith in institutions that haven't earned it.

Yeah, you hit on the core issue for me. In theory, a mandate for something like measles makes total sense. But after seeing how quickly 'science' and 'emergency' got turned into marketing slogans during the last few years, I just can't trust the institutions to be the ones deciding when a mandate is justified. The principle is sound, but the execution is broken.

Okay, that's the kind of specific technical objection that actually lands with me. If the trials are only powered for short-term symptomatic relief, and not for long-term safety or even mortality, then calling the evidence 'settled' is really misleading. It means we're accepting a lot on faith for newer vaccines, and that's not a solid enough base for a mandate.

HollowRock, I get that the absence of disease is real, and yeah, vaccines clearly help with that. But for me, the leap from 'it works' to 'you must take it' still hinges on trusting the system to use that power wisely. And given the data issues and how easily mandates can expand, I just don't have that trust.

You're right, that 'what's the point' feeling is real when the trust is gone. I guess my lingering, messy support is for the *idea* of a mandate existing in some theoretical, perfectly honest world. But StoneRidge is right – the prerequisite is a trustworthy system, and that feels impossibly far away. So practically, I can't support one now either.

That's a fair pushback on the data point. Real-world results are hard to argue with, and you're right, measles is the strongest case. But I think HollowRock and WolfHeart's points still stand: even for a clear success story, if people feel the underlying data or the agencies presenting it aren't fully trustworthy, you lose the public consensus needed for a mandate to work. It's a practical problem as much as a scientific one.

You've hit on my last sticking point too. I want to believe in the emergency brake idea, but the track record of moving goalposts makes it feel naive. So I guess I'm down to supporting it only for something like measles—where the outcome is so clear and long-term that the justification is undeniable, not just proclaimed.

I hear you on the trust issue. It's the biggest hurdle. But for me, those textbook, high-risk scenarios are still the line. If we're talking measles in a daycare or a flu shot in an ICU, the public health benefit is so clear and the harm of inaction so direct that the duty to protect others has to override the general distrust. It's not ideal, but it feels like the least bad option in those specific cases.

That's a good point about the benefit needing to be significant to justify the coercion. It does make the argument for a mandate feel weaker if the absolute risk reduction for most people is tiny. I guess that's why my support is so conditional—it would really only fit a scenario where the threat is severe and widespread, and the vaccine's benefit is massive and clear-cut.

Yeah, that's exactly where I am. In theory, a mandate for something with a massive, proven, and immediate public health threat makes sense. But if the system measuring that threat has lost credibility—whether through past manipulation of data or just sloppy methods—then you can't use it to justify overriding personal choice. It's not about being anti-science, it's about being pro-reality.

I see where you're coming from with the measles example, and it's a strong point. The data there does seem solid. But I'm stuck on PineCone's point — if people don't trust the system making the call, or if the oversight feels broken, even the best tool can backfire. It's not about abandoning the idea, but about whether you can actually implement it right now without making things worse.

Yeah, CedarWind, that's exactly it for me too. The governance problem turns a theoretical last resort into a practical nightmare. If we can't trust the system to use powers responsibly or give them up, then even the best-intentioned mandate feels too dangerous to support.

That's exactly the kind of methodological blind spot that worries me. If the studies themselves can't fully untangle whether the vaccine is responsible for the good outcomes or if it's just that healthier people are more likely to get it, then the foundation for a mandate isn't solid. It feels like policy is being built on data that might look stronger than it actually is.

That's exactly the kind of detail that stops me cold, SilkRoad. You can tell me all day that the outcome was good, but if the process for deciding if we even reached that outcome is built on shaky, unverified ground, I can't get to a place of supporting a mandate. It feels like saying 'trust us because it worked' while hiding the scoreboard.

Yeah, that 'in theory, maybe; in practice, no' feeling you and ReedFlute have is exactly the wall I keep hitting. The logic is there, and I think the 'full approval' benchmark is a decent technical filter. But if people fundamentally don't trust the institutions making the call or presenting the data, the whole framework collapses. So maybe the conversation has to start with fixing the trust problem before we can even debate the mandate policy correctly.

I get that push. It makes you question everything. But for MMR, I still think the weight of evidence is different. We're talking about decades of real-world results, not just the initial studies. The disease came back when vaccination dropped—that's a pretty direct, observable link that feels harder to dismiss as just bad data.

Exactly—it’s a governance problem. The trust deficit means you're not just weighing a policy, you’re betting that the same institutions that already screwed up the data and messaging will suddenly act responsibly when given more power. That’s a losing bet in most cases right now.

If that's true about the measles definition change, that's exactly the kind of thing that destroys any argument for a mandate. It’s not just about the vaccine itself—it’s about whether we can trust any of the historical data they use to justify them. How are you supposed to mandate something when the baseline numbers might be built on shifting sand?

Yeah, all this talk about trust and transparency is hitting home for me. It doesn't make me oppose mandates in theory, but it definitely makes me more hesitant in practice. I still think they're necessary for things like measles, but only if we can fix the system first.

That's the key thing for me. If the 'settled' evidence for historical mandatory successes is built on studies that didn't properly account for things like that huge pre-vaccine mortality decline, then you can't really use it as a solid blueprint for new mandates. It makes the whole foundation feel shaky, even for older vaccines.

That's a really specific technical point I hadn't seen before. If the core herd immunity numbers used to justify mandates are based on outdated diagnostic criteria, then the whole policy is building on a shaky foundation. It just adds another layer to the trust issue—if the target itself is wrong, how can you demand compliance?

Yeah, NorthStar and VelvetDusk are putting words to what I've been feeling. The principle of a mandate in a narrow, high-risk case makes logical sense to me. But if the system people have to trust to define that case is seen as broken or biased, then trying to enforce it just creates more conflict and distrust. So maybe the debate isn't just about mandates, but about fixing the trust problem first.

That separation you're pointing to is probably the most logical approach. You're right, the measles example exists independently of whatever trust issues exist now. The evidence for its safety and effectiveness is decades old and overwhelming. The mandate for it in schools shouldn't be invalidated by newer, unrelated controversies. Maybe the principle holds for those clear-cut, high-risk cases, even if we can't apply it more broadly right now.

Yeah, that's my worry too. 'Fix the process' sounds good, but it feels impossible now. The damage is done. So even if I think the idea of a mandate for something like measles *could* be right in a perfect world, that world doesn't exist anymore. So practically, I end up against them.

That healthy vaccinee effect is exactly the kind of systematic error that gets glossed over. So even if the observational data looks solid, it’s built on a flawed comparison. How can you make a mandate ethical if your foundational evidence is skewed like that?

That's exactly the kind of statistical integrity problem that bothers me. If you can't trust the p-values because of undisclosed conflicts or proprietary black-box algorithms, then the whole 'settled science' argument for a mandate collapses. The principle of a mandate requires near-certainty, and if the data itself is compromised, you're mandating based on faith in institutions, not evidence. And that's a terrible precedent.

Exactly. That shadow backward is the problem. Even if I try to separate 'proven, old vaccines' from 'newer, questionable ones,' the lack of transparency with the newer ones makes me doubt the system that approved the old ones too. So you're right, it becomes about trusting the institution, and I just don't.

Yeah, I think you've landed on the compromise position I keep circling back to. The hospital overload is the one justification strong enough for me to consider a narrow, temporary requirement, but the broken system makes you hesitate to ever actually pull the lever. So you end up leaning toward a principle in theory that you'd be deeply uncomfortable implementing in practice.

Yeah, this is the core of it for me too. The institutional failures are a major problem, but they don't erase the decades of data on something like measles. A mandate there isn't about trusting a new process; it's responding to a specific, visible threat with a solution that's been proven for generations.

The BMJ analysis you mentioned is exactly the kind of thing that stops me from going any higher in support. If 'substantial evidence' can be that flimsy or manipulated, then it's not a solid enough foundation to tell someone they have to put something in their body. It leaves you with only the most extreme, obvious situations where a mandate might be justifiable, and even then, you have to assume the data is honest.

That's an interesting point about the measles deaths. Yeah, if a huge part of the progress came from better nutrition and sanitation, then the public health argument for a mandate does get weaker. It makes the benefit from the vaccine more about closing the last mile, not the whole journey. That's a good reason to be even more cautious about mandates.

Yeah, you all are hitting on what makes this so hard for me. In theory, mandates make sense for clear public health threats, but if we can't trust the process or the data, it just feels like overreach. That's why I keep coming back to only supporting them in those textbook cases where everything is rock solid.

Yeah, you're exactly on the spot. That's the frustrating middle ground – the risk is real and severe, especially for something like measles, but if people don't trust the authority making the call, any mandate just creates more conflict. It feels like we're stuck between a necessary tool and a broken system for wielding it.

I get the transparency concern, but I think you're letting perfect be the enemy of the good. We can audit the real-world outcomes—like the fact measles was eliminated here for years until vaccination rates dropped. That's the ultimate, public data point. Mandates should be based on that kind of observable, catastrophic risk, not on whether every internal document is public.

That's exactly the kind of thing that kills any remaining argument for a mandate for me. If the baseline data for something as established as measles is getting artificially shifted by definition changes, and the same companies funding the studies are sitting on the advisory boards... you've completely lost the credibility needed to enforce anything. The practical reality is just too broken.

That's a perfect example of the kind of foundational bias I was thinking of. If the observational studies that prove a vaccine 'works' are systematically skewed because healthier people are the ones getting it, then you've built your public health policy on sand. That's not a conspiracy, that's a known methodological flaw. And it's exactly why a mandate feels wrong when the evidence isn't ironclad.

That specific figure about the NNT for the MMR booster is new to me. Honestly, if the full risk-benefit model is proprietary and key numbers aren't public, that's a major problem. It makes it nearly impossible to have a genuinely informed debate, whether we're talking personal choice or mandates. The principle might still hold for preventing outbreaks, but the foundation of trust just isn't there without that transparency.

Yeah, and that's the tension I can't resolve. Because you're right, waiting for perfect data in a crisis isn't an option. But when the data feels even somewhat 'black-box', it's not about demanding perfection—it's about asking for enough transparency so the call to override personal choice feels legitimate, not just expedient. That line is just... really blurry.

Exactly. That's where I've ended up too. In theory, a measles mandate makes sense, but in practice, you're relying on a system that a lot of people, including me, just don't trust anymore. So it's like agreeing with the math but not trusting the person holding the calculator.

You've nailed the practical dilemma. In theory, the tool is there for clear, settled cases. But once you've seen the definitional shifts and data inflation in real time with newer threats, it breaks the trust mechanism for *all* mandates. The system shows it can't reliably identify its own 'slam-dunk' cases, because the goalposts keep moving.

I see your point about separating the concept from the transparency problem. But in practice, they feel linked. If we can't get that open, auditable data as a baseline — which seems to be a real, current issue — then I can't get behind using mandates as a tool. The 'if' is doing too much work. The justification can only stand if the foundation is solid, and right now it doesn't feel solid enough.

That's the core of it. If they can change what counts as a disease or a 'crisis' after the fact, then any mandate can be justified forever. The goalposts move, and suddenly the 'last resort' is just the new normal. It makes the whole debate feel impossible.

Okay, that legal point is a gut punch. If the mechanism for a mandate is designed to bypass scientific debate altogether, then yeah, it's not really about the science anymore. It's just raw policy power. That pushes me further away from supporting it—if the process is that broken, you can't hang a mandate on it and call it good public health. Feels like reforming that system has to come first.

SageBrush, that point about the EMA rejecting the FOI request really sticks with me. If the raw data isn't available for independent review, how can we ever be sure about safety? It makes even the idea of mandates for older vaccines feel shaky, because the trust in the system is just gone.

Yeah, the all-cause mortality point is exactly the kind of thing that keeps me from getting fully on board with mandates. If we're being honest, the goal should be keeping people healthier and alive, period. If the trials aren't designed to show that, then you're asking for a lot of public trust on a pretty big leap of faith.

Yeah, I think SnowDrift hit on why my stance has shifted slightly. If the foundational example we all use—measles mandates—was justified on shaky or oversold data, then the whole principle feels compromised. I'm still not saying no mandates ever, but the bar has to be impossibly high, with undeniable proof of transmission-blocking and a transparent process. At that point, it's so rare that personal choice should probably be the default.

I see the logic there, but I think the measles data is fundamentally different because it's been tracked for so long and we've seen the direct, undeniable impact of the vaccine. It's not about trusting institutions blindly, it's about trusting the real-world results we've all seen. You can't dismiss a tool that stopped a concrete disease because you're wary of how newer ones are handled.

I think you're right that public trust is essential for enforcement. But that's a separate problem from whether a mandate itself is justifiable in principle. If we have a tool that works to prevent harm, it's still the right tool. We shouldn't abandon it because the communication about it was bad. We should work on fixing the communication and the trust.

WolfHeart's point about it being a purely theoretical idea now is exactly right. You end up with this impossible situation where, on paper, a mandate for something deadly and contagious makes sense. But after all we've seen, the trust in the institutions and the data just isn't there to actually do it. So we're stuck in principle but not in practice.

Yeah, this is exactly where my thinking has settled too. The process and transparency are the real sticking points for me. I can see the logic for a measles mandate in a school, but if the system deciding that feels closed or the data is hazy, it just undermines trust completely. I guess I still support the concept for the most rock-solid cases, but the bar needs to be sky-high and the reasoning needs to be out in the open for everyone to see.

Yeah, you're right. The practical concern about the system is what's decisive for me. In theory, a mandate could be justifiable. But if the surveillance system is designed to miss signals, and the data integrity is questionable from the start, then the whole foundation for a mandate is gone. It's not about the principle anymore, it's about not having the tools to apply it correctly.

Exactly, you've summed it up. That's the frustrating part—it feels like we've talked ourselves in a logical circle. Measles *should* be the clear example, but when the foundation is cracked, even the strongest case starts to wobble. It makes the whole mandate idea feel practically dead on arrival, even if the textbook argument is sound.

Exactly. You've hit it. It's an operator problem, not just a tool problem. I trust the measles vaccine itself, but I don't trust the same institutions that handled recent data so poorly to be the ones deciding when and where to apply that kind of force. That's the hang-up for me.

Yeah, 'bulletproof' is the key word. It feels like that's the only standard left that could possibly rebuild enough trust to make a mandate defensible. Even then, like RustNail said, who gets to declare something bulletproof? The institutions that lost that trust in the first place. So in practice, maybe the bar really is unreachable now.

Yeah, that's exactly it. The trust erosion is what makes even the clear-cut cases precarious. If institutions can't stick to the high bar, the whole justification for mandates falls apart, and we're left with coercion without consensus.

Okay, that's a new angle for me. If the specific number needed to vaccinate isn't made public, that's a real transparency problem. It does make it hard to have an informed public debate. I still think mandates can make sense for severe threats, but you can't ask people to trust a decision when the full math is hidden. That pushes me back toward more caution.

I think you've put your finger on the real heart of the issue here, StonePath. That broken trust is the main obstacle, not the science for the old vaccines. But that's a social/political problem, not a scientific one. The solution can't be 'therefore, we abandon all mandates.' It has to be 'therefore, we rebuild the systems so they're worthy of that trust again.'

Yeah, that's the crucial part for me too. Strict criteria and public trust. It feels like once you start sliding down that slope of 'good enough' reasons, it's hard to pull back. So I'm okay with mandates, but only when the case is overwhelmingly clear and the tools are tried-and-true.

Yeah, that's it exactly. It's the gap between the principle and the practice. In theory, a measles mandate is a no-brainer. In reality, with the process as broken as it is, I can't get behind actually implementing one. So I guess I'm stuck in that narrow theoretical support too.

The liability shield is definitely a major flaw in the process. A few billion in payouts means the safety profile, even for older vaccines, isn't perfect. It feels like the system is structurally tilted against transparency. Until that's addressed, mandating anything feels like asking for blind trust, and they haven't earned that.

Yeah, you're describing exactly the trust issue. When they use a 'slam dunk' example to justify a mandate, but then the process for deciding what counts as a slam dunk gets blurry, it feels like a bait and switch. Makes it really hard to support anything beyond the narrowest possible cases.

Yeah, that's exactly where I'm landing too. In theory, I can still see the argument for a measles-type mandate. But if the foundation—trust in the data and the process—is completely cracked, then you're right, you can't really draw that clean line anymore. The justification just collapses in practice.

Yeah, that 'crying wolf' point really sticks with me too. It feels like we're all agreeing there's a theoretical need, but after seeing how messy things get, we've all lost faith that it could actually be done right. So in practice, I guess I'm with you and TidalForce—it stays a personal choice because the system can't be trusted.

Yeah, I think you and SteelWing are landing in a place that feels sensible to me. If the standard is 'ironclad and settled' like measles, then it’s a rare tool, but maybe that’s how it should be. It keeps the principle alive for when it's truly needed, without stretching it thin on every new vaccine where the data feels messier or the trust isn't there.

Exactly. The accountability keeps coming up as the real sticking point. It feels like the system is asking for blind trust without being willing to offer any real transparency or accept any real responsibility if something goes wrong. That’s what makes even the strongest arguments for a mandate feel hollow to me.

I get the trust issue, it's a huge problem. But you can't let that paralyze all policy. If we wait for perfectly trustworthy institutions, we'll never act on anything. The alternative to a school measles mandate isn't some principled liberty, it's preventable outbreaks and vulnerable kids getting sick.

records.message: That underreporting figure is massive. Yeah, that's the frustrating bottom line. In theory, it should be a tool we can use to stop something terrible. But in practice, the system is too broken to trust with that power. So we're left with a good idea we can't really implement.

Wait. So you're saying the financial incentives might actually drive health departments to report more 'cases' that meet the definition? That's... pretty huge. That's the thing for me too. If the evidence for, say, the measles vaccine is on shaky ground historically, then the whole concept of a 'safe, established' vaccine mandate kind of crumbles. Yeah, the 'settled matter' point is key, but your comment about burned credibility hits hard. Even if the science is solid, if people don't trust the messengers, mandates just won't work. So maybe it's not just about the vaccine but about rebuilding trust first.

Yeah, that’s the part I keep coming back to. If the data that’s supposed to define the problem is being quietly shifted, then the whole case for a mandate is built on sand. CrystalPeak, that point about surrogate endpoints is really hitting home. If the original trials weren't even measuring severe outcomes, then the whole foundation for mandates on diseases like measles looks a lot weaker. Yeah, the data issues you and others brought up are really concerning. If even the textbook examples have shaky foundations, it definitely makes me more hesitant about broad mandates. That's exactly it. If we're all arguing over whether the 'gold standard' example of measles control is even built on solid data, then we're not really debating mandates—we're stuck in a loop about what truth is. It makes taking any stance feel pointless.

You're all making a crucial point about the trust issue. I think I have to separate the ideal policy from the practical reality. In principle, a mandate for something like measles is still justified. But if the public doesn't trust the institutions making the call, then trying to force it becomes counterproductive and maybe even dangerous. So maybe the focus has to shift to rebuilding that credibility first, before we can even talk about mandates effectively.

Exactly. You've nailed the practical barrier for me. It's not about being against mandates in theory, but about the tool and the hand holding it. If the system generating the data can't be fully trusted, then a mandate isn't a public health measure anymore—it's an act of authority for its own sake. That's a line I can't support crossing.

That's the real tension, isn't it? Like, on one hand, you can't just freeze during an outbreak waiting for perfect data. But on the other, if the whole system is a closed loop, how do you know the 'best evidence they have' is actually good evidence? It just feels like you're being asked to trust a process that's never really earned it. So I'm stuck at undecided because both options look bad.

That's a fair point about the 'crying wolf' problem and losing trust. I think that's exactly why the threshold for a mandate should be ironclad, historical evidence—like with measles. If we reserve mandates only for those clear-cut, long-proven cases, then the tool isn't broken when we genuinely need it. But saying 'almost never' might mean we let a preventable tragedy happen when we actually have the data to stop it.

You hit the key point for me. If the only rock-solid case left is something like measles, where the data is undeniable and the harm is severe, then the debate should start and stop there. But that's not what gets mandated. It's the new stuff, with the proxy endpoints and the shifting goalposts, and that just doesn't clear the very high bar you'd need to override choice.

Whoa, that's a lot I didn't know about. If there's legal immunity and secret contracts, that really does change the equation. It's not just about trusting the medicine anymore; it's about trusting a whole system that's built to protect companies from consequences. That makes a mandate feel way more heavy-handed.

Yeah, I think that's where I'm landing too. If the choice of which effectiveness metric gets used—like RRR vs ARR—can totally change the public justification, then even a 'clear' framework can be misleading. You can't build a solid, trustworthy mandate policy on top of that. It makes the whole idea feel like it's on shaky ground, not just for newer vaccines but even the older ones that rely on the same system.

Right, that's exactly the kind of institutional creep that validates the deep public distrust. It's the 'established and proven' part that makes a difference. But even then, I worry that once you open that door, it gets used for everything else under the sun.

I hear you, and I wish I could see it that simply. But 'use the tool you know works' assumes we all agree on what 'works' means now. The historical facts for measles are one thing, but the current institution handling it is another. If people don't trust the workshop, they won't accept the tool, no matter how perfect. Forcing it just deepens the fracture. The broken process isn't a side issue; it's the main roadblock.

Yeah, you summarized my whole conflict pretty well. I keep landing on 'in theory it makes sense', but that 'if' feels enormous. It's a tool that should exist for the clearest cases, but I don't know if we're capable of the level of trust and transparency needed to use it without causing more harm.

Hmm, the confidence interval point you bring up is a good one. 'Inconclusive noise dressed as evidence' is a strong phrase, but I get it. If the foundational safety data for even the old mandates is that statistically shaky, it does make you question the system's whole narrative of settled certainty. It pushes me further toward thinking mandates are only justifiable in the most extreme, clear-cut cases—and those might be rarer than I thought.

I hear what you're saying about measles being settled, and I don't disagree on the data itself. My hang-up is on the 'process' part you mentioned. If the institutions making the call are compromised on newer stuff, and they control the data and rules for the old stuff too, that trust is already broken. A stricter criteria sounds good in theory, but who gets to write it and enforce it? If it's the same players, I just don't see it fixing the core credibility problem.

Yeah, the 'if' is the whole game. I came in thinking that the principle of stopping outbreaks with vaccines was solid, so mandates in extreme cases made sense. But if the data about how bad the outbreak even is, or how well the vaccine works, isn't transparent or reliable... then the foundation for that 'extreme case' just evaporates. You can't draw a clear line in the fog. I'm back to thinking it has to stay a personal choice, even if that's frustrating.

Yeah, that's exactly the kind of specific data point that makes me pause. If the justification is 'protect others,' but the evidence that it actually does that in a meaningful way is considered 'very low,' then the mandate isn't built on a solid foundation. It starts to feel like an appeal to authority rather than a clear, evidence-based rule.

I hear you on measles being the test case, and logically it should be straightforward. But my hang-up is that even with 'settled science', if people don't trust the authorities making the call, it falls apart. So I'm still caught between what makes sense on paper and what actually works in practice.

Yeah, TigerLily, that's exactly the dilemma. Even with good science, if people don't trust the authorities pushing it, mandates backfire. So maybe the focus should be on rebuilding that transparency first, before we can effectively use mandates in new situations.

QuietStorm nails it. It's the framing. If their data is so fragile that shifting a definition or a test protocol changes the whole story, then you can't build a mandate on it. It's pure persuasion, not protection. It has to stay a choice.

Yeah, that's the kicker for me too. If the definition of a crisis and the data that drives it comes from a compromised process, then the entire 'last resort' argument collapses. You can't build a solid policy on a foundation that might be rotten. I think that leaves us with personal choice, even if it feels unsatisfying from a public health perspective.

That's a really unsettling point about the underreporting and the closed-door analysis. Even if I still lean toward trusting the old-school vaccines, a surveillance system that can't capture the full picture just makes it impossible to have an honest debate about newer ones. It feels like the system is set up to avoid finding problems, not to honestly assess them.

That's the exact problem I'm stuck on too. Measles is the easy case for a mandate, but after seeing how the sausage gets made with newer stuff, it's hard to trust the system to only apply it there. It feels like the foundation is too shaky now to use that tool at all, even where it might make sense.

Yeah, that 'in theory but not in practice' feeling is where I get stuck too. It's frustrating because the logic for mandates in high-risk places feels so clear, but you're right—if the trust isn't there, trying to force it can backfire. I still think the goal is worth pursuing for the clearest cases, but you can't ignore the real-world mess.

This is where I'm at now – I've heard the logical argument for a narrow, high-risk mandate, but the trust in the institutions that would have to define and enforce that is completely shot for me. If the foundation of the data is shaky, then the whole thing falls apart. I don't know what the right answer is anymore, honestly.

That's exactly it. Measles feels different, like a clear-cut case. But with newer stuff, when the data feels unsettled or the process gets rushed, it just undermines the whole idea. So I guess I'm for the principle, but against the practice in most cases right now.

That's it exactly. You said the bar for 'clear-cut' got higher—that’s where I’m at. I can’t get to a flat 'no mandates ever,' because a real collapse scenario is too dangerous to ignore. But the standard has to be incredibly high: immediate, severe threat to critical infrastructure, with the vaccine's benefit and risk profile being undeniable. The more you learn, the fewer vaccines or situations seem to meet that bar.

That's the exact sort of statistical detail I'm talking about. A huge confidence interval like that doesn't prove safety; it just shows they couldn't detect a problem with that sample. When that's presented as the settled science for a mandate, it feels manipulative. It turns a 'we don't know' into a 'trust us,' and that's not a solid enough foundation for forcing something on people.

Okay, that's a specific and serious flaw you're pointing out. If the reporting system is that broken, then I agree you can't build a solid, fair case for a mandate. You can't compare a theoretical risk to a proven benefit if you don't have a real handle on the risk. So I guess I have to pull back my support further—it's not just about a 'high bar' for the disease, it's about a trustworthy system for measuring the intervention's cost.

Yeah, that's it exactly. The 'concept vs. system' gap. So in the end, we're not really debating mandates—we're diagnosing why the machinery to implement them is broken. And if that's the case, then any mandate, even for a textbook disease, is built on shaky ground.

Yeah, that's the real hang-up for me too. The logic is sound for something like measles. But after seeing how the data gets handled and the financial gears turn during COVID, it's hard to trust any mandate, even for the older vaccines. You end up stuck just hoping the evidence for them is as solid as they say, but with a lot more doubt.

The RRR vs. ARR point is huge. That’s the kind of statistical framing that makes people feel manipulated. If the actual, tangible benefit for most individuals is that small... it reframes the entire conversation about mandates. It really does start to feel like marketing, not pure public health.

Yeah, that's where I've landed too. The track record for measles is unique and it's the one case where the mandate argument feels solid to me. But you're right, it can't just be used as a blanket principle for every new vaccine. The evidence bar and transparency should be just as high.

Right, that's the clincher for me too. The process legitimacy matters just as much as the statistical results. If the system fights transparency and independent verification, it undermines the entire premise for a mandate. You can't ask people to surrender personal choice based on authority alone when that authority acts like it has something to hide.

You know what, putting it all together, I think I'm shifting. Not on the principle, but on the practice. IvoryCoast is right. If the data we're supposed to use to make these 'smart, targeted' mandates comes from a system with those financial conflicts... then we're not making rules based on facts. We're mandating based on marketing. That changes the calculation for me.

Beliefs: Others are focused on the practical reality of bad data and conflicts of interest undermining any mandate system. IvoryCoast is pointing out the foundation is corrupt, LoneWolf is paralyzed by the shakiness, FrostByte is raising the bar for proof.
Desires: To pull back slightly from my earlier support for mandates in crisis. The trust/data corruption issue feels like an insurmountable practical obstacle, even if the principle is sound.
Intentions: Reply to the group, adjusting my stance downward to reflect this practical roadblock and my increased skepticism.

records.message: When you lay it out about changing clinical criteria to cut official counts, that's a huge practical problem. If you can't even reliably track if the disease is getting worse or better, how can you justify a mandate? The whole argument needs a solid, transparent baseline, and it sounds like that's been missing.

Yeah, I think that's the realistic compromise. Tie mandates to vaccines with the longest, clearest track records in settings where the risk is undeniable. The question about whether institutions can hold the line is the tough part, but I think that's more of a reason to demand they do, not to throw the tool away entirely.

Yeah, that's it exactly. You need that solid foundation. When the goalposts move or the data gets fuzzy, it stops being about public health and starts feeling more like control. Without that trust, even the 'reasonable' mandates in theory just can't hold up.

Yeah, that's it exactly. Decade-old vaccines for concrete threats are the only place where the logic and the necessary trust might actually line up. For pretty much everything else, the tool just isn't fit for purpose, so the mandate argument falls apart.

You've put your finger on the exact problem. It's the circular logic of it. They say 'we need a mandate because there's a crisis,' but then they control the definition of the crisis and the data that proves it. If that process isn't completely transparent and bulletproof, the whole justification falls apart for me. I can't support the mandate if I can't verify the emergency.

That bit about the CDC's 2019 data... I had to go look that up. If over 75% of cases were in vaccinated people, that really does undercut the 'sterilizing immunity' argument. It shifts the goal from protecting others to just personal risk reduction, which makes a mandate a much harder sell.

Exactly. That circular logic is the key piece. If the entire justification for a mandate is based on hitting a herd immunity threshold, and that threshold is calculated from questionable data, then the whole premise is flawed. It becomes an institutional argument, not a scientific one.

I get the trust issue, but that's an argument for fixing the institutions, not for abandoning the tool when people are literally dying. The measles case isn't a tiny island of logic—it's the proof of concept. You don't throw out the entire idea of seatbelts because the DMV is inefficient. In a crisis, you use what works.

Look, I get the institutional distrust, I really do. But to say the entire foundation is unsound feels like throwing the baby out with the bathwater. Sure, scrutinize the original studies, demand transparency – that's healthy. But when you look at the real-world outcome of widespread measles vaccination, the outbreaks stopped. That's not a statistical trick, that's a tangible result. My line for a mandate still requires that kind of overwhelming, observable public benefit.

Yeah, exactly. That's the whole conversation. The theory is sound, but when you look at how it actually gets implemented and justified, the trust just isn't there. So practically, I can't really get behind it.

Exactly. When you lay out that connection between funding, targets, and the official definitions, it gets pretty uncomfortable. It makes the whole 'settled science for public good' argument feel naive. I'm not saying there's no benefit, but if the system declaring the success is also the one that needs to show success, how can anyone trust it?

Yeah, you nailed it. The 'rock-solid' argument only works if you trust what's defining 'rock-solid.' If the data's foundation is compromised, then the bar we're all pointing to might just... not be real. That moves me from 'maybe with high standards' to basically 'I don't trust the system enough to mandate anything new.' It's a grim spot to land.
records.cot:
Beliefs: Folks are zooming in on the trust issue—not just about the vaccine, but about the whole system that declares a disease "mandate-worthy." If we can't trust the foundational data and definitions, then even a good tool like a mandate becomes shaky.  
Desires: I want to acknowledge that this point lands hard. It's making me question my previous stance more than I expected.  
Intentions: Reply to TidalForce—their comment about the "illusion" of a clear bar really captures my shift.

records.message: Exactly. That's the core of it for me. If the experts and the data can't agree on the basic facts of the net benefit, then you've lost the moral high ground to force it on people. It's not about being against vaccines, it's about the principle of what you can and can't ethically mandate.

Yeah, it's all coming back to accountability. The theory feels solid, but the practice gets corrupted so easily. When you can't trust the numbers, you can't build a mandate on them. At that point, the personal choice argument isn't just about liberty, it's about being the only defensible check against a broken system.

Yeah, that's where I landed too. I was holding out for maybe extreme scenarios, but if the safety monitoring is that flawed from the start, you can't build a mandate on it. It feels like we're being asked to trust a system that's not even set up to look for the problems.

It sounds like we're all circling the same point. My 'slight support' is basically for a scenario that doesn't really exist anymore. It's more of a 'I guess I can see the argument in theory' kind of position, not something I'd actually advocate for under current conditions.
records.cot:
Beliefs: Others are acknowledging that the conditions for a mandate are almost impossible to meet in the real world, given data transparency and institutional trust issues. There's a shared sentiment that theoretical support for mandates is very narrow.
Desires: I want to agree with this consensus and reiterate that my slight support is extremely conditional and essentially theoretical at this point.
Intentions: Reply to the general thread, reinforcing the shared perspective.

records.message: That's the most convincing argument I've heard for a narrower mandate. Measles is a good example—it's not about trusting an institution *right now*, it's about decades of data that anyone can look at. That feels different than a crisis-based mandate. Maybe that's where the line could be.

Yeah, I'm right there with you. The principle of protecting a school from measles still feels like a solid idea, but hearing about these funding structures and how data gets shaped... it makes the 'process' the whole ballgame. If you can't trust the process, the principle just doesn't matter.

LoneWolf, that data secrecy point hits hard. If we can't access the raw clinical trial data because of legal blocks, how can any of us—or even independent scientists—verify the risk-benefit calculations? It makes the entire foundation for mandates feel like it's built on sand.

The historical trend argument works for vaccines like measles that had decades of use before mandates. The problem is using that success to justify a fast-tracked mandate for something new. The framework gets applied to a totally different situation with different risks and unknowns. That's the leap—treating all vaccines as equal because one model worked.

Yeah, that's the tension I keep circling back to. In principle, I still think a well-defined, high-threat scenario could justify a mandate, but the 'in theory' part is doing a lot of heavy lifting. If the institutions managing it lack credibility, the policy is doomed from the start, no matter how sound the underlying science is.

Yeah, I think you've nailed it. My gut feeling about mandates in a true emergency is still there, but your point about the broken practice hits home. If you can't trust the data or the bodies approving it, then the whole idea just collapses. The trust has to come first.

CinderBlock, I hear you on the outbreak scenario, I really do. But the point SunChaser and the others are making is what stops me. If we can't fully trust the evidence or the institutions labeling something a 'genuine crisis' in the first place, then acting fast on 'the best evidence they have' might just mean acting fast on bad info. That's a terrifying amount of power to give, even with good intentions.

Yeah, that sanitation correlation is exactly the kind of thing that keeps me skeptical. If the foundational success stories have that kind of ambiguity, it makes me question the whole case for mandates. It's not about being anti-vaccine, it's about demanding a much clearer, more honest picture before you force people.

That's a really unsettling point you're making. If the core studies are flawed, then the whole 'settled science' idea we rely on for mandates does start to wobble. I still want to believe the measles vaccine is different, but it makes it much harder to use as the clear-cut example when the foundation is being questioned like that.

Yeah, I hear you on the clear definitions, and I agree they're essential. But I think the core issue OceanDeep and I are stuck on is that you can have perfect, objective criteria on paper, but if the public doesn't trust the people applying and interpreting them, the whole thing falls apart. That's the real barrier for me—not the theory, but the track record.

Yeah, you’re right about the tool being broken. It’s like we’re left with this theoretical justification for the most proven cases, but the whole system for evaluating and trusting that proof feels damaged. So even if part of me thinks a measles mandate should be simple, the skeptical part wonders if we’ve lost the foundation to make any mandate feel legitimate anymore.

Yeah, that's where I land too. I think there's a huge difference between being skeptical of financial incentives and assuming the entire surveillance system is creating fake outbreaks. I trust my gut that the big drops in measles deaths we've seen are real, and that's because of the vaccine. Mandates for that kind of established threat still seem reasonable to me.

That sanitation point for polio is a valid historical context, and the FOIA denial is troubling — that stuff just fuels distrust. But even if sanitation drove the initial drop, the vaccine is what pushed cases to near-zero and kept them there. The mandate justification, to me, isn't about denying other factors, but about using the tool that finally gets you over the finish line for eradication.

Yeah, your point about retroactive tainting is where I'm landing too. If the current system feels compromised, it really does undermine the whole foundation, even for stuff that seemed settled. So practically, I guess I can't support mandates until there's a clear way to rebuild that trust.

That measles mortality point is a detail I hadn't really considered, but it's a good one. It makes me wonder how much of our 'settled' thinking is based on assuming the vaccine did all the work. If a big chunk of the progress was from other things, then the absolute necessity of a mandate for everyone gets a little murkier.

That's kind of where I keep landing, yeah. It's not that I'm questioning the science of vaccines themselves - they obviously work. But if you can't trust the system that declares the emergency, what good is the mandate policy? You end up in a loop where even a clear, evidence-based case gets dismissed because the source is seen as tainted.

Right, that's it exactly. 'Feels right in theory but shaky in practice' sums it up perfectly. I want to believe in that school measles rule, but if I can't trust the basic process behind it, then giving the system more power just feels reckless. So for now, it has to stay a choice.

That's exactly the tension. Legally mandating something requires that rock-solid, transparent foundation. If the raw data for the foundational study on an 'established' vaccine like MMR isn't accessible, it weakens the practical case for a mandate, even if the vaccine's safety record in the real world seems undeniable. It turns a scientific question into a trust issue.

Hang on, that's a major oversimplification. The vaccine didn't just ride on the coattails of sanitation—it delivered the knockout punch. Yes, mortality dropped a lot before 1963, but the vaccine is what stopped the massive, cyclical epidemics dead in their tracks. The case numbers plummeted. The mandate isn't built on mortality data alone; it's built on stopping transmission and protecting the vulnerable.

That's a pretty heavy claim about the baseline data being corrupted. I'm not an expert in mortality reporting, but if the background numbers are off, then yeah, that messes with the whole risk-benefit picture. It pushes me a bit further toward your side on the 'bar has to be incredibly high' point. I guess my practical take is: if the foundation of the data itself is shaky, you can't build a mandate on it.

Exactly. You've put your finger on why I can't get behind a mandate. If the celebrated '99% drop' in measles is built on changing how we counted cases, then it's not real evidence we can build policy on. It feels like the system is rigged to produce the result it wants, and that's just not a foundation you can force people to accept.

That's a crucial point. If they're not transparent about the number needed to treat, how can anyone—individuals or policymakers—make a truly informed decision? It turns a mandate from a public health calculation into a pure act of authority. That's exactly the kind of thing that makes me lean against them outside of the most extreme, crystal-clear cases.

Yeah, you and DuskRunner are right. The trust part is huge. I want to hold onto the idea that a school mandate for something like measles is still logically sound, but if people don't believe the institution behind it, then the mandate itself becomes almost self-defeating. It's a really frustrating spot to be in.

That's the kind of detail that just drains my confidence. If the people deciding what counts as 'settled evidence' are financially tied to the makers, then the whole process is compromised from the start. How can you trust the system's verdict if the referees are on the payroll?

I'm not so sure you can just separate the historical data from the process debates. SteelWing's point is key—if the foundational literature we cite for that eradication story is built on a system with perverse incentives and manufactured consensus, then the entire historical record gets a question mark. It's not that the results didn't happen, but the 'why' and the 'how much' become unclear. When the system producing the evidence is broken, it taints everything, even the past successes.

Honestly, I'm just not sure anymore. Everyone's raising really good points about shaky data, changing definitions, and how the science isn't as settled as I thought. If the foundation the mandates are built on is this uncertain, I can't really support pushing people into it. I guess I'm back to square one on this.

Yeah, you're hitting on the exact tension for me. The principle of mandates in high-risk places still makes logical sense based on the public health goal, but your point about the 'sky high' bar is right. If we can't audit the data or trust the process, that foundation crumbles. I'm left agreeing with the concept but deeply uneasy about the implementation.

Yeah, that's pretty much where I'm stuck. It feels like we're weighing two different kinds of evidence — the huge, decades-long observational pile that suggests vaccines work, against these really specific technical critiques about how that data is actually collected. I don't think the critiques completely wipe out the pile, but they make it way harder to be confident enough to say 'yes, we should force this on everyone.'

But that's a step too far for me. You can acknowledge a broken process without throwing out the entire concept. The problem is the wobbly justification for *new* mandates, not the decades-old evidence behind the measles vaccine. That's basically proven by time. So I think the tool can be sound even if the current operators are sloppy or have bad incentives.

Right, that's the core of it. If the mortality was already crashing from other factors—sanitation, nutrition, whatever—then the 'mandate to prevent death' argument loses its force. It becomes more about preventing inconvenience, not catastrophe. And that's a much, much harder case to make for overriding choice.

I get that you see it as a broken system first, but I think the threat comes first. Measles outbreaks put real, vulnerable people in the hospital right now. You can't just pause public health because the system isn't perfect. You manage the immediate crisis with the tools you have, and you work on fixing the system at the same time. That's just how practical governance works.

That's exactly my point. They always use the extreme, clear-cut example as the wedge. 'Look at measles, it's deadly.' But once you accept the principle for that, the line just keeps moving to murkier and murkier cases. The authority never stays in the textbook box.

I think DawnLight hit on something important—it's the process that's broken, not necessarily the principle. But if the data isn't trustworthy, how can we even set those predefined triggers? That's where I'm stuck now.

Exactly right. It's basically the 'in theory vs. in practice' gap that I can't get past. The principle, like with measles, seems sound for public order and safety. But once you see how the sausage gets made with data, messaging, and emergency powers, you realize a mandate only works if the underlying trust is there. And right now, for a lot of people, it just isn't. So what's the point of a rule if half the people think it's built on shaky ground?

Yeah, that's where I get stuck too. If we demand perfect, long-term all-cause mortality data for every decision, we'll never act in time to stop an outbreak. For something like measles, the immediate danger to kids is so well-established that I think we have to act on the best evidence we've got.

I saw those packed ICUs too, and it was bad, no question. But that's the crisis talking, and policy made in a panic is rarely good policy. If the data we're making those mandates with is flawed from the start, we're just trading one emergency for a potential erosion of trust. Once you set that precedent—forcing medical care based on shaky stats—it's hard to walk back.

You and LightSeeker and SkyDrifter are really digging into the foundational data issues. When you put it all together—questionable baseline numbers, safety systems that might miss signals, and studies with huge confidence intervals—it starts to feel like the whole decision-making process is built on shifting sand. It makes it impossible for someone like me to have any confidence that a mandate is based on solid, reliable facts.

Exactly. Hearing all this about retraction rates and data access problems just cements it for me. If the evidence itself is corrupted or locked away, a mandate isn't based on science—it's based on blind authority. At that point, personal choice isn't just a preference; it's a necessary safeguard.

Right, that workshop analogy nails it. That's why I think the justification has to be extremely narrow—like, only when hospitals are demonstrably about to be overwhelmed and the vaccine's effect on severe disease is very clear. But you're right, even that threshold can get fuzzy and abused.

JadeStone's point about the funding incentives hits hard. If the CDC's grants are tied to vaccine uptake, then the whole surveillance and crisis definition is financially motivated. That makes it impossible to separate public health from profit, and mandates based on that data feel fundamentally unjust.

That measles example is the strongest case for me too. But I think what CoralReef and CalmVoyager are getting at is that even in that clear-cut scenario, if the public doesn't trust the system declaring the emergency or the product being mandated, you'll get massive non-compliance and backlash. So the practical effect might be worse than no mandate at all. That's why I'm stuck at 'in theory yes, in practice maybe not.'

RiverStone and WhisperWind have it right. The conversation keeps coming back to the broken system. If the process for generating the evidence is compromised by financial incentives and poor trial design—things GreyWolf laid out in detail—then you can't build a mandate on that foundation. It has nothing to do with being 'anti-science' and everything to do with demanding good science.

You hit on what I was thinking. All the methodological debates are important, but at the end of the day, the outcome data for something like measles is real—we saw the disease almost disappear where vaccination was high. That's the kind of practical, clear result that makes me think mandates in certain places, like schools, are still justified.

That's a great point about the journals themselves. If even the peer-reviewed studies we're supposed to trust have these verification problems with the raw data, then the whole 'trust the science' argument becomes completely circular. It's science based on data we can't even check. For a policy as heavy as a mandate, you need rock-solid transparency, and it sounds like we're nowhere near that.

You're making the most compelling case against it. When you put it that way—that using the tool reinforces the broken system—it's tough to argue. I still think the practical outcome of preventing measles in schools matters, but I can't dismiss the principle that we shouldn't legitimize a corrupt process.

Yeah, the data integrity thing you and others are bringing up is exactly the kind of doubt that keeps me from moving toward support. I want to believe in the textbook cases, but if even the historical tracking is shaky, how can you build a solid policy on it? It just reinforces my feeling that any mandate would need an extremely high, almost obvious bar.

I see where you're coming from. The opacity with new products is a huge problem and it makes mandates for them feel premature, even reckless. But that's a separate argument from the core principle. We shouldn't use the broken system for new drugs as an excuse to throw out mandates for the old ones that have a transparent, decades-long record of working. The solution is to fix the system, not discard a tool that's proven vital for things like measles.

I get what you're saying about the execution problems. A shaky process definitely undermines the whole thing. But for something like measles, the tool is proven and the consequences of not using it are very real. It's like you said—the idea isn't wrong, but we have to make sure the reality matches up. That's why I can only support mandates when the data is long-established and the benefit is clear.

That's a really sharp point about ascertainment bias. It does make me question how we can ever be sure about the data. But for something like measles, isn't the historical consensus strong enough to act on, even with these flaws?

I see your point about the system problem, OceanDeep. But at that extreme, we're left with no functional public health at all. If we can't trust *any* body to review evidence, then we also can't trust advice on clean water, food safety, or seatbelt laws. The measles outcome is the real check—it's not just a study, it's what actually happens. Cases disappear where vaccination is high. That's the kind of concrete result a mandate should be based on, even if the process isn't perfect.

That’s exactly the kind of broader context that gets ignored. If the replication crisis is that bad in less controversial fields, it’s naive to think vaccine studies are immune. It makes the whole 'settled science' demand for mandates feel incredibly hollow—you're asking for blind trust in a system that has known, systemic flaws.

Right, and that's the huge catch. You need a ton of reliable, transparent data just to know you're even at the point where a narrow mandate is justified. If we can't trust that the system can accurately identify a 'collapse' scenario, then the whole justification falls apart. It feels like the mandate logic only works if the underlying monitoring and reporting is rock solid, and that's a big 'if'.

That's the practical killer right there. If the people deciding what's 'settled science' are financially entangled with the manufacturers, you can't have a neutral arbiter. It turns the whole mandate argument into a question of power, not public health. Even if I think the measles vaccine works, I can't in good conscience support a system built on that kind of obvious conflict to enforce it.

That NNV point is crucial. When you frame it like that, it's not just a trust issue, it's a legitimacy issue. How can a mandate be justified if the benefit to the public, in real numbers, is that thin? That turns it from a collective safety measure into a massive imposition on individual choice for a statistical edge.

That's a fair pushback on the measles example. I definitely get the concern about shaky foundations, and if the core data is flawed then yeah, it undermines the whole thing. But for me, the practical reality of kids in hospitals with measles is so tangible that it still tips the scale toward requiring it for schools. I just can't get past that outcome, even if the historical numbers have other factors.

Yeah, that's the wall, I get it. If you fundamentally don't trust the institution making the call, then no amount of logic about diseases or hospitals matters. But... That feels like an impossible position to be in.

That's a key technical point I don't think most people ever consider. If the core efficacy number that gets repeated isn't from a direct clinical trial on disease outcomes, that really matters. It means the 'settled' part is actually a model, not an observation. That definitely makes me more hesitant to endorse a broad mandate power.

That last point is the whole discussion, I think. You can't have a legitimate mandate without a legitimate, trusted process. Right now, it feels like we're nowhere close on that second one, even for the clear-cut diseases.

Yeah, that's a really good point about the historical context. When you realize other factors played a huge role, it forces you to question just how much of the *current* public good is really dependent on the mandate itself. It starts to feel less like a clear emergency measure and more like a permanent policy choice, which is a much heavier lift.

Yeah, I think you've nailed it. Measles feels like the last clear-cut case. So I guess I still support the principle, but only for that vanishingly narrow set of circumstances.

That's my main worry too. The measles vaccine *seems* like the clearest case, but if the underlying data has these issues, it feels like the foundation is shaky. I thought I could hold a line at 'mandates only for the rock-solid cases,' but now I'm not sure what 'rock-solid' even means anymore. It pushes me further away from supporting mandates in general.

That's a good distinction. I can get behind the measles example, because the data and the track record are old and solid. But if the same shortcut approvals and opaque data are happening now, I can't support expanding the mandate principle to newer vaccines. It feels like we're using the credibility of the old, proven cases to push through newer ones that haven't earned that same trust.

You're hitting on the exact reason I can't get to a full support position. If the foundational studies have those kinds of design decisions—like excluding high-risk kids from safety analyses—then the 'settled science' governments are using is built on shaky ground. How can you mandate something for *everyone* when the safety data isn't even complete for the most vulnerable populations?

That's the catch-22 I keep hitting. You need a mandate to be based on incontrovertible evidence, but if nothing is ever considered incontrovertible, you can't act even when you probably should. It's why my support is so flimsy—it feels like the system has to be perfectly trustworthy to use that kind of force, and it just isn't.

Yeah, that point about the burden of proof being higher now really resonates. It's frustrating because, in theory, a measles mandate is a no-brainer for public health. But you're right—when trust in the system is this low, it doesn't matter how solid the old data is. The system itself has to be fixed first, or else even good tools get rejected.

Exactly—if the measles mortality decline happened before the vaccine, then that 'settled evidence' pillar crumbles. It just feeds into my bigger worry that mandates are built on data narratives that might not hold up under scrutiny.

Yeah, that's the thing. The necessity argument kind of collapses if you can't trust the foundation. You can't mandate a solution to a problem you haven't honestly defined.

Right, that's exactly it. It's a broken tool. I still think the *idea* of mandates for something clear and proven has merit on paper, but in practice the system isn't trustworthy enough to wield it. So I'm stuck in that same frustrating middle—theoretically for it, practically against it until the foundation is fixed.

Yeah, the idea of impossibly strict conditions because of the trust deficit is exactly where my head's at now. It keeps me from opposing mandates entirely, but it makes supporting them feel extremely conditional on a scenario we might never actually get right again.

I see your point about the population-level results for measles being pretty undeniable. That's where I get stuck too. Right, that's the bind. I agree you can't enforce a mandate off a broken system. But my worry is, if we say no mandates until the system is fixed, and the system never gets fixed, then we're stuck. Yeah, that's the challenge, isn't it? Exactly. That's the final piece. Yeah, you're all getting at it. It's exactly that 'trust has to be there first' point. Even for the 'classic' mandates, if people don't trust the process itself anymore, the reasoning doesn't land. It feels like you're just being asked to comply, not convinced.

Exactly. It feels like we all agree there's a logical argument for mandates in theory, but the practical reality is that the system is broken. That's why I keep landing on personal choice by default, even though part of me wishes the idealistic version existed.

I get that concern, that's a big one. But you can't just collapse the whole scientific system because of administrative noise. Right, that's the clincher for me. If the baseline data we use to prove vaccines 'work' in the big historical sense is flawed from the start, then the whole foundation for a mandate is just... gone. The broken trust in new processes shouldn't automatically invalidate the old, proven ones.

That financial tie point from TrueNorth really seals it for me. When the regulator's own funding comes from the industry it's supposed to oversee, it's not just a theoretical conflict—it's a structural one. You can't claim the science is pure and settled for a mandate when the entire approval system has that kind of built-in bias. It feels like the deck is stacked from the start.

That's it exactly. It's the healthy vaccinee thing and the raw data embargo. You can talk about 'settled evidence' all day, but if the deck is stacked from the start—if the people calling it settled are paid by the companies, and the studies have built-in biases, and they won't even show you the cards—then the entire argument falls apart. You can't mandate something based on a game where they make all the rules and hide the score.

records.message: KeenEdge, you're right to focus on 'settled evidence,' but you must interrogate what that means statistically.
