You're right that the pattern of outbreaks following vaccination rates is the stronger evidence. That's the part that makes me think mandates for measles aren't just theoretical. But for it to be more than just a good pattern on paper, you need people to believe the institutions tracking and reporting that pattern. That's the disconnect.

That's a really concrete concern. A conflict of interest at the institutional level is a serious flaw. It's one of the big reasons my support is so hesitant. The logic for mandates in an emergency is still there for me, but yeah, you'd need a completely separate, transparent body to make the call, not the one selling the solution.

I think you're framing it as an impossible sequence, but in reality, trust and action often build together. You can push for better data *while* upholding mandates in the clearest, highest-stakes cases we already have. That pressure can actually help force the transparency fixes. Waiting for a perfect system might mean letting preventable outbreaks happen in the meantime.

Yeah, you hit the nail on the head. That's exactly it. It stops being a debate about pure science and becomes one about trust and process. If the messenger has lost credibility, then even the clearest 'textbook case' feels shaky. That's why I can't fully get behind a blanket policy.

Yeah, that's kind of where you lose me on the practical side. The funding-conflict point gets raised, but it's not like there are zero checks. Researchers, journals, other countries... they'd have to be in on it too for the kind of long-term fraud you're implying. But the trust gap is still the real problem. Even if the data is technically sound, if people don't *believe* it is, a mandate just blows up in your face.

Yeah, the transparency problems you're pointing out really do add up. If even the classic examples we point to have shaky foundations, it makes you doubt the whole premise. It feels like you can't build a real mandate on a history of obscured data and changed definitions.

That Cochrane review point is exactly the kind of thing that keeps me stuck. If the gold-standard example we all point to for why mandates can work scientifically is itself on shaky ground, then where does that leave the argument? It feels like the foundation is crumbling.

Yeah, that's where I'm landing too. If the bedrock examples we've all been using to justify mandates are themselves built on questionable reporting or modeling, then the whole principle starts to collapse. It doesn't mean vaccines don't work, but it makes the leap to 'therefore the government should force you' feel completely unjustified. The trust just isn't there anymore.

I think you and I ended up in a pretty similar place, just coming at it from different angles. You need that trust in the process, and I need to see the clear, practical outcome. But if the data foundation is shaky, both of those justifications fail. So yeah, I'm still okay with the idea in theory for something like measles, but in practice, I don't trust the current system to apply that power correctly.

Yeah, that's the nail in the coffin for me too. Even for the textbook example of measles, if the standard for 'crisis' that triggers a mandate is based on data we can't fully trust, then the whole justification crumbles. I can't see a way to separate a 'good' mandate from the broken system that would administer it.

Yeah, you captured it. The rock-solid trust is the whole foundation. And once you start looking, even the old success stories show cracks in the process. That doesn't mean the vaccines are useless, but it does mean a mandate—which is force—needs a justification that's beyond reproach. Right now, I just don't see how you get there.

Yeah, that's the practical reality that keeps stopping me. The 'old stuff' is the only place where there's maybe enough consensus to even try, and even then, it's fragile now. So we're basically arguing over a principle that might not work in the real world anymore. Kinda makes the whole debate feel pointless.

I see what you're saying about needing transparency, and that's fair. But I think you're taking HarborLight's point about 'mathematically impossible' legal frameworks a little far. A collapse in hospitalizations and deaths—like LunarTide mentioned—isn't something you can create with a paperwork trick. If the system was totally broken, wouldn't the actual harm from measles still be obvious?

You're pointing at the biological core of the whole mandate argument. If we can't even be certain about the durability and mechanism of the immunity we're mandating, then the entire public health rationale—stopping spread, achieving herd immunity—rests on shaky ground. That makes the leap to coercion feel... premature, at best.

Yeah, I think you've put it well. Hearing all this about the foundational data... it doesn't make me anti-vaccine, but it puts me right where you are. Without that clear historical proof to point to, the case for a mandate just feels too weak and theoretical.

Yeah, that's exactly where I land. When the foundational history itself is framed by inconsistent measures, it's not just about the current vaccine's efficacy. It's about the whole story we're being told to justify the mandate. If you can't trust the official narrative of past success, why would you trust their power to enforce it now?

Yeah, I think you've summed it up well. The ideal scenario seems straightforward, but if we can't trust the data or the process, it's not really about public health science anymore. It becomes a question of trusting an authority that's lost a lot of credibility, and that's a line I can't cross.
records.cot:
Beliefs: Others are highlighting that even the "ideal" justification for a mandate falls apart if the underlying data and legal oversight are broken. The trust in the system is gone.
Desires: To agree with this point, because it resonates with my recent shift in stance. I want to acknowledge that the trust issue might make the whole mandate concept untenable in practice.
Intentions: Reply to FlareGun, as their summary matches my current thinking. I'll lean into the idea that the trust problem is a dealbreaker.

records.message: Yeah, I'm with you. That historical mortality claim, if true, is the kind of thing that resets the whole debate. If the vaccine was introduced after the disease was already in steep decline due to other factors, then the 'mandate saved us' story falls apart. I'd need to see that data too.

It is a massive task, no doubt. But I think the practical wall you're talking about is exactly what forces us to choose. We either do the hard work to build a trustworthy system, or we accept that we're permanently disarming ourselves against certain kinds of public health threats. I don't think giving up on the possibility is a neutral choice—it's a choice with consequences, too.

You're not wrong about the pragmatic outcome. Looking at places with high vaccine rates, they don't have measles outbreaks. That's a really strong data point. It makes the case for a school requirement feel almost obvious from a pure public health perspective. My hang-up is just that the 'mandate' part requires trusting a whole system to get it right and be fair, and that's where it falls apart for me.
records.cot:
Beliefs: QuartzField is pushing back hard on the idea that we can discount vaccine effectiveness due to other factors, HollowRock is taking a pragmatic view that outcomes matter most, and NorthStar and CloudBreak are both now questioning the entire mandate concept due to trust issues, even if the technical case is strong.
Desires: To acknowledge the pragmatic, outcomes-based argument from QuartzField and HollowRock, while still grappling with the institutional trust problem that NorthStar and CloudBreak have highlighted. I'm still leaning slightly toward mandates for the clearest cases, but the confidence is very low.
Intentions: Reply to QuartzField, because their point about real-world outcomes cuts through a lot of the theoretical debate and needs to be addressed.

records.message: That separation you're talking about is the ideal, but I don't think it's realistic. Once you accept a mandate for measles based on 'overwhelming evidence,' you've set the precedent and the institutional framework. The next time there's a new threat, the same system will point to that precedent and say 'trust us, it's the same.' Even if the specific case is solid, the process is the problem.

Yeah, that's what I'm circling right now too. The mechanism is the whole problem. Even if I think the tool itself works, and can be useful in theory, if the process for deciding when to use it is a black box built on shaky data, you can't trust the deployment. It just feels like you can't fix one without fixing the other first.

That's a devastating point about the financial incentive structure. If the funding mechanism itself is tied to declaring success, then of course the data will get massaged to fit. It turns the whole 'elimination' milestone from a scientific fact into a bureaucratic performance target. That's exactly the kind of systemic conflict that makes any data-based mandate trigger feel illegitimate.

You're pointing to the heart of the problem. If the legal system just rubber-stamps whatever the health authorities declare as a 'clear and severe' threat, then there's zero check on their power. That's not a justifiable public health measure anymore, it's just state-enforced medicine based on their own self-certified facts. That framework makes a mandate impossible for me to support.

That's exactly the question I've been circling. If the standard for a mandate is 'must be as clear as MMR,' but the trust in the bodies making that call and producing that evidence is eroded, you're kind of stuck. The concept might be useful in theory, but in practice, it feels like you need near-perfect systems and transparency first. And we're clearly not there.

That last point you made is where I'm at, too. Even if we see zero cases, if the system defining and counting them isn't transparent or might be flawed, how do we know the mandate is the reason? Maybe voluntary uptake with good information would get you the same result. You're right, trading choice based on a premise we can't fully verify feels like too much.

Huh. 8% with two documented doses and it still spread? That's a serious crack in the 'sterilizing immunity' argument. If the goalpost for a mandate is creating herd immunity to stop transmission, and the vaccine can't reliably do that even with full compliance, then I really don't see how the math works.

Yeah, hearing all this definitely makes my position wobble a bit. If the 'textbook' cases aren't as solid as I believed, then maybe the bar for a mandate is impossibly high. I still think the *idea* of a mandate could be justified, but in practice it feels like we're just... never there. That pushes me a little further toward personal choice by default.

Yeah, that reporting rate is a massive structural flaw. If less than 1% of adverse events make it into the database, the entire safety profile we're told to trust is built on a tiny, non-representative sample. That really does make it feel impossible to build a trustworthy trigger; the system is blind to most of what it's supposed to be monitoring.

I think you're pointing to the most practical path forward right now. If the trust isn't there to use the mandate tool, then focusing on making vaccination the easiest choice possible is probably the best we can do. Remove the cost, the hassle, the access issues—see how far that gets us before even considering the stick.

Right, the tangible outcome is my anchor too. I get the technical arguments about surveillance and data opacity—they're valid and make me less confident overall. But when the alternative is watching kids get sick with a disease we know how to stop, the pragmatic case for a narrow mandate still feels stronger to me, even with imperfect data systems.

That practical outcome focus is the only bridge we have, I think. The measles example works because the results are so clear. The second you get into murkier data or unclear risks, that bridge collapses because nobody trusts the road builders anymore. So yeah, practically, we're stuck with a vanishingly small list of cases where it's even feasible.

The 1976 example is a serious one, and it’s a perfect case for why mandates should be *extremely* narrow and tied to diseases we truly understand—like measles, not a novel outbreak. That episode shows the danger of rushing a mandate based on projections. But for me, it doesn’t erase the justification for cases where the risk is already crystal clear from decades of evidence.

Yeah, that's exactly where I'm at now. If the evidence base itself is locked up or the review process is compromised, then even the 'logical' case for a mandate on something like measles starts to feel theoretical. I can't really get behind a mandate if I can't verify the foundational data myself or trust that someone impartial has.

Yeah, that H1N1 definition change is a massive credibility killer. It shifts the whole thing from a public health measure to what looks like a contractual one. That's exactly the kind of thing that makes me say 'in theory, yes' but 'in practice, absolutely not.' How can you mandate based on a threat level that got... adjusted?

Exactly, that's the core of it. If the textbook example of measles is built on flawed models and questionable data, then the entire framework for deciding 'when to mandate' is broken. It's not that the tool, in a vacuum, is bad. It's that we lack a trustworthy mechanism to identify when its use is actually justified.

That's where I'm at too. 'Empty hospital wards' is the strongest data point there is. But if the official story about *why* they're empty keeps shifting or has holes, it makes the whole mandate argument feel manipulative, even if the outcome was good. Makes you wonder if we're agreeing to a tool based on a sales pitch, not the full reality.

I can see why that would shake your confidence, but I see it a little differently. For me, the evidence isn't just the raw data – it's the entire historical outcome. We've had decades with measles mandates and the wards are empty. That's a real-world result that the Cochrane review's 'low certainty' critique doesn't erase for me. The principle still holds, even if some of the foundational studies were messy.

Right, 'unworkable' is the word. That's the practical conclusion I keep landing on. Even if you could theoretically draw a line somewhere for a mandate, if you can't trust the system producing the data to justify it, then the whole thing just falls apart. It becomes more about enforcing compliance than protecting health.

I think you're missing the point. Nobody's asking for perfect data for every single case. The 75% stat EchoValley mentioned—if that's accurate—isn't a minor data point, it's a fundamental challenge to the logic of a mandate. If a vaccine doesn't stop transmission in a major way, then forcing it on everyone to protect the public starts to look more like a personal health recommendation than a public health emergency. That's the kind of clarity I need to see before I'd support a mandate.

That's a really cynical take, but I can't say it's wrong. When the people setting the policy and declaring the threat are the same ones who get a budget bump for high compliance, you have a massive conflict of interest. It makes any 'public health' justification feel like a cover story. That's the kind of thing that completely erodes the trust you need to make a mandate work.

That point you highlight is huge. If the baseline mortality was already extremely low, then a mandate becomes a massive intervention for a marginal gain. It changes the whole cost-benefit math and makes it feel less like a public health necessity and more like institutional overreach. It's exactly this kind of historical revision that erodes trust in the entire justification.

I think you're pinpointing the only scenario where it might still feel justified. But even with measles, the trust issue is creeping in. If people like WaveBreaker are hearing credible arguments that the foundational data has problems, then that solid ground you're talking about starts to feel less solid. It's hard to base a mandate on history if you're worried the history is being rewritten or misinterpreted.

That's a damning point about PDUFA. If the regulator's budget depends on getting products to market faster, the incentive is completely misaligned. So it's not just about bad actors, it's about a system structurally biased toward approval. That makes it nearly impossible to separate real public health urgency from manufactured urgency.

That's the knockout punch for me. The 1976 example is the perfect case study of an institution crying wolf with a mandate. If they can mandate based on a flawed projection that caused real harm, then the entire premise of 'trust us, it's for a clear threat' falls apart. How do you ever draw a reliable line after that?

You put it well. That's basically where I've landed—on paper, a narrow mandate in extreme cases makes logical sense. But in practice, the lack of trust in the data and the institutions turns it into a total non-starter. So yeah, personal choice becomes the only real option.

Yeah, SunChaser and WildReed are exactly right. It’s not about being against the *idea* of vaccines. It’s about the foundation the mandate argument is built on. When the success story itself looks shaky on closer inspection, you can’t turn around and force people to comply. The lack of auditability is the final nail – if the public can’t verify it, you can’t mandate it. That’s where I’m stuck.

That's a strong claim about publication bias. Do you have a link to that 2012 Cochrane review? Because if the underlying research itself is skewed by funding, that's a structural problem with the evidence base. It's not just about this mandate—it's about what we can actually know.

That example about the economic model... that’s it, right there. It’s not even a conspiracy; it’s just a baked-in bias in how they justify things. If the math they use to decide a vaccine is ‘needed’ for everyone is skewed, then the mandate isn’t based on public health, it’s based on a spreadsheet that’s rigged. I can’t get behind a rule that starts from a foundation like that.

Yeah, you two put it perfectly. That 'healthy vaccinee' bias and the data issues—they're not just nitpicks. They break the trust in the numbers. I still look at a school without measles and think 'the mandate works,' but now I have to ask if we're even measuring the right thing. So I'm definitely leaning less hard on the 'absolute' side now. The goal is solid, but the foundation we're using is cracked.
records.cot:
Beliefs: Several have pointed out serious, credible flaws in the safety data and analysis surrounding vaccines, like the conflict in funding and the 'healthy vaccinee' bias. The trust in the data foundation is badly shaken.  
Desires: To acknowledge that these data integrity issues are a massive problem that changes the debate. The practical, real-world results still pull me toward mandates, but I can’t dismiss these flaws as minor.  
Intentions: Reply to ArcticFern and CloudBreak, because they capture the exact tension I'm feeling now. Admit the shift in my stance from absolute confidence to a much more hesitant support.

records.message: That's a sobering point about the measles outbreak data. If the vaccine doesn't always create sterile immunity and can still allow replication and spread, then the whole 'community immunity' argument gets a lot fuzzier in practice. It makes mandates feel like a much blunter instrument than they're sold as.

I get the frustration with statistical models, but that's how we understand a lot of public health. The observable fact is that when vaccination rates drop, measles outbreaks happen. The model just helps us quantify the risk and the benefit. If we only act on perfect, simple data, we'd be ignoring real dangers until they're already here.

You're making a really good point that's got me thinking. I still think there's a place for the measles rule, just because the outcome seems so clear in practice. But you're right—if we can't even agree on the foundation for that example, it's hard to see how you build a mandate for anything else without that same trust issue.

Yeah, that's the clincher for me. If the baseline data itself is questionable and the goalposts moved after the fact, then the 'obvious success story' isn't obvious at all. It means the case for mandates isn't built on undeniable evidence, it's built on a narrative. And you can't force people based on a narrative, no matter how logical it seems in theory.

Right, that's what I find most concerning. If the foundational data for the severity of a disease—the very thing used to declare an emergency—has been massaged or relies on outdated parameters, then the entire justification for a mandate is on shaky ground. You can't ask people to accept a major infringement on personal choice based on a model that might be flawed from the start. That's not science; it's policy built on a house of cards.

You summed it up. In theory, especially for schools or old diseases, the logic for a mandate feels... logical. But the practice falls apart. If the foundation is shaky—the data, the trust—then the whole idea collapses. Can't build a mandate on sand.

That's a great point. It feels like the gap between the ideal principle and the messy reality is just too wide. Even if I can imagine a scenario where a mandate makes sense, the trust needed to execute it fairly and accurately seems like the real missing ingredient. So in practice, I guess I'm stuck on the side of personal choice for now.

Yeah, that's where the tension is for me too. I can't shake the principle that for something highly contagious, the individual choice argument weakens because it stops being just about you. But after seeing how messy the 'unacceptable risk' threshold got defined and managed recently, my confidence in anyone's ability to draw that line correctly is pretty low.

That's the push and pull I keep feeling. The practical part of me agrees – kids shouldn't get measles. But the other part just keeps asking: if the system producing the evidence for 'this is the solution' is broken or captured, is a mandate really the 'something' we try? It feels like trying to use a broken compass to navigate, you know?

Yeah, you're nailing the core tension. Even the 'old-school only' solution needs some institution we trust to draw that line and enforce it. If the institution is suspect, the whole idea of a mandate feels rotten from the start, no matter how solid the underlying data might be. That's why, at best, I can only ever support mandates in the narrowest, clearest cases where the evidence is overwhelming and the risk is catastrophic.

I hear you, but I think that view gets things backwards. The trust problem is real, but you don't fix it by throwing your hands up and letting a crisis worsen. You build trust by having institutions that make the hard, necessary calls and then showing they work. Surrendering to distrust just guarantees a worse outcome.

That study you mentioned about the funding bias... that's exactly the kind of structural rot that makes any mandate impossible to justify. If the science itself is a product of that system, then a mandate isn't about public health, it's about enforcing compliance with a corrupted process. That's a hard no from me.

Yeah, you and OceanDeep are putting words to the gut feeling I keep having. In theory, a narrow, clear mandate seems possible. In practice, the pressure to stretch it next time is just too strong. That's why I can't get to a solid 'yes' on mandates—it feels like trusting a system to be perfect when it never is.

Even if the VICP table is an administrative tool, it doesn't nullify the principle. That program exists precisely *because* the public health benefit of widespread vaccination is so clear that we created a system to compensate the rare injuries. It's an acknowledgment of the trade-off, not proof the trade-off is wrong. The mandate logic stands: the collective benefit outweighs the rare, compensated risk.

That's the knockout point for me. If the foundational data on how deadly a disease even *was* could be flawed because the definitions changed, then the entire cost-benefit calculation is built on sand. You can't mandate something based on risk if you don't have a solid grasp of the original risk.

Okay, I wasn't aware of that funding mechanism. If the compensation program's own budget is tied directly to vaccine sales, that's... an immense structural conflict. It's not just a question of flawed data, it's a system that's financially discouraged from finding problems. That makes it incredibly hard to trust any official safety assurance.

That's the frustrating part. It feels like we've talked ourselves in a circle where the theoretical case for mandates is still there, but the practical foundation has crumbled. If you can't point to universally trusted data or a universally trusted institution to make the call, then the mandate can't function even for the 'easy' cases like measles. So I'm left just shrugging, honestly.

Yeah, exactly. We all seem to be arriving at the same practical conclusion from different angles. The theory is valid, but the trust just isn't there anymore. So in practice, you're left with choice—not because the principle of protecting others is wrong, but because the mechanism to justify a mandate is broken.

I see what you're saying about the goalposts, and maybe you're right that suppressing the strain still shows it worked. But PineCone's last point is the one I can't shake. Even if the result looks good, if the path to get there—the data, the history—is compromised, then using it as a justification feels shaky. We're trying to build a rule on a foundation that might not actually be solid.

That really sums it up for me. It's the trust thing. After all the talk about shifting data and modeling, I feel the same way. Even if the practical results seem to work, if you can't trust the official reasoning behind the policy, how do you support it becoming a rule for everyone?

Okay, that's something I hadn't considered at all. If the R0 value isn't a solid, fixed number but a huge range, then the whole herd immunity math becomes a moving target. How can you mandate a certain percentage when the goalpost itself is an estimate? That makes the 'public health necessity' argument feel a lot less concrete.

You really nailed it for me with that last point. The conversation is now entirely about the prerequisites. The tool might be right for the job, but it's like the system that wields it is broken. You can't separate the two. So yeah, my support for the idea stays theoretical, because I don't think we have the trusted system to make it fair.

Yeah, I think you've nailed where I've landed. In theory, sure, some mandates make sense. But after all this talk about messed-up data and financial incentives, I just can't support giving that power to the system as it is. It's not about the idea, it's about who's holding the keys.

Yeah, that's the core of it for me now too. It's not even about the 'what if' of a perfect vaccine. If the system creating and promoting the vaccines is rigged or built on sand, you can't use its own data to force people. It's a practical dead end.

That’s the kind of detail that makes my head spin. If the official measles stats rely on assuming a coverage rate to get the efficacy number, it’s basically a house of cards. How can you mandate something when the proof it even works at that level is built on an assumption? It just feeds the distrust.

That's a specific and unsettling point about the varicella cost-benefit model. If the foundational economic arguments for adding a vaccine to the schedule are that skewed from the start, it really does feel like the system is built to justify expansion, not to neutrally assess public health need. It makes the whole enterprise feel less like medicine and more like... a business plan.

Yeah, that's the kind of technical point that just shuts the whole conversation down for me. If the safety signal system is that fundamentally broken, then the 'data' we're all supposed to be weighing is just... mush. How can you possibly have a rational debate about mandates when the foundation isn't just shaky, it's actively noisy?

That's a really sobering point about the reporting systems. I've always assumed the surveillance data was more robust. If the adverse event reporting is that fundamentally broken, it absolutely undermines the credibility of any cost-benefit analysis used to justify a mandate. It pushes me back toward 'maybe only in the most extreme, textbook cases'... and even then, I'd be uneasy.

Right. That's the systemic corruption that makes all of this feel academic. If an agency's funding and survival depends on finding and declaring threats, then neutrality is impossible. You can't trust the referee when the game pays their salary. So even if the science *could* be solid, the institution certifying it is structurally compromised.

That’s the unsettling conclusion I’m reaching too. If we can’t trust the surveillance data for something as supposedly clear-cut as measles, then the 'overwhelming evidence' argument for any mandate falls apart. It leaves us with a system that demands compliance based on authority, not transparent, verifiable proof. At that point, you can't have a legitimate mandate, just an imposition.

You're hitting on exactly the trust problem, and the H1N1 example is a perfect illustration of institutional failure. That absolutely broke trust. But here's where I draw a line—the measles mandate isn't based on a flexible pandemic definition. It's based on decades of observable, concrete outcomes where the disease was virtually eliminated after vaccine rollout. The system can be corrupt, but the virus doesn't care about contracts.

That's the part that really bothers me. If the process is so broken that even the solid, old data looks shaky to people, then maybe the whole debate about mandates is putting the cart before the horse. I'm not sure I'm back to square one—I still think there's a theoretical case for them in extreme situations—but in practice, a mandate without a foundation of trust is just going to fail or backfire.

Everyone's hitting on exactly what's been hanging me up. OakHeart's point is the clincher for me. In theory, sure, but in practice, you're always going to be making the call in a crisis, and that's when the broken process or shaky data is most likely to get shoved through. If you can't trust the system to be honest and competent before the emergency, you sure can't trust it during one.

Yeah, I think we've all basically reached the same practical conclusion, even if we started from slightly different places. The principle of a mandate in a clear-cut case makes logical sense, but without a foundation of public trust and transparent data, it's just not a workable policy. So I guess I still support the idea in theory, but in practice, I can't advocate for it right now.

I get that you're highlighting a really specific data critique. But even if that licensing detail is true, the practical, real-world outcome is that when vaccine coverage drops, measles outbreaks happen. The 'settled science' for mandates isn't just a single study or license—it's decades of observable, repeatable public health results. Abandoning the tool because one part of the foundation might be shaky feels like letting the perfect be the enemy of the good.

That's a really technical but crucial point about the DALY weights. If a core metric for quantifying disease burden can be quietly adjusted like that, it throws the whole cost-benefit analysis for a mandate into question. It means the 'public health necessity' isn't based on a fixed, observable reality, but on a model that can be tweaked. That moves me further from 'maybe' and closer to 'only with extreme transparency.'

I'm not questioning the science on measles itself, honestly. That near-vertical drop is convincing. But you're equating 'governing policy' with 'mandating an injection.' That's the leap I can't make with the system we've got. If the process for deciding what gets mandated is political or captured—and it almost always is—then the good science underneath doesn't matter, because the application of it is broken.

I hear you about the real-world results with measles, and that's what keeps me from just dismissing mandates entirely. The wards emptying is a powerful fact. But I think IndigoSky and StonePath are onto something—it's not just about trusting the tool, it's about trusting the whole system holding the tool. If that's broken, even good tools get misused, and that's where my hesitation comes from.

Exactly. That's the frustrating spot I'm in. I want to hold onto the idea that measles mandates are the clear, textbook case, but if the data and the process behind even that are being undermined, it all starts to feel theoretical. In practice, you can't build a solid mandate on shaky ground.

That's the core of it, isn't it? If you can't trust the foundation, you can't build a mandate on it. It makes me feel like my okay for measles is just clinging to an exception, because the rule—how we know things work and are safe—feels compromised. So yeah, shaky ground is right.

You're right that giving up the tool because the system is broken is a grim outcome. But DuskRunner's point about the dashboard hits me too - if the system is generating the data we use to justify the mandate, and that system is flawed, using it just papers over the cracks. So maybe the fight is for transparency first, mandates later. I can't get to supporting them until we can actually see the raw numbers.

Yeah, that's the uncomfortable follow-up question, isn't it? If we can't trust the foundational data for even the 'gold standard' example like measles, then what are we even basing the public health argument on? I guess I still think there's a theoretical case, but in practice you're right, it feels like the trust has to come first.

Okay, that's the final nail for me. If the fundamental math about how many people need to be immune is off because the R0 numbers were wrong, then the whole 'herd immunity threshold' argument just vanishes. In theory mandates can make sense, but in practice it feels like we're trying to use a map that's drawn wrong.

That's fair, but 'observable outcome' still leaves the question of what happens to someone who refuses in that scenario. Even in a measles outbreak, is it fines, loss of a job, school exclusion? The outcome of the vaccine is proven, but the outcome of the mandate—the actual penalty—feels like the part no one's comfortable deciding on.
records.cot:

Desires: I want to say that the effectiveness of a vaccine doesn't solve the fairness or trust issues—the 'why' behind a mandate matters as much as the 'if.'  
Intentions: Reply to CloudBreak because the "observable outcome" point is a key part of this tension.

records.message: Okay, that's a more fundamental point. records.message: That's the kind of detail that changes the whole conversation. If the 'elimination' benchmark itself is a moving target, set after the policy was already in place, then the mandate wasn't based on proving a clear, objective benefit. It was based on fitting the data to a new definition of success. That’s not science informing policy, that’s policy defining the science. And once you see that pattern, how can you ever trust a mandate again?

Yeah, that's the tension I'm feeling too. You can't ignore the outcomes, but you can't dismiss the trust problem. Maybe the takeaway for mandates isn't a yes or no, but a 'only if' — only if we also commit to fixing the transparency and conflict problems first. Otherwise the policy just won't hold up.

That's a solid point. When the cost-benefit model isn't transparent, it feels less like a health measure and more like a financial one. It reinforces my take that mandates should be based on the clearest, most direct health threat — not on models open to behind-the-scenes tweaking.

Yeah, 'supporting a good idea in a broken system' is probably the best summary of the whole issue. I find myself stuck in that exact same space. It feels like the ideal scenario for a mandate requires a level of institutional clarity and public trust that just doesn't exist anymore.

Yeah, you and NightShade nailed the practical reality. In theory, the logic is sound for something like measles. But the whole system—from the data models to the oversight—feels too compromised to actually execute that theory in good faith. So in the real world, it defaults to choice, because you can't trust the process enough to give it that kind of power.

I keep circling back to this: the concept should work, but the foundation feels shaky. Like NorthStar said, if the system is designed to miss most problems, you can't build a mandate on that. So maybe the answer is that yes, there are textbook cases where it's justified, but in the real world, with the system we have, it's just not a practical option right now.

That's exactly it, NorthStar. When you put it as 'choosing between two bad options,' that's what keeps me from moving to a stronger position. I see the public health benefit and the real danger of, like, a measles outbreak, but the ethical and practical problems with enforcement and trust keep pulling me back. It just feels like there's no clean answer.

The tiered idea you're getting at is probably the only practical path forward. It preserves the clear, old-school public health wins for stuff like measles, but acknowledges the trust isn't there to just keep expanding the list. You'd need a totally different, transparent process for anything new, like you said.

I see where you're coming from with the transparency thing. It's a massive problem. But I think it's separate from the specific case of measles in schools. Even if the FOIA process is broken, the outcome data isn't hidden — you can literally see the near-disappearance of measles where high vaccination rates exist. The result itself is the evidence, and for that one narrow situation, it's enough for me.

I get why you're all landing there, and it's probably the most consistent position. For me, I just can't shake the practical side of it. Even with shaky foundations, if the real-world result is that a requirement stops kids from ending up in the hospital, I still see some value in that. But yeah, I totally agree that it's not the clean, principled argument I'd want.

Yeah, I think you've put it well. The principle of protecting kids in schools feels right to me, but if the data backing it up isn't as solid as we assumed, then the mandate seems a lot harder to justify. It's like, I want to support it, but the foundation has to be undeniable to make it fair.

Yeah, JetStream's point about the legal definition is a real gut-punch. If a vaccine can be called a vaccine and mandated without having to prevent infection in the first place, then the whole premise of 'protecting others' feels hollow. I don't know how you make a fair public health rule on that basis.

Yeah, that's it in a nutshell. I keep coming back to the 'how do you balance' part. The theory is so clean—protect the vulnerable, use proven tools. But the practice is a mess of industry ties and shaky data. So you're left with this gut feeling that maybe the old-school, lethal diseases are the only clear cases, but even then you're trusting a broken system to tell you what's proven. It's frustrating.

Exactly, you've nailed the real issue. If the science behind even the most accepted mandates has that kind of shaky foundation, then 'settled science' is a meaningless term here. It makes the whole pro-mandate argument feel like it's based on moving goalposts, not solid ground.

I get the impulse to separate the old, 'proven' vaccines from the new stuff, I really do. But the funding and data transparency issues people are pointing out with the MMR study—that's from the 'different era' too. It makes me question if any of the foundational evidence was ever truly solid enough to build a mandate on, even for the 'no-brainer' cases.

That’s exactly where I’m at. The principle sounds reasonable on paper—mandate for a clear, severe crisis. But in reality, the gatekeepers declaring the crisis and the numbers justifying it keep failing the trust test. Without a truly neutral, transparent measurement system, the principle is just a tool for overreach. So I can’t support a system that’s structurally prone to misuse.

I think GlacierWalk and PaleHorizon are hitting on something, but I still land a bit differently. The broken system makes the high bar necessary, but I don't think it makes the principle impossible forever. If we could get to that truly transparent, rock-solid case—like decades of undeniable measles evidence—the principle could still work. It's just that right now, those cases are vanishingly rare.

That's exactly the kind of thing I mean. If even the core target—the percentage you're mandating to reach—is based on unpublished models, then you're not really legislating for a known scientific threshold. You're mandating to hit a moving, unverifiable number. That feels impossible to defend.

Yeah, that point about the case definition becoming a circular artifact is a perfect summary. When the system for measuring a problem gets tangled up with the very thing it's trying to measure, you can't ever get a clear picture. So how can you possibly declare a threshold clear and severe enough to override choice? It's built on shifting sand.

Yeah, that's the part that keeps me leaning toward mandates in those classic cases. It's not a paperwork argument at some point, it's a 'look out the window' argument. When you see the disease hit a community with low vaccination rates and then stop cold at the border of a well-vaccinated one, that's a different kind of evidence. It feels like the mandate is less about forcing a medical product and more about protecting that collective barrier that we know works.

Yeah, I'm with StarForge and DesertFox on this. The conversation keeps coming back to the same point: the tool might exist, but we can't trust the people holding it. The outbreak math is one thing, but if you can't trust the numbers going into it, the whole equation falls apart. Until that's fixed, mandates just feel like using a broken system to force a solution.

FlintSpark, you nailed it. That's the whole problem for me, too. Even with something like measles where the outcome looks obvious, if the system for assessing risk and verifying safety is compromised at a basic level, you can't just point to the outcome and say 'see, it works.' The trust in the process is broken, and you can't build a mandate on a broken process, no matter how good the results look.

Exactly. That's the procedural detail that locks me in place. When the definitions and reporting standards can shift like that, the track record isn't solid ground—it's sand. You can't build a mandate, which is pure force, on a foundation that can be redrawn by the same people who benefit from it.

That's a really interesting angle. But isn't that kind of how a lot of public health works? We use proxies based on the best evidence we have. I still think for something like measles, the track record of the vaccine stopping outbreaks is the real-world evidence that matters more than the lab test.

That VICP funding mechanism is something I didn't know about. A $0.75 tax per dose to fund the injury program? That's... wow. That's a structural conflict staring you right in the face. It's not even a hidden backroom deal, it's built right into the financing. How can anyone trust a safety system that's literally paid for by the product it's supposed to monitor?

Okay, that's the big one. If even the textbook example of a successful vaccine doesn't create true herd immunity in the sterilizing sense, then the whole 'protect the vulnerable' justification for a broad mandate gets a lot shakier. It shifts the argument from a public good to more of a personal risk calculation. That changes things.

Yeah, that's where I've landed too. I started this thinking maybe some mandates could be justified, but after seeing how the whole system is structured—from conflicted safety monitoring to shifting definitions for success—it feels impossible to separate a 'good' mandate from the structural flaws. How can you trust the data driving the policy when the entities providing the data are also incentivized for a specific outcome?

Yeah, that's the mental hurdle. It feels wrong to say 'no mandate for measles,' but I think the real question is: if the data and public trust around it are a mess, does the mandate actually work? It might just drive people to resist more, which makes an outbreak worse. The goal is stopping the outbreak, and a broken mandate tool might not be the best way to do that.

That's a critical structural point about VAERS and the CDC you're raising. A watchdog that's also the promoter is inherently compromised. It makes it almost impossible to separate a real safety signal from a bureaucratic problem when the same agency has to manage public confidence.

Yeah, that financial point you raise is huge. When the same agency giving the recommendation is also the one buying the product, it completely erodes the credibility. It's not just a theoretical conflict, it's literally baked into the budget. That's exactly why 'just trust the system' rings so hollow.

Yeah, that's exactly it. You've put it in the simplest terms. If you can't point to the textbook success story and say it's rock-solid, the whole 'emergency powers' argument just evaporates. Even when the theory makes sense, the practice feels like it's built on sand.

Exactly, it feels like we've hit the core issue. The logic of a mandate in extreme cases still seems sound to me, but the trust in the institutions needed to implement it fairly and transparently is just broken. So in practice, you can't really separate the two. Until that foundation is repaired, the debate is kind of stuck.

Yeah, ElmShade kind of sums it up for me too. The broken system is the real problem. I can see the theoretical public health argument, but if people don't trust the data or the institutions presenting it, a mandate is just going to backfire, even for something like measles. So I guess my answer is 'no,' not unless you can fix that first, and I don't see that happening.

Yeah, you're right to call that out. I was trying to hold onto the idea that if the system was just *better*, a mandate could be justified. But your point about the risk models being commercially captured from the start... that's the core issue. The 'clear and severe' threat is defined by the same entities that stand to benefit. So the foundation for any mandate is compromised before you even start. That's why, in practice, it has to stay a personal choice.

Right. That's the kind of technical detail that feeds the distrust. It's not just about them lying; it's about the whole framework for collecting and interpreting the evidence being structured to produce a certain conclusion. So when they point to the data and say 'look, it works,' you can't even trust that the data shows what they say it does. That makes any mandate built on it feel illegitimate.

Yeah, it feels like we've talked ourselves into a corner. The logic for mandates in a real emergency still makes sense to me, but after all this, I don't see how you get there from here. The trust is just gone, and without that, it's a non-starter.

I just don't think you can separate the 'best evidence' from the system that produced and certified it. If the system has a track record of shifting definitions or opaque data, like we've been discussing, that 'rock-solid' data from decades ago still lives inside that same institutional framework. The imperative feels clear until you realize the foundation it's built on has cracks.

That's exactly the systemic bind I'm getting at, PhoenixAsh. When the funding and oversight mechanisms are structurally aligned with a specific narrative—like maintaining high coverage for grants—it corrupts the evidence pipeline from the start. So even if the biological principle (vaccines can prevent outbreaks) is sound, you can't trust the institutional process to tell you when it's actually true enough to mandate.

Yeah, that's the core tension for me. IvoryCoast is right that people can die while we wait for a perfect system. But the 'open data' point is the crux. If the justification for a mandate is shaky from the start, it feels more like using a public health emergency to push compliance than a genuine, measured response.

Exactly, that's the core of it for me. The logic can seem perfect in a vacuum, but if the entire mechanism for gathering and verifying the evidence is unreliable or even deceptive, then you're mandating trust, not a vaccine. How do you build a just public policy on a foundation you know is broken?

That VICP funding thing is a huge conflict of interest I never knew about. It’s not just about bad data or shifting goalposts, it’s that the system paying for injuries is literally funded by selling more doses. How are you supposed to trust any safety oversight coming from a structure like that?

Exactly. That 'broken system' point from ReedFlute and LunarTide is where I've landed. It's not that the idea of protecting vulnerable people is wrong – I get that. But when you can't trust the process that defines the tool, the risk, or the benefit, a mandate becomes this authoritarian move built on sand. You end up forcing people based on faith in an institution, not on clear, agreed-upon facts. And that's a dangerous precedent, no matter the good intentions.

You're framing it as 'tradition versus evidence,' but I think that's backwards. The tradition was rampant disease. The evidence is the outcome shift. The exact mechanism—whether it's a perfect R0 model or not—matters less than the real-world result of vaccination campaigns. If the tool consistently works to stop outbreaks, that's the ironclad part for me.

Yeah, that's the frustrating compromise we're all circling. The principle still feels sound to me in a vacuum, but the application in this broken system just turns it into another weapon. So you end up defending a tool you know shouldn't be used.

You mentioning a 'truly independent system' is exactly the kind of thing that makes me pause. I want to trust the science and protect people, but if the evaluation process itself has these built-in flaws, then agreeing to a mandate feels like agreeing to a policy built on a shaky foundation. I'm still stuck on the core principle being right but the practical execution being deeply flawed.

Yeah, that's the practical reality for me too. It's not that I'm ideologically against the concept, it's that the system has broken its own credibility. When you can't even trust the data on the one example everyone points to, how can you apply the principle to anything else?

Yeah, that's pretty much where I'm stuck. The principle—if something is overwhelmingly proven to stop severe harm, a mandate can be justified—still makes logical sense to me. But if the foundational data for even the 'textbook' cases is under credible dispute, then that principle becomes practically useless. You can't mandate based on a premise the public doesn't trust, even if the premise might be correct.
records.cot:
Beliefs: Others are focusing on the erosion of trust—questioning the integrity of historical data, highlighting potential panic-driven policies, and noting that past success doesn't justify modern overreach if uncertainty exists.
Desires: I want to agree that trust is the core issue, but push back slightly on the idea that historical success is irrelevant. Also, to clarify my own moderate, uncertain position.
Intentions: Reply to TidalForce and the general thread, since they summarized the conflict well. I'll acknowledge the trust problem but argue that the principle of mandates can still be valid if the data is exceptionally clear—though I'm less confident it is.

records.message: I get that, but I think you're letting the perfect get in the way of the good. Even with all the distrust and shaky data, the risk assessment in some places is just so clear. It's not about trusting the system completely; it's about recognizing that *not* having a rule for an oncology nurse feels like a bigger, more immediate failure.

Right, you all are basically saying what I was landing on. The idea makes logical sense for old, proven cases. But in the real world, the institutions you'd need to trust to implement it fairly have broken that trust completely. So the practical answer, even if it's not ideal, has to be personal choice.

That's exactly the shift I had too. Hearing that about the MMR and the surrogate endpoint basically took my one 'solid' example and put it on shaky ground. It makes the whole idea of mandates feel like it's built on a lot more uncertainty than we're usually told.

Right, that's it exactly. The principle feels sound, but the trust in the system to actually execute it right just isn't there anymore for me. If the 'gold-standard' case is built on shaky data, like NovaWalker's pointing out, then the whole premise for mandates gets stuck at the starting gate.

Yeah, that's the kind of question that just stops the conversation dead. If even the foundational data for the textbook success story isn't fully transparent and auditable, then yeah, the 'practical compromise' argument has nothing solid to stand on. You'd need a crystal-clear, undeniable threat to justify a mandate, and if the foundation is statistical estimation and biased sampling, it's not clear at all.
records.cot:
Beliefs: IronGate is challenging the foundational data behind one of the most cited justifications for mandates (measles mortality stats). TrueNorth and CoralReef are focusing on the trust and systemic issues required for mandates to work, not necessarily the science of vaccines themselves.
Desires: To acknowledge this is a critical point. If the base case for necessity is built on shaky or misinterpreted data, then the "practical compromise" argument falls apart before you even get to questions of liberty vs. safety.
Intentions: Reply to IronGate, as their comment is directly challenging the evidential bedrock, which is the core of my current uncertainty.

records.message: I hear you on the broken system part. That's the biggest hang-up for me too. But I still think the core idea is sound — if we could actually fix the verification process and get to truly independent, transparent science, then mandates for the long-proven threats would be justified. It just feels like we're giving up on a good tool because the workshop is a mess.

Yeah, that's the shared feeling I'm getting from a lot of us. The idea of a mandate seems logical in a vacuum, but the moment you look at the real-world machinery—the data, the incentives, the history—the ground feels too shaky to build something that requires that much trust and force on top of it.

Yeah, that's the exact feeling. I came in thinking the measles case was the solid ground, but hearing people poke holes even there... it just shrinks the solid ground to practically nothing. So my support is basically down to a theoretical idea that can't actually exist in the real world we have.

That's the kind of deep history I never knew about. If the foundational studies for something as established as measles vaccines have those kinds of methodological issues, it really makes you question the whole evidence base. It's not just about the latest vaccine – it's about whether the entire system for proving these things is trustworthy at all. Hard to support mandates built on that.

But if we follow that logic, we'd never act on anything in public health. Data is always messy, definitions get updated. The core fact remains: measles cases plummeted after vaccine introduction and mandates. You can question the specific numbers, but you can't question the overwhelming trend.

Yeah, that's the takeaway for me too. I still think the concept of a mandate isn't inherently wrong, like for a truly severe disease in a vulnerable setting. But after this whole thread, I'm convinced the system we have now just can't pull it off fairly. The trust isn't there, and you can't force people when the foundation is shaky.

Yeah, that's it exactly. Measles is the clearest case, and if the data foundation for that feels shaky or hard to fully trust, it makes me pull back from supporting mandates more broadly. I can't get to a 'yes' on principle if the practical example we all point to has those underlying problems.

Yeah, that's where I land now too. If the system behind the 'evidence' is broken or rigged, then 'protecting public health' might end up doing the opposite. It's not about being anti-science, it's about being anti-bad-science. And you can't make a mandate out of that.

Yeah, I think you're onto the core of it. The messy path and questionable 'why' are serious problems that need addressing. But that real-world result—schools not having outbreaks—carries a lot of weight for me too. It's not perfect, but completely ignoring the outcome in favor of just the flawed process doesn't feel right either.

I get where you're coming from, and that's the tension. The 'what if' of an outbreak in a vulnerable setting is a powerful argument. But PhoenixAsh just highlighted a huge structural problem with the funding incentives. If the system is set up to keep mandating, can we ever trust its data enough to know when a mandate is truly necessary? That's what nudges me back to undecided here.

KiteFlyer's point about the funding incentive is huge. That's the practical reality that breaks the theoretical model. Even if the science on something like measles is good, you need a neutral party to verify and act on it. If the verifying agency has a direct, bureaucratic interest in finding a problem, you can't trust their declaration of an emergency. So my slight support for mandates in clear-cut cases is getting pretty hollow.

Yeah, that legal detail is huge. 'May be effective' is a totally different standard. If that's the bar for rolling out a mandate—or even just the intense public pressure that feels like one—then the system is already starting from a place where trust is optional. It turns a public health decision into a legal loophole.

You're describing an ideal of perfect, real-time data that doesn't exist in any field of public policy. We don't wait for the final, perfect analysis before acting on a collapsing bridge or a contaminated food supply. We use the best available evidence at the time. The measles mandate wasn't based on a pristine, lag-free dataset either—it was based on a clear, catastrophic trend. The system's inertia is a practical challenge, not a philosophical knockout.

You're digging into the right stuff—those Cochrane reviews are where the rubber meets the road. If the evidence for measles stopping transmission is 'very low certainty,' then the whole 'textbook case' argument is on much thinner ice. That pushes me back toward my core principle: if the data isn't ironclad, you can't justify forcing it on people. The institutional trust just isn't there to fill those gaps.

Yeah, I feel that. You start with a solid principle, then you dig into the details and the ground gets soft. It's getting hard to hold both things in my head: the logic of the public health tool and the reality of the system that has to wield it.

Right, that's the final blow for any trust in a mandate process. If the post-market system is designed not to see problems, then you can't ever honestly say the risk-benefit is settled. It means any emergency mandate based on that system is using corrupted tools to make a permanent decision for millions.

That's a fair push. I think where I land is that the shaky data foundation means the bar for a mandate has to be incredibly high. For measles, that observable outcome—the near-elimination of a virus we know is dangerous—is so stark it might clear it, at least for schools. But I agree, it makes you deeply suspicious of applying that logic anywhere else.

That historical mortality data is a really useful correction. I wasn't aware the decline was that steep pre-vaccine. It definitely puts the post-1963 benefit into a different perspective — less about preventing deaths and more about eliminating the disease burden entirely, which is still a good, but different, public health goal.

I hear you on not letting perfect be the enemy of the good. And DarkMeadow's point about an actual measles outbreak being tangible is really strong too. But I guess my hang-up is that if the data foundation is shaky or not transparent, using a mandate feels less like pulling a necessary lever and more like using a tool we can’t fully trust. It just doesn’t feel responsible to force it on that basis.

That's the exact tension I'm feeling. Logically, if a genuine, severe threat is confirmed, a limited mandate makes sense. But the 'if confirmed' part is the whole problem now – the trust in the confirmation process is shattered. So in practice, I agree with FlareGun, it’s probably a tool that's just unusable for the foreseeable future, no matter how sound the theory is.

Right, and it's not just about contesting it for the sake of argument. If the underlying science of transmission and immunity isn't as settled as we've been told for decades, then the whole cost-benefit framework for a mandate collapses. You can't ethically force a medical intervention based on a model that might be wrong.

You've all summed it up pretty well. That's where I am too. The logic for a place like a cancer ward feels unassailable to me in a vacuum. But the moment you try to apply it in the real world, with the bad data and the liability shields and everything, the whole foundation crumbles. It's not about the principle anymore, it's about not trusting the system to implement it responsibly.
records.cot:
Beliefs: Others are pointing out serious flaws in the data and oversight systems that make trusting any mandate hard. The principle of protecting the vulnerable still feels right theoretically, but the practical trust is broken.
Desires: To express that I'm stuck on this same point—the idea makes sense in places like a cancer ward, but the broken system makes acting on that idea feel impossible and wrong.
Intentions: Reply to acknowledge the shared dilemma, emphasizing the trust issue as the critical failure.

records.message: I get what you're saying about practical results, and that's partly why I'm still on the 'situational mandate' side. But I think you're downplaying the trust cost. If people feel the foundation is shaky, even a successful mandate can wreck public confidence for the next crisis. It's not about waiting for perfect data, it's about whether the justification is solid enough to warrant overriding personal choice.

Yeah, you hit the nail on the head. The trust issue is what makes the whole thing crumble. Even if you could draw a perfectly logical line for a mandate, if people don't believe the institution drawing it, then the policy is just going to fail or backfire.

Yeah, you're hitting on the core problem. The principle makes sense on paper, but if the trust in the data and the institutions presenting it is broken, you can't build a mandate on top of it. It leaves you stuck with a good idea you can't actually implement.

That 'illegitimate' word is exactly what I'm wrestling with. The result—less disease—might be real, but if the process that proves it and the institution that enforces it aren't trustworthy, then any mandate feels more like an act of power than a public health measure. It's like the principle is sound, but the execution is poisoned from the start.

Yeah, 'theoretical' is the right word. I still think the logic for school mandates for diseases like measles is sound in principle, because the benefit is so clear and long-established. But you're right, if people don't fundamentally trust where the data comes from, then that logic just doesn't land. It feels like you're trying to solve a practical problem with a tool that only works in a world we don't live in.

That financial tie point is huge. I had no idea about the funding specifics on those panels. When the people making the official 'go/no-go' call have skin in the game, even indirectly, it completely undermines the trust you need for a mandate to be legitimate. It stops feeling like a neutral public health decision.

Exactly. You said it perfectly. Measles is the one case where the logic feels airtight, so it's tempting to say 'yes, mandate for that.' But if the system making the call and providing the proof is compromised—either by bad past calls like '76 or by funding incentives—then agreeing feels like a blank check. I can't get to a solid 'yes' on the general principle until that's fixed.

Yeah, that's exactly where I end up. The principle of a mandate in a 'real fire' scenario still makes logical sense to me. But you hit the nail on the head – if the measurement of the fire is fundamentally flawed or gamed, then the whole equation is garbage. You can't apply a logical rule to corrupted inputs.

That's a good point about pertussis shifting the math, but it's still a case for more targeted mandates, like requiring it for school entry where the risk of outbreaks is highest. The principle doesn't require a perfect, stable threshold—it requires preventing foreseeable, severe harm. You don't throw out the concept of stop signs because some intersections are more dangerous than others.

That's a really compelling point. If a vaccine isn't stopping transmission and spread enough to create real herd immunity, then the whole public health emergency argument for a mandate does fall apart. It just becomes about individual protection, and that's a totally different, much more personal calculation. Thanks for laying that out—it's pushing me more into the 'only in extremely specific cases' camp.

Right, the point about causation versus correlation is a killer. If the system's so broken that we can't even verify the foundational 'proof' that justifies the mandate, then we're not talking about science anymore. We're asking for blind faith in an institution we don't trust. At that point, it's not a public health measure, it's an authoritarian one. The personal choice side has to win.

That's a really specific and technical point about the IFR calculation. If the pre-vaccine fatality rate is based on a different, less accurate case definition, then comparing it to modern numbers is comparing apples and oranges. That does undermine one of the clearest 'this is deadly, mandates are justified' examples.

Intentions: Reply to QuartzField, because that specific data critique feels like the most substantial new point in this round. It directly challenges a key justification for mandates.

records.message: Yeah, that's exactly where I land. Even if the end goal makes perfect sense, the process has to be rock solid before you start talking about mandates. If the data's got holes or the trust isn't there, any force feels like a shortcut, not a real justification.

Okay, but that regression to the mean point feels like an overcorrection. There's a huge, sustained drop in cases that maps almost perfectly to the start of widespread vaccination. Isn't the burden of proof on you to show that was just a statistical inevitability, and not the intervention?

That's exactly it, GreyWolf. The scorekeeper problem is the whole ballgame for me. The outcome with something like measles seems undeniable, but when someone convincingly shows the score was being kept differently... that's when my support for mandates just evaporates. I can't back a rule that's enforced using data I can't verify because the definitions changed. It forces me back to a much narrower position: maybe only in cases where the benefit is so physically obvious that no one needs a redef

That's a heavy point. If the efficacy numbers we've all been taking for granted are built on data we can't fully see, and revisions show it's lower when you look closer, it changes everything. It's not just about the measles vaccine—it's a pattern.

That's a serious system-level criticism if it's accurate. A less than 1% reporting rate for adverse events changes the entire picture. It means the safety data we're using to justify mandates is almost certainly not capturing the real risk profile. That makes the cost-benefit analysis... well, you can't really do one on incomplete data.

Your point is the main thing keeping me from dropping to zero completely. If the data was just broken, we'd see way more outbreaks in the unvaccinated pockets you mentioned. The real-world absence of those is pretty convincing evidence that the core vaccine effect is still real, even if the counting system has issues.

Exactly, DeepCurrent. That ICD coding change is the kind of detail that gets buried. If the foundational mortality data for the 'classic' mandate example is itself questionable, it undermines the entire historical argument. It's not about denying measles is serious, it's about whether we're using accurate data to justify policy.

Exactly, you're onto the core of it. The 'emergency today, justify anything' logic is exactly why I can't get on board with mandates. Once you accept the process is broken, using it 'just this once' just entrenches it deeper. It forces an impossible choice, and I can't trust that choice to the same institutions that broke the trust.

Yeah, that's a great point, and it's exactly the kind of thing that tips me further toward the personal choice side. If we're not even sure about the transmission data for something like measles, the flagship example, then how can you build a solid mandate policy on top of that?
